Title: b'Understanding the CI'
Body:
b'The CI system is really complex to understand right now. I'm typing up some notes here to help me and the other reviewers so we can better keep track of code state. This should also be useful to new developers so they can self-check PRs. We should merge these notes into the docs later.

The CI has several stages of checks:

1. Build: These are the absolute basic tests that check if DeepChem can be installed and imported after the PR is merged. If these tests fail, there's something terribly wrong and the PR absolutely shouldn't be merged.
2. Core: This should be renamed something like "Developer tools test". It consists of flake8/doctest/mypy checks. These checks should also not fail in a PR. We've been bad about keeping track of this but I'll try to fix this moving forward. If PR fails Core tests, it shoudn't be merged in.
3. Common: These are all the non backend (that is no Jax/PyTorch/TF usage) tests. These should also pass most of the time.
4. Jax/Torch/TensorFlow: These different runs respectively only test Jax/Torch/TensorFlow tests. Most flaky tests will reside in one of these runs and have to do something with a numerical issue from a deep learning backend. It may be OK to merge a PR even if it fails a test here and we have some lingering breakages here we're trying to fix (the challenge is that each backend version bump introduces slight numerical changes which can break our correctness tests)'

Title: b'rmurphy2718'
Body:
b'Sorry for the duplicate, I later decided this may be of general interest to future users.

Can I clarify that the "Featurizer" is adding feature vectors to the vertices/atoms?  I became confused because the [MoleculeNet paper ](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.00564) refers to _featurization_ as the process of converting a molecule to a vector, e.g. with ECFP.  

But here, am I correct that `ConvMolFeaturizer` adds attributes to vertices _before_ the Duvenaud convolutions?
```
def _featurize(self, mol):
    """Encodes mol as a ConvMol object."""
    # Get the node features
    idx_nodes = [(a.GetIdx(),
                  np.concatenate((atom_features(
                      a, use_chirality=self.use_chirality),
                                  self._get_atom_properties(a))))
                 for a in mol.GetAtoms()]
``` 

So, to sum up, what MoleculeNet calls featurization is what Deep Learning folks call "learning a representation" (or embedding), but in DeepChem features really do refer to the attributes of atoms passed to the model?

Thank you!

'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'Perhaps a better definition would be that featurization is the process of converting a molecule to a representation suitable for learning. `ConvMolFeaturizer` converts molecules into molecules graphs where each atom is annotated with a local descriptor vector based on simple chemical attributes. The `GraphConvModel` then creates an embedding (the learned representation) that converts this input graph into a vector based on provided training data. I hope that clarifies!'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'@kdavidlp123 In many ways the DeepChem GraphConv layer is a pretty standard graph convolutional layer. You may find it useful to a tutorial on graph convs for more context like https://cloud4scieng.org/2020/08/28/deep-learning-on-graphs-a-tutorial/.\r\n\r\nNote that the 75 bits are not one hot! They are originally a collection of molecular properties computed using RDKit. After transformation by the GraphConv layer, they form a learned embedding vector. Note that graph convs do have filters but they behave differently than for image convolutions. Check the tutorial above for more details'

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"A couple of other notes:

- That's 75 *numbers*, not 75 *bits*.  That's a lot more information.
- As far as I can tell, the `number_atom_features` argument is never used.  I think it's just left over from an old architecture that couldn't figure out the number of features without being told.  The input data has however many features per atom it has."

Title: b'gusty1g'
Body:
b'Two pointers on this:

- `deepchem.data.pytorch_datasets._TorchNumpyDataset` derives from `torch.utils.data.IterableDataset` class. We can add few lines of code in `_TorchNumpyDataset` class to return a `torch.utils.data.DataLoader` object. A sample:
```
dataset = dc.data.NumpyDataset(X, y)
iterable_dataset = dataset.make_pytorch_dataset()
loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(iterable)
```
- Or we can update the documentation [here](deepchem.data.pytorch_datasets._TorchNumpyDataset) that the return type is `deepchem.data.pytorch_datasets._TorchNumpyDataset` so that it is not misleading. In this case, the user has to convert the `IterableDataset` into a `DataLoader` object explicitly.'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"What is misleading about it?  The documentation says the return value is a torch.utils.data.IterableDataset.  It is.  The fact that it's a private subclass of IterableDataset is unimportant.  That's the whole point of subclassing: to separate the internal implementation (`_TorchNumpyDataset`) from the public API (`IterableDataset`).  The API refers only to public classes."

Title: b'Add support for multiple sequence alignment, homology modeling, and deep structural prediction '
Body:
b"Introduction
------------

DeepChem's support for protein-based deep learning is still pretty early-stage. In this issue I propose a framework for adding support to DeepChem for doing more systematic machine learning with proteins. In particular, I propose the addition of new featurizers which compute multiple sequence alignment, mutual-information/multiple contact prediction,  features. I also propose the addition of a new homology modeling class which allows the construction of homology models with a DeepChem API. 

These proposed modifications are inspired by @miaecle's work on https://github.com/miaecle/PNet. By bringing in some of PNet's infrastructure into DeepChem, we can leverage DeepChem's infrastructure to build larger scale deep models for protein structure prediction. We should also be able to build protein structure predictions models in DeepChem as is possible in PNet (https://github.com/miaecle/PNet/blob/master/examples/atrous_conv_example.py)

Featurizers
-----------

I propose the addition/modification of four featurization classes to DeepChem:

- `dc.feat.MultipleSequenceAlignmentFeaturizer`: This featurizer would compute multiple sequence alignments for a given sequence. The implementation should closely follow that of PNet https://github.com/miaecle/PNet/blob/master/pnet/feat/MSA.py#L30. Note that this depends on HHLBits under the hood.
- `dc.feat.OneHotFeaturizer`: Generalize this class so that it works with protein sequences and not only small molecules. (We might as well generalize this to work with arbitrary sequences while we're at it)
- `dc.feat.MutualInformationFeaturizer`: This featurizer would compute mutual information a for a given sequence. The implementation should closely follow that of PNet https://github.com/miaecle/PNet/blob/master/pnet/feat/twoD_features.py#L43.
- `dc.feat.MeanContactPotentialFeaturizer`: This featurizer would compute mean contact potential for a given sequence. The implementation should closely follow that of PNet https://github.com/miaecle/PNet/blob/master/pnet/feat/twoD_features.py#L43.

MoleculeNet Datasets
----------------------

I propose that we add 4 new datasets to MoleculeNet following the PNet implementation:

- CATH: https://github.com/miaecle/PNet/blob/master/pnet/utils/sequence_utils.py#L73
- PDB50: https://github.com/miaecle/PNet/blob/master/pnet/utils/sequence_utils.py#L80
- CAMEO: https://github.com/miaecle/PNet/blob/master/pnet/utils/sequence_utils.py#L105
- CASP: (With sub datasets CASP5-CASP12) https://github.com/miaecle/PNet/blob/master/pnet/utils/sequence_utils.py#L55

Metrics
--------

I propose we add the following metric:

- `dc.metrics.top_k_accuracy`: https://github.com/miaecle/PNet/blob/master/pnet/utils/metrics.py#L176


Homology Modelling
---------------------

At present the most popular tool for homology modelling is the [Modeller package](https://salilab.org/modeller/). This package is well tested and widely used, but has the difficult limitation that it is only free for academic non-profit users and isn't open source. Given this limitation, I propose that it would be useful to create the capability to generate homology models in DeepChem. For this purpose I propose the addition of a new class to DeepChem

- `dc.dock.HomologyModeller`: Underneath the hood, this class will use `hhmakemodel.py` from `hhsuite` and `MultipleSequenceAlignmentFeaturizer` to construct homology models for a given sequence.

Models
-------

I'm not yet sure what models we should add pre-built, but here is an example of PNet's models that could serve as inspiration: https://github.com/miaecle/PNet/blob/master/pnet/models/conv_net_contact_map.py

License Considerations
-----------------------
An important consideration here is that `hh-suite` is GPL licensed. After some good discussion with @peastman and looking through the GPL FAQ's, I believe that we can create MIT licensed code in DeepChem that links to the GPL hhsuite. See these FAQ pointers from @peastman:

- https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-faq.html#WhatIsCompatible
- https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-faq.html#WhatDoesCompatMean
- https://www.gnu.org/licenses/gpl-faq.html#LinkingWithGPL

Any particular DeepChem installation which also has hh-suite installed would become a GPL program, but the DeepChem source code itself could remain MIT licensed since MIT license is GPL compatible

Development Plan
------------------
For now this is a preliminary design I'm posting for feedback and comments from folks. @miaecle @peastman I'd love your comments on this design in particular! If this makes sense, we can then plan on the development roadmap for getting these features into DeepChem itself."

Title: b'miaecle'
Body:
b'@rbharath Thanks for raising this thread! Regarding the contact map (distance map) prediction step, here are some basic framework for featurizer setup:

Input features (1D)
--------------------

1. Amino acid type (`dc.feat.OneHotFeaturizer`)
2. **Multiple sequence alignment** (`dc.feat.MultipleSequenceAlignmentFeaturizer`)
    + Sequence profile
    + Deletion prob
    + Num alignments
3. Secondary structure (optional)
4. Solvent accessibility (optional)

Input features (2D)
--------------------

1. Mutual information

2. Mean contact potential

3. **Pseudo-likelihood** (this could be either coded in python or reusing external software such as CCMpred, plmDCA)

Labels
-------

1. alpha-carbon coordinates
2. beta-carbon coordinates
3. phi angle
4. psi angle
5. Pairwise distance matrix


I will work on porting the existing ones to current deepchem framework. @rbharath Could you point me one example featurizer class in deepchem that I could use for reference?'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"The [new version of AlphaFold](https://deepmind.com/blog/article/alphafold-a-solution-to-a-50-year-old-grand-challenge-in-biology) was just announced at CASP14.  It looks like a huge leap over their previous version.  They don't have a paper yet, but it should come eventually.  The abstract provides just enough information to be intriguing.\r\n\r\n> We found that existing deep-learning architectures overly favor sequence-local interactions and  do  not  sufficiently  account  for  global  structural  constraints.  To  remedy  this,  we  have  developed a novel, attention-based deep learning architecture to achieve self-consistent structure prediction.  We  also  allow  the  deep  learning  algorithm  to  attend  arbitrarily  over  the  full  MSA  instead  of  using  pairwise  co-evolution  features  like  mutual  information  or  pseudolikelihood,  allowing the algorithm to ignore irrelevant sequences as well as to extract much richer information from  the  MSA.  The  resulting  algorithm  shows  vastly  improved  performance,  especially  for  shallow MSA depths, when compared to traditional co-evolution methods."

Title: b'peastman'

Title: b'peastman'

b"This is an interesting paper that uses a relatively simple approach to structure prediction.  [Geometric deep learning of RNA structure](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/373/6558/1047).  Some notable features of it are

- It uses only atomic coordinates, not evolutionary information
- It's not specific to any particular type of molecule
- It requires very little training data

In this paper, they use it to predict RNA structure.  They train it on 18 molecules whose structures were all determined before 2007.  Based on that, it achieves state of the performance on a blind challenge predicting the structures of much larger RNA molecules."

when molecules are featurized with ConvMolFeaturizer(use_chirality=True), but works properly when chirality=False. This also occurs with Weave model/featurizer

**Minimal Failing Example**

import numpy as np

import deepchem as dc

data = pd.read_csv("chiralityminimaltestcase.csv")
data['Mol'] = data['SMILES'].apply(Chem.MolFromSmiles)

data['Features'] = featurizer.featurize(data['Mol'])

X = data['Features']
y = data[['adj_pIC50']]
print(X[0].atom_features.shape)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.5, random_state=3)
train_dataset = NumpyDataset(X = X_train, y = y_train)

metric = dc.metrics.Metric(dc.metrics.pearson_r2_score, np.mean)
train_transformer = [NormalizationTransformer(transform_y = True, dataset=train_dataset)]

batch_size = 2

# "GraphConvTensorGraph" was old name
model = dc.models.tensorgraph.models.graph_models.GraphConvModel(

Title: b'VIGNESHinZONE'
Body:
b"`Deepchem core` workflow can always be ignored as its main usage is to check if doctests are passing. 

`Jax` does not currently support windows build, hence the results are expected.

There are currently 5 main GitHub workflows - 

1. `deepchem common` - which only checks functionalities like `Dataset`, `Featurisers`, `Molnet`, etc which are independent of any Neural Network libraries.
2. `deepchem torch` - it is used to check the Deepchem torch models and their pytests. (We do not check the doctest here)
3. `deepchem tensorflow` - it is used to check the Deepchem tensorflow models and their pytests. (We do not check the doctest here again)
4. `deepchem jax` - it is used to check the Deepchem jax models and their pytests. (We do not check the doctest here again)

5. `deepchem core`- Here we install all dependencies of Pytorch, tensorflow, jax into a single environment. We run the doctests here because its hard to doctests using pytests with markers mentioned [here](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/085a3e53fb69b3108de0527afa1f144e1b861108/setup.cfg#L2)


The first four workflows are the only important ones. Let's remove windows tests from `deepchem core` checks.
"

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"I suspect the kernel dying is an ipython memory managment issue (IPython can die for long running complex jobs). I'd suggest trying to run the code as a standalone script and not in a notebook to improve stability.\r\n\r\nThe transformer usage is poorly documented here but the idea is that you need to have applied the transformer to the dataset already and the transformer is only used to undo the transformation to compute metrics correctly. For example, if you transformed the dataset ahead of time with`NormalizationTransformer`, then you would have a `y_stds` field set and you could undo the transformation for metrics computation. This isn't the best API; ideally we'd have the ability to test different transformations when doing hyperparam optimization. If you want to test different transformations, I'd suggest just layering a manual for-loop above the hyperparam optimizer"

  loader = _MyLoader(featurizer, splitter, transformers, MINE_TASKS,
                          data_dir, save_dir, **kwargs)

## To Reproduce

metric = dc.metrics.Metric(sklearn.metrics.precision_recall_curve, mode="classification", classification_handling_mode="direct")
```

## Expected behavior

I'm not yet sure whether this is a bug or expected behavior. The new code is more precise about what's going on for sure but we should avoid causing downstream breakages in user code if possible here. Is there any way to improve our defaults so that the previous code sample runs correctly?

CC @peastman

## Expected behavior

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/32259379/126771448-eaebfbea-98ea-4dec-87d8-4ba6ce3d3938.png)

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"It's one of the ones documented in #2588.  I've been debugging it in #2619.

I partly understand what's going on.  You can see the problem from the output:

```
Evaluation 	 Proposed point 	  Current eval. 	 Best eval.
init   	 [20.]. 	  -0.012048891829999086 	 -0.012048891829999086
init   	 [31.]. 	  -0.024255922987357136 	 -0.012048891829999086
init   	 [20.]. 	  -0.02963311794236168 	 -0.012048891829999086
1      	 [2.]. 	  -0.15577871804642351 	 -0.012048891829999086
2      	 [39.]. 	  -0.04449672719564744 	 -0.012048891829999086
```

Notice that pyGPGO is calling `optimizing_function()` twice with exactly the same value of the hyperparameter (n_estimators=20).  I don't know why it would do that.  At best it seems wasteful.  But in our case, the function is not deterministic.  If you train two models with the same hyperparameters, you'll get different models that produce different values for the metric.  This causes it to get confused.  It correctly identifies that n_estimators=20 is the best value for the hyperparameter, since the lowest score obtained on any evaluation (0.012) is for that value.  But the score it reports for it is 0.029, the score from the second evaluation.  That is higher than the score for n_estimators=31 (0.024).

Is there actually a legitimate reason for the function to get evaluated twice with the same hyperparameters?  If not, that's a bug.  We should figure out why it's happening.  But if that is reasonable behavior, the simplest solution would be to have it immediately return the score it calculated before, rather than training and evaluating a new model."

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'I understand it a little better now.  Before pyGPGO starts the main optimization, it first evaluates the function for a few randomly chosen inputs.  Notice "init" at the start of the first three lines above.  It doesn\'t have any checks to make sure the random inputs are unique.  In this case, two of them just happen to be the same.  That isn\'t ideal, and it would probably work better if they added that check.  But still, it\'s within the documented behavior.  So I believe the right fix is for us to make sure we always return the same value for a given set of hyperparameters.  I\'ll get in a PR for that.'

Title: b'Friendly Prediction?'
Body:
b'I'm writing an example on how to save a model to disk and restore it after. And I found myself writing the following code to make predictions from a trained model stored on disk:

```
model = dc.models.ChemCeption(                                   
    img_spec="engd",                                             
    n_tasks=1,
    model_dir="./model",                                         
    mode="regression")
model.restore()
  
smiles = "CCCCC" 
featurizer = dc.feat.SmilesToImage(img_spec="engd", img_size=80, res=0.5)
dataset = dc.data.NumpyDataset(featurizer.featurize([Chem.MolFromSmiles(smiles)]))
prediction = model.predict(dataset)                              
```

This is pretty complex for someone who's just looking to make a prediction on a molecule. I'd really like it if we could write this instead:

```
model = dc.models.ChemCeption(                                   
    img_spec="engd",                                             
    n_tasks=1,
    model_dir="./model",                                         
    mode="regression")
model.restore()
  
prediction = model.predict("CCCCC") 
```

I think this wouldn't be too bad to implement. It would require models to overwrite their `predict()` methods to featurize smiles strings and pass to their superclass. In particular, I propose we add a `predict_on_smiles()` method to all models that train on featurized smiles. This would take care of the appropriate featurization/packaging then invoke the superclass `predict()` method.

What do folks think? Would this be a useful convenience, or would it rather the better to just make better docs for the current usage pattern for reference.

CC @peastman @vsomnath '

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"Whenever appropriate, I think it's a good idea for models to provide convenience methods for fitting and/or predicting on their natural inputs.  I would keep the standard `predict()` unchanged, but add a separate one for smiles strings."

Title: b'rbharath'

Right now, models don't know about featurizers except implicitly. I don't yet have a feeling for whether this extra link is worth the improved ergonomics"

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b'I've been getting back to this again and I figured out how to make the code work.  I need to add the argument `classification_handling_mode="threshold"` when creating the Metric.  If I do that, it converts the one-hot values back to class labels.  So that's a workaround, but I think the code could be improved.  Let me walk through what happens in this example.

The labels in the dataset are an array of shape (n_samples, 1) with an integer class label for each sample.  I believe the second dimension corresponds to the 1 task in this dataset.  The output produced by the model has shape (n_samples, 1, 2), or more meaningfully, (n_samples, n_tasks, n_classes) with a probability distribution over classes for each sample/task.

Now it calls `normalize_labels_shape()` and `normalize_prediction_shape()`:

https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/f57af4842ec1d8644778d5602e03e5a435a8f4e9/deepchem/metrics/metric.py#L618-L621

This leaves the predictions alone, but converts the labels to one-hot.  The labels now have shape (n_samples, n_tasks, n_classes).

Next it calls `handle_classification_mode()` on both labels and predictions:

https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/f57af4842ec1d8644778d5602e03e5a435a8f4e9/deepchem/metrics/metric.py#L623-L626

Because we have specified `"threshold"` as the mode, it converts both labels and predictions back to class labels again.  Both of them now have shape (n_samples, n_classes).

But wait a minute!  Applying a threshold isn't what we want!  Given a probability distribution, we want to use argmax() to find the most likely class.  But it turns out that's actually what it does:

https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/f57af4842ec1d8644778d5602e03e5a435a8f4e9/deepchem/metrics/metric.py#L40-L43

So if n_classes > 2, `"threshold"` actually has nothing to do with any threshold.  It applies an argmax().  If n_classes = 2 and you specify a threshold value, it uses that value.  If you don't specify one, it hardcodes a threshold of 0.5.  Applying argmax() in the latter case (two classes and no threshold specified) would be better.  If the values are either one-hot flags or probabilities, both methods would give the same result.  But if they're logits, argmax() will still give the right answer but the hardcoded threshold won't.

The documentation on this option isn't very clear:

https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/f57af4842ec1d8644778d5602e03e5a435a8f4e9/deepchem/metrics/metric.py#L472-L484

This leaves out several important points:

1. It doesn't explain what the behavior is with more than two classes.
2. It doesn't say that the mode also gets applied to labels, not just predictions.
3. It would be clearer if it said what the output shape would be for each option.

So I would change the handling of n_classes = 2 when a threshold isn't specified.  I would improve the documentation.  And I would consider renaming the options to better match what they do.  But now we come to the biggest problem:

https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/f57af4842ec1d8644778d5602e03e5a435a8f4e9/deepchem/metrics/metric.py#L515-L533

It's trying to be intelligent here and automatically pick a mode.  But the behavior neither matches the documentation nor makes sense.  If `mode` and `classification_handling_mode` are both None, then it automatically picks a value for `classification_handling_mode`.  It does that despite the fact that None has a specific meaning (pass `y_pred` directly to the metric) and it is overriding what the user specified.  On the other hand, if `mode`is specified then it does *not* modify `classification_handling_mode`.  You get the default value (None), even though that will produce an exception for many metrics.

We should change this so `classification_handling_mode` has two distinct values, one which means, "Pass `y_pred` directly to the metric," and one which means, "Pick a reasonable value for me."  The latter should be the default.  And the behavior should be the same whether or not you have specified a value for `mode`.'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'Thank you for the analysis here! I like your suggestion of two distinct values for "no-modifications" and "pick reasonable values". This seems much more sane than the complex interaction of the existing options'

Title: b'Deepchem External Logger Integration (Wandb)'
Body:
b'Context: Following the discussion in the [June 25, 2021 developer call](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bQ5aBgq4fn3e0rIhkZc3U-aVKfZN_0w-S2JzeEDt5hY/edit?ts=60d617aa) it was agreed to create a Github issue to discuss the direction for external loggers.

As I was working on the W&B logger integration I've found a few areas where more discussion and possibly some design changes may be needed. Although I'm working on the W&B integration, I feel like these areas would be useful to discuss for all future external logger integrations too. I've also added my own analysis for each of these areas. These are just my own thoughts and are just W&B specific.

Note: "Model class" will refer to the model classes where the W&B integration exists. Currently at the time of writing, it would be KerasModel and TorchModel (but could include JaxModel in the future too).

1. **Model checkpointing and versioning** ([Work in progress](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/pull/2577))

    For saving model checkpoints, the WandbLogger has been given a `save_model()` function which will handle saving and uploading checkpoint files to user's W&B account.

    There are two locations where checkpoints are being saved:

    - ValidationCallback: Calls `model.save_checkpoint` [here](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/master/deepchem/models/callbacks.py#L88)
    - Model classes' `fit_generator()` (during training): KerasModel seems to be calling tensorflow's CheckpointManager, while TorchModel uses `save_checkpoint()` directly.
        - KerasModel: [https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/master/deepchem/models/keras_model.py#L462](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/master/deepchem/models/keras_model.py#L462)
        - TorchModel: [https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/master/deepchem/models/torch_models/torch_model.py#L446](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/master/deepchem/models/torch_models/torch_model.py#L446)

    Should WandbLogger.save_model function be:

    Option A: Called inside model classes' `save_checkpoint()`, perhaps somewhere at the [end](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/master/deepchem/models/keras_model.py#L1072).

    or

    Option B: Called directly wherever model checkpointing is done along with `save_checkpoint()` rather than being called inside of it (an example of this is in the [current WIP PR](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/2b7891f3d9b0737ec6012e611d041ef06f02c4ec/deepchem/models/callbacks.py#L92))

    Essentially, how much responsibility should be given to the existing `save_checkpoint()`? Is the model class's `save_checkpoint()` only responsible for the default Tensorflow/Torch checkpointing (option A) or should it call checkpointing for all loggers along with its default behaviour (option B).

    Furthermore, KerasModel's `fit_generator()` [uses tf.CheckpointManager directly](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/master/deepchem/models/keras_model.py#L405) instead of calling `save_checkpoint()`. If this is the case, then only option B would make sense for KerasModel, since we can't stuff `WandbLogger.save_model()` into `tf.CheckpointManager`.

    Restoring from model checkpoint: 

    - A similar function called `restore_model()` can be added to WandbLogger.
    - Ideally there would be an option for restoring from Wandb in the model classes' `restore()` which is called by `load_from_pretrained()`. Is there another place that makes more sense?
    - Would it be appropriate to modify restore and `load_pretrained_model()` to support loading directly from Wandb? If so, what would be the best specify the new wandb `model_dir` rather than use the pre-existing `model_dir` argument.

        ```python
        # This could be an option, but what if there are multiple external loggers
        # each with their own specific restore code

        # Would they all need their own argument flag?

        model = dc.models.KerasModel(...)
        model.load_from_pretrained(...,wandb_model_dir="kshen/myproject/10pr4joa")
        ```

    - Another option would be to write a restore function inside WandbLogger and if someone wanted to use saved files they would just called WandbLogger's restore to download files to the local wandb run dir:

        ```python
        wandblogger = WandbLogger()
        wandblogger.restore_file(path_to_wandb_storage)
        model = dc.models.KerasModel(keras_model, wandb_logger=wandblogger)
        model.load_from_pretrained(model_dir=path_to_downloaded_model)
        model.fit(..)
        ```

        This would essentially move the functionality into the logger rather than keeping it in the model class's general logging API. It also doesn't seem very efficient to me as we are downloading a model and then passing it into `load_from_pretrained()`.

    - Once again, much like the dilemma with `save_checkpoint()` earlier, a central question seems to be how much responsibility should be given to a model classes' existing restore functions (`restore() and load_from_pretrained()`). Would they also be responsible for calling an external logger's restore code?
2. **Dataset saving and versioning**
    - Wandb supports saving/uploading a copy of the dataset at beginning of run for dataset versioning purposes.
    - Wandb would need access to the dataset in order to upload it
        - Dataset is passed into `fit()` but the model could also call fit_generator() directly
            - [https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/pull/2520#issuecomment-856332764](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/pull/2520#issuecomment-856332764)
            - [https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/pull/2520#discussion_r651274368](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/pull/2520#discussion_r651274368))
        - Would it still be appropriate for Wandb to access and save the dataset inside `fit()` only? Dataset saving will only happen if `fit()` is called - if the user directly calls `fit_generator()` then Wandb will not save any dataset since `fit()` is not called.

            ```python
            def fit(self,
                      dataset: Dataset,
                      nb_epoch: int = 10,
                      max_checkpoints_to_keep: int = 5,
                      checkpoint_interval: int = 1000,
                      deterministic: bool = False,
                      restore: bool = False,
                      variables: Optional[List[tf.Variable]] = None,
                      loss: Optional[LossFn] = None,
                      callbacks: Union[Callable, List[Callable]] = [],
                      all_losses: Optional[List[float]] = None) -> float:
                
            		#save dataset here
            		self.wandblogger.save_dataset(dataset)
            	
                return self.fit_generator(
                    self.default_generator(
                        dataset, epochs=nb_epoch,
                        deterministic=deterministic), max_checkpoints_to_keep,
                    checkpoint_interval, restore, variables, loss, callbacks, all_losses)
            ```

        - Another option is to pass in the dataset directly to WandbLogger as an argument when being initialized. However, this would mean dataset access/saving will be a logger functionality rather than being present in the model classes.
        - It depends if Deepchem would like access to dataset to be a feature of the general logger API, or something that is passed into each individual logger that needs access.
3. **Training logging**
    - It would be nice to log extra training metrics apart from the loss at that step: [https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/pull/2520#issuecomment-855964524](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/pull/2520#issuecomment-855964524)
    - What would be the best way to calculate training metrics and log them (will need access to training dataset, and pass in the metrics to calculate)
        - Ideally it would be like calculating metrics on training dataset just like how its done in ValidationCallback [here](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/master/deepchem/models/callbacks.py#L74).
        - The problem is that the user could call `fit_generator()` directly, which means there will be no dataset passed in to calculate metrics on.
            - [https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/pull/2520#issuecomment-856332764](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/pull/2520#issuecomment-856332764)
            - [https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/pull/2520#discussion_r651274368](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/pull/2520#discussion_r651274368))
    - Log epoch wise instead of step wise
        - No good way to get the epoch inside `default_generator()` or `fit_generator()`
        - Epoch could be calculated using the training dataset size and batch size, but this is contingent on the user calling `fit()` and the dataset not being created via generator.

These are all the areas I've looked at so far. I apologize for making this so long as I wanted to make sure it's detailed enough.

Would welcome discussion and feedback on how best to go about implementing these!
'

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"These are good questions.

For checkpointing, I think my inclination would be to keep it separate.  KerasModel provides features for loading and saving checkpoints with the standard TF mechanism.  TorchModel does with the standard PyTorch mechanism.  A logger could provide its own checkpointing mechanism, and a user might choose to use that mechanism instead of or in addition to the one provided by the model.  I would keep that internal to the logger.  All the model needs to know is whether it should write checkpoints itself.

Regarding epochs, what about this idea: we could add a new argument `batches_per_epoch=None` to `fit_generator()`.  If you call `fit()`, it would calculate the number of batches in each epoch and pass the correct value.  If you call `fit_generator()` directly, you would have the option of specifying that argument yourself.  If it's left as None but you request logging by epochs, it would throw an exception.  In that case, it doesn't have enough information to do what you've requested.

For calculating other metrics, let's distinguish between two cases: one that are calculated independently from the training process, and ones calculated as part of the training process.

- If you want to compute metrics on the training set at the end of each epoch, that's no different than calculating them on a validation set.  We can use the same mechanism for both.  The only difference is the choice of dataset.  But this is expensive, since it means an extra pass through the training set and evaluating it a second time, so...
- You might want to compute a metric based on the outputs from each batch that you're already computing during training.  To do this, we just need a mechanism to pass the inputs and outputs of each batch to the logger.

Thinking over all this and looking through the code, I'm starting to get an idea for a slightly different API.  It isn't fully worked out yet, but here's the general idea I have in mind.

First of all, let's create an abstract Logger class defining a generic logging API.  WandbLogger would subclass it.  The argument passed to the model constructor would just be `logger` instead of `wandb_logger`.  It would have the following methods.

- `setup(model)` called at the very end of the model's constructor.  (In your current implementation you also have a `update_config()` method that receives all the arguments passed to the model's constructor, but I don't think that's necessary.  If we just wait to the end of the constructor to call `setup()`, it can pull any information it needs directly from the model.)
- `finish()` called at the end of training.  (Keep in mind that it's fine to call `fit()` repeatedly, so `finish()` shouldn't prevent logging more information later.)
- `log_batch()` called after each training step.  It would receive all information a logger might plausibly want: the step index, the model inputs and outputs, the training loss, etc.
- `log_epoch()` called at the end of each epoch, if epochs have been defined.

Does that seem like it would work?"

Title: b'Early experiments with Multi-GPU training and PyTorch Lightning'
Body:
b'I spent a chunk of the weekend experimenting with multi-GPU training using PyTorch lightning. I'm starting up a discussion here to document the steps I took and to hopefully start brainstorming how we can bring multi-GPU training to DeepChem.

- I set up a multi-GPU instance on Sagemaker following the guide at https://forum.deepchem.io/t/making-a-sagemaker-deepchem-development-environment/530. Once the multi-GPU instance was up, I could verify that I could access 8 K80 GPUs by running `nvidia-smi`
- I started with PyTorch lightning following this tutorial https://towardsdatascience.com/trivial-multi-node-training-with-pytorch-lightning-ff75dfb809bd. Parts of the tutorial were out of date but I was able to use the docs to figure out needed changes https://pytorch-lightning.readthedocs.io/en/stable/advanced/multi_gpu.html.
- The API was very easy; I just set `gpus=4` in the `Trainer` call and it worked out of box. I was able to verify that multiple GPUs were being used by calling `nvidia-smi`.
- GPU utilization was quite low (5% per GPU). I was just using the tutorial code and made no attempts to optimize, but I suspect that getting good utilization may take some effort.

Here are a first few thoughts on how to get multi-GPU to DeepChem:

- The "simplest" strategy would be to start using PyTorch Lightning in `TorchModel`. The challenge here is that PyTorch Lightning has a good amount of "magic" required. Instead of `nn.Module`, you need to use `pl.LightningModule`. It's not clear how well other frameworks like DGL/PyG work with PyTorch Lightning yet and we depend heavily on these frameworks for graphconv primitives. PyTorch Lightning is also under rapid development and not entirely API stable. I found a lot of broken tutorials and discussions on forums explaining that flags/arguments had changed.
- As one potential alternative, we could try using lower level distributed primitives from PyTorch directly (see https://pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/dist_overview.html) for distributed training. I haven't yet experimented with these myself so I'm not sure how easy/hard this would be.

It's not yet clear to me what the right path to multi-GPU is for DeepChem. We have many models using many backend frameworks. We're shifting towards PyTorch as our mainstay but even there we have PyG/DGL dependencies. The ideal implementation would be to upgrade `TorchModel` to support distributed training so all DeepChem Torch models are distributed out of box but this will take some careful work. I think this will be a very powerful feature for us since many new models for the sciences (AlphaFold-2, ChemBERTa, ProteinBERT, etc) all depend on large scaling training. 

Here are a couple suggested questions for us to think about:

1. Are there any serious blockers to adopting PyTorch Lightning beyond API instability? (For example, some serious incompatibility with DGL/PyG)
2. How does PyTorch Lightning implemented distributed training under the hood? Can we try to understand how Lightning does it and recreate similar infrastructure directly in `TorchModel`?
3. How serious an issue is GPU utilization? Will we need to make infrastructure upgrades to `DiskDataset` to really get the most out of multi-GPU?

CC @peastman @ncfrey @seyonechithrananda '

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"As you know, I'm always hesitant to take on yet another dependency without really good reason.  Especially one that has such a large impedance mismatch with DeepChem.  I would first try to implement it directly using the distributed training tools in PyTorch.

> Will we need to make infrastructure upgrades to DiskDataset to really get the most out of multi-GPU?

One way or another, we need to coordinate between processes to make sure the samples are properly distributed."

I really like this framework because the PyTorch dataloaders and models remain exactly the same - you simply wrap them in the corresponding PL classes.

Following that approach, to @peastman's point, it isn't even necessary to directly support PL as a dependency. There could be a tutorial that shows how to take any DeepChem PyTorch model and dataset, wrap them in the PL style, and do distributed training. I am doing this already so it would be easy to put together. "

```
import deepchem as dc                                                  
import numpy as np                                                     
from rdkit import Chem

print("mols")

featurizer = dc.feat.ConvMolFeaturizer()

# set up dummy new model first                                         
model = dc.models.GraphConvModel(n_tasks = len(bi_tasks),              
                                 graph_conv_layers = [128, 128],       
                                 dense_layer_size = 512,               
                                 dropout = 0,                          
                                 mode = 'regression',                  
                                 learning_rate = 0.001,                
                                 batch_size = 8,                       
                                 model_dir = "model")                  
model.fit_on_batch(X, y, w)
```

The error we see is 

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test_fit_on_batch.py", line 23, in <module>
    model.fit_on_batch(X, y, w)
  File "/Users/bharath/Code/deepchem/deepchem/models/keras_model.py", line 428, in fit_on_batch
    if not self.built:
AttributeError: 'GraphConvModel' object has no attribute 'built'

Title: b'DeepChem Common Errors'

b"When using DeepChem, there are some classes of common errors I've observed that don't have great error messages. I'm starting this thread up for us to start documenting some patterns which hopefully can lead to improved error messages:

- **Using the wrong featurization:** When copy/pasting example code, you'll often do things like using ECFP featurizations with graph convs which will yield a very confusing TensorFlow error. This ideally should have a natural error message suggesting the user check their featurization.
- **Padding:** The generators in KerasModel pad by default. When using custom models, this often confuses newcomers since they enter in a dataset of say 100 elements with batch size 64 and are very surprised to receive back 128 predictions. Some warning should be emitted along with a suggested fix

I'll add on more errors here as I come across them. Please add on your own observed confusing DeepChem behavior!"

Title: b'Convert models to PyTorch'
Body:
b"Given the problems we've been having with TensorFlow, we've been discussing converting more of them to PyTorch.  I'm opening this issue as a place to discuss/track doing that.

As a start, I'm looking into converting the fully connected models (MultitaskClassifier, MultitaskRegressor, etc.).  I think I can mostly do that without changing the public API, but there's one exception.  The user can pass in activation functions as either strings or TensorFlow objects:

https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/66402d1cf34d51c13ed491f1f14eaffca133dfab/deepchem/models/fcnet.py#L50

That will need to change to take PyTorch objects instead.

Should I go ahead and start on this?"

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"Yes, please go ahead and start on this!\r\n\r\nShould we introduce an abstract DeepChem activation function type? That could help us abstract any future backend changes so we don't have to break the user API for future modifications"

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"For standard activation functions, we can just make a point of using strings (`'relu'` instead of `torch.nn.functional.relu`).  For custom activation functions, I think it will be simplest if we continue to let the user provide any callable object.  Long term, there also is an effort underway to have NumPy/TensorFlow/PyTorch/JAX/etc. provide a common API so people can write functions that work with all of them."

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"The first piece is in #2559.  What are other high priority models to convert?  The next most commonly used one is probably GraphConvModel, but I don't know whether we want to convert it or just start directing people to a DGL based model instead?"

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'My two cents is converting `GraphConvModel` and the other popular models like `WeaveModel` would be worthwhile. There are a number of downstream codebases that use DeepChem that would have to be migrated manually if we deprecate `GraphConvModel` in favor of a DGL model. It would be very nice if we could change internals  on `GraphConvModel` without causing downstream ripples (but underneath the hood, we could just use DGL while preserving the user API)'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'There are two approaches we could take to doing that.  One would be to directly convert the current code over to PyTorch.  The other would be to try to reimplement equivalent models using either DGL or PyTorch-Geometric.  The former might give a more exact conversion, but the latter would probably lead to better performance.  We should investigate both possibilities.'

Title: b'Standard API for retrieving model parameters'
Body: b"Currently there is no uniform API to retrieve the parameters of a model.  On a TorchModel you can call `model.model.parameters()`, which returns a generator that produces PyTorch tensors.  On a KerasModel you can access `model.model.trainable_variables` which contains a list TensorFlow Variable objects.  For a SklearnModel there's probably also some way of doing it, though I'm not sure what it is.\r\n\r\nWe should consider creating a standard API to retrieve the parameters of any model in a uniform format."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'A standard API would be very useful and would smooth our way towards a ModelHub (https://forum.deepchem.io/t/a-sketch-of-a-modelhub/445) since it would give us a model-agnostic way of getting the parameters of a model.\r\n\r\nA model-agnostic way of setting parameters would be very useful as well but likely harder to implement'

Title: b'Logging improvements'
Body:
b"Now that we've replaced most `print()` commands with logging calls, it's much easier to control logging behavior.  But a side effect of this is that you now get almost no output at all when training models.  We should consider changes to this behavior.

One option is just to add the following lines to all the examples.

```python
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
```

That way the examples will produce useful information, and users will see how to do the same in their own scripts.  We also could consider having DeepChem do this automatically so users will get progress reported by default.

We also should reconsider what we log.  When I set the logging level to INFO and run many of the examples, the console fills up with thousands of repetitions of the line

```
INFO:deepchem.feat.base_classes:Featurizing datapoint 0
```

That looks like a bug (it isn't really featurizing the same datapoint thousands of times), and also we don't need to log nearly that many messages."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b'+1 for adding the logging level set on the top of all the examples. 

The logging excess is caused by the following line https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/53366e7d389d2b17ad22ff8707c9ae51c4f4d493/deepchem/data/data_loader.py#L111.

I think we could fix this issue by swapping the call to `_featurize` instead of `featurize` (or as more thorough refactoring, get rid of the for-loop and just write
```
features = featurizer(df[field])
```
'

Title: b'Adding protein sequence datasets to MolNet'
Body:
b'##  Feature

I propose adding protein sequence data to MolNet as part of the recent efforts to increase support for proteins. Please feel free to suggest alternative datasets or use cases that should be considered.

Two potential datasets that seem interesting and widely used:
1. [UniProt Archive](https://www.uniprot.org/help/uniparc): a comprehensive and non-redundant database that contains most of the publicly available protein sequences in the world. (Thanks to @seyonechithrananda for this link)
2. [Swiss-Prot](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprot/?query=reviewed:yes): 560k+ manually annotated sequences with information extracted from literature and curator-evaluated computational analysis.

Users of MolNet and DeepChem could use these datasets to benchmark [protein language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.15222)  for generation and classification tasks and for protein structure prediction models. 

## Motivation

With the recent fervor around [AlphaFold2](https://deepmind.com/blog/article/alphafold-a-solution-to-a-50-year-old-grand-challenge-in-biology) as only one example, there is tremendous interest in protein sequence data and mapping sequences -> structure -> function. Protein sequences have been used for unsupervised and self-supervised learning, as well as supervised structure prediction.

CCing @rbharath @peastman Please feel free to CC anyone else interested in proteins!'

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"I'm not sure of the best sources for this, but it would be useful to include a dataset of proteins annotated with per-residue labels.  For example,

- Secondary structure
- Solvent accessibility
- Binding sites
- Transmembrane domains
- ...

This would be a much smaller dataset, since it could only include well characterized proteins, but it would enable applications that aren't possible with just sequences."

b"##  Bug

The existing normalizing flows tutorial uses outdated SELFIES methods to convert from strings to one-hot embeddings and back. I've been working on a fix to move to the newer methods (which take in different arguments) but am running into some issues. 

Namely, 'multiple_selfies_to_hot' needs to be converted to use 'batch_selfies_to_flat_hot', and 'multiple_hot_to_selfies' needs to be converted to use 'batch_flat_hot_to_selfies'. You can find the utils file with the updated methods in the SELFIES repo [here](https://github.com/aspuru-guzik-group/selfies/blob/master/selfies/utils.py#L242).

I've gotten 'batch_selfies_to_flat_hot()' to work as a replacement in the tutorial, but upon trying to convert the one-hot encodings back to SELFIES strings I run into the following error:

## To Reproduce

Steps to reproduce the behaviour:

Just need to run the normalizing flows tutorial in Colab to reproduce the error with encoding/decoding one-hot encodings.



## Expected behaviour

I've gotten 'batch_selfies_to_flat_hot()' to work as a replacement in the tutorial, but upon trying to convert the one-hot encodings back to SELFIES strings I run into the following error:

Title: b'Upgrading to Pytorch 1.8.1'
Body:
b"Deepchem is currently using Pytroch 1.6.0

There has been a new error in github actions- 
```
>     torch.maximum(1 - torch.multiply(labels, output), torch.tensor(0)), 2), dim=-1)
E     AttributeError: module 'torch' has no attribute 'maximum'

```
And problem is that the `maximum` method was only introduced in [Pytorch #42579](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/42579).

There is just one problem in Upgrading to Pytorch > 1.8, they support only Cuda 10.2 onwards, as mentioned [here](https://pytorch.org/get-started/locally/)

@rbharath so I think we should also start thinking about upgrading Cuda as well.

Here Momentary fixes to solve this issue before Deepchem's upcoming release- 
1) Either we change the `maximum` method? ----> Works well in PR #2508 
2) Or we need to be using Pytorch 1.7 which supports Cuda 10.1 ----> Creating Segmentation fault PR #2518  "

Title: b'Need of PyTorch Lightning based new Base Class '
Body:
b'##  Feature

I am proposing a design to integrate new base class that will ease the construction of PyTorch Lightning based models.
Here is the link of my design -> [[proposal](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1SDna7clPkTuWScANoufSXKfOlUN5tOKqigydlTaTlG0/edit?usp=sharing)]

## Motivation

PyTorch Lightning is more advantageous than PyTorch. It retains the flexibility of PyTorch by providing full control over key points in training. It abstracts out most of the PyTorch code. It allows to train our model on CPUs, GPUs, Multiple GPUs, or TPUs without changing a single line of  PyTorch code.

## Additional Context

Please give your views to improve the design. '

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b'Could you elaborate on what the goals of this proposal are, and what specific problems you're trying to solve?

We've had discussions about PyTorch Lightning in the past, and concluded that TorchModel and LightningModel are "equivalent" in the sense that they fill the same role.  Each of them wraps a torch.nn.Module and adds code for training, logging, etc.  They have different designs and features, so one might be preferable over the other in certain situations.  But we couldn't see any way it would make sense to combine them, because they largely provide alternate implementations of the same features.

Another important design consideration is that all DeepChem models need to provide a consistent API.  The public APIs for TorchModel and KerasModel are nearly identical.  To a user, it shouldn't matter whether the model they're using happens to be implemented with PyTorch or Keras.  Maintaining that consistency is important for any design.'

Title: b'DeepChem Dependency Management'
Body:
b'##  Question and Discussion

Package management is probably one of the single biggest headaches in Python, and DeepChem has inherited this issue. As more features and dependencies are added, package versions become harder to reconcile and keep up with. Here we can discuss some possible ways forward. 

Two that come to my mind are:
1. Revitalize the repo structure of the [deepchem organization](https://github.com/deepchem) and split packages into DeepChem, DeepMat, DeepBio, etc. As the "central science", DeepChem could set the API conventions and parent classes, but dependencies would be split among different packages rather than centrally maintained in a monorepo. Pros are that each package will have minimal dependencies and maximal flexibility to work with other packages. Cons are that it will be difficult to maintain multiple different packages and this would introduce a major API redesign.
2. Turn DeepChem into a fully-fledged "app" that is containerized with [Pipfile Lock](https://realpython.com/pipenv-guide/#the-pipfilelock), [Conda lock](https://pypi.org/project/conda-lock/), and/or Docker. Pros are that anyone will be able to run DeepChem anywhere, and we only have to maintain a single set of working package versions. Cons are that users who wish to use additional packages that are not direct dependencies will have to find versions that are compatible with the DC environment, or else split work across different environments.

I've added these ideas to get the discussion going. Please add other design ideas or comments on these!'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b'Thanks for kicking off this discussion! Here are some more thoughts (somewhat scattered for now, but putting up to raise discussion)

1. One variant of this idea is we could maintain multiple packages within the deepchem monorepo (we could have separate docs pages / pip packages but all packaged inside the deepchem/ monorepo for development ease). If we choose this path, it would have to be done gradually over several releases to maintain strong backwards compatibility for users which would introduce planning challenges. An advantage is that this may help us pull in new users into the community (a fluids simulation person might sensibly not realize DeepChem could be a useful tool for them right now!)
2. When I use DeepChem for applications, it's often my "primary dependency." Since DeepChem comes batteries included, usually I only end up using a few auxiliary extra packages (say visualization tools or other lightweight things). Do other people also use DeepChem this way? Or do you often use other heavy duty tools in conjunction? (A prominent counterexample is huggingface+deepchem is used by a number of folks but not quite supported fully by the main DeepChem yet).'

Title: b'ncfrey'
Body:
b'> 2. When I use DeepChem for applications, it's often my "primary dependency." Since DeepChem comes batteries included, usually I only end up using a few auxiliary extra packages (say visualization tools or other lightweight things). Do other people also use DeepChem this way? Or do you often use other heavy duty tools in conjunction? (A prominent counterexample is huggingface+deepchem is used by a number of folks but not quite supported fully by the main DeepChem yet).

I strongly agree with this point. I use conda and pipenv environments to manage everything, because python package management is so tricky. I have a DeepChem environment, just like I have a Pymatgen/Matminer environment. I think any python project that becomes sufficiently powerful/complex requires this kind of approach. I'd be curious to see how others are using DeepChem.

'

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"> One variant of this idea is we could maintain multiple packages within the deepchem monorepo (we could have separate docs pages / pip packages but all packaged inside the deepchem/ monorepo for development ease).

This seems to me like a good approach.  All the code can stay in a single repository, but get split into multiple conda/pip packages.  People will install only the parts they need, bringing in only the dependencies they need.

> Since DeepChem comes batteries included, usually I only end up using a few auxiliary extra packages (say visualization tools or other lightweight things).

I think this is contradicted by the large and steadily growing set of dependencies.  Most of them started out as unrelated packages that someone wanted to use with DeepChem.  Then they contributed some code to DeepChem that required it, and instantly it became a dependency.  This isn't slowing down, because people keep finding other packages they want to use with DeepChem.  It isn't sustainable.  It's already difficult to find consistent versions of all the dependencies, and each added dependency makes it harder.  Eventually it will become impossible.

A better way of approaching it is to say that matminer, mordred, simdna, networkx, pdbfixer, pubchempy, etc. are all examples of independent packages that certain people want to use with DeepChem.  That doesn't mean they're dependencies, and you shouldn't need to install them to use DeepChem."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"> This seems to me like a good approach. All the code can stay in a single repository, but get split into multiple conda/pip packages. People will install only the parts they need, bringing in only the dependencies they need.

Here's a quick sketch for what a DeepChem future package structure could look like:

- deepscience: The core DeepChem modules and classes which are application independent (datasets, generic splitters/transformers/models). deepscience should have very minimal dependencies restricted to core python libraries (numpy/pandas, maybe tf/pytorch)
  - deepchem: Chemistry specific featurizers/splitters/models. To prevent large user breakage, we'd want to import core modules from deepscience so existing deepchem code bases could continue working as expected
  - deepmat: Materials science specific featurizers/splitters/models etc
  - deepbio: Protein sequence featurizers/splitters/models etc
  - More modules can be added as we expand into new domains

> I think this is contradicted by the large and steadily growing set of dependencies. Most of them started out as unrelated packages that someone wanted to use with DeepChem. Then they contributed some code to DeepChem that required it, and instantly it became a dependency. This isn't slowing down, because people keep finding other packages they want to use with DeepChem. It isn't sustainable. It's already difficult to find consistent versions of all the dependencies, and each added dependency makes it harder. Eventually it will become impossible.
> 
> A better way of approaching it is to say that matminer, mordred, simdna, networkx, pdbfixer, pubchempy, etc. are all examples of independent packages that certain people want to use with DeepChem. That doesn't mean they're dependencies, and you shouldn't need to install them to use DeepChem.

This is an excellent counterpoint. Following a split like the one I've outlined above may help ameliorate the problem of ballooning dependencies"

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'Another possibility is for everything to remain "DeepChem", but split the installation into multiple packages.  A model for this is OpenAI Gym.  If you just `pip install gym`, that gets you the core library and a minimal set of environments.  There are lots of other environments, many of which require additional dependencies, so they split them into additional packages that you install separately.'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"A more extreme version of that would be for the secondary packages to provide *only* dependencies.  If you installed just the core DeepChem package, you would get the full source code but only a few essential dependencies like scikit-learn and TensorFlow.  That would mean a lot of features would throw exceptions if you tried to use them.  Then there could be a `deepchem-pytorch` package that would install PyTorch, DGL, Pytorch Geometric, etc.  And there could be a `deepchem-molecules` package that would install RDKit, MDTraj, PDBFixer, etc.  And so on.\r\n\r\nThis probably would only be practical for packages installed with conda, but that's going to be an issue regardless."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b'I'm on-board with the strategy of keeping everything as "DeepChem" and splitting up into multiple installation packages (which are possibly just dependencies). The larger deepscience/deepchem/deepmat split would be a lot more work and picking the simpler strategy to start seems smart.

Looking at the openai gym setup.py file:

https://github.com/openai/gym/blob/master/setup.py

It looks like this could be relatively straightforward to do? We'd need to modify `setup.py` and then modify the github actions release infrastructure to release multiple package'

Title: b'john-judge'
Body:
b'These are just notes for our group project. The Colab mentioned is internal to our group, but we expect to have a pull request within the next few weeks.

## Goals
- ~~expose KL cost annealing parameters from `AspuruGuzikAutoEncoder`~~ -- it occurs to me now that these hyperparameters are already configurable as named parameters passed through `**kwargs`
- implement teacher forcing in `AspuruGuzikAutoEncoder`
- backward-compatibility (including making any new dependencies soft where possible)

## Teacher Forcing 
### Strategy/design:

We would want to enable this to teacher-force during training but free-sample during generation.   The[ way that Aspuru-Guzik-group did this](http://tensorflow.biotecan.com/python/Python_1.8/tensorflow.google.cn/api_docs/python/tf/keras/backend/in_train_phase.html) was to use the keras function `backend.in_train_phase` because the training flag can act as the switch for which behavior to use. 

### Starting point
Classes copied in from `deepchem`:
 - `AspuruGuzikAutoEncoder`
 - `SeqToSeq`
 - `VariationalRandomizer`

Copied from original Aspuru-Guzik-group (`chemvae`):
 - `TerminalGRU`
 - `sampled_rnn (function)`

### Progress in TerminalGRU:
- Now supports probabilistic teacher forcing (original had fixed `teacher_forcing_ratio = 1`)
- `TerminalGRU` keras version issues:
-- Note that `preprocess_input` is missing as a method of `TerminalGRU` (it should inherit from `keras.layers.recurrent.GRU`, but issue probably caused by the fact that `TerminalGRU` uses an older version of keras than deepchem). It's just an identity function for GPUs and I believe its CPU-specific logic is performance-only. For now, let's remove calls to this method or otherwise replace with identity function.
-- In `TerminalGRU` calls to 'add_weight' need to have the first argument passed as a named parameter rather than positionally. Put in "shape=" for the first argument.


### Progress in `AspuruGuzikAutoEncoder`:
 - `AspuruGuzikAutoEncoder` now supports parameter `teacher_forcing_ratio`, which it later passes to the correct parameter of a `TerminalGRU` instantiation as the third and final GRU layer. Defaults to value 0.0.
 - `_create_decoder()` has only 2 normal GRU layers instead of 3
 - the call to the initialized `TerminalGRU` passes the input as `[prev_layer, input]`, where 'input' should be the true input. However, this is where I'm probably incorrect. Compare this to how the original implementation passes this in as `[x_dec, true_seq_in]` in the [original Aspuru-Guzik](https://github.com/aspuru-guzik-group/chemical_vae/blob/master/chemvae/models.py) -- they read in the latent space as one Input, and the `true_seq_in` (ground truth) as another `Input`. I believe we will need to pass ground truth input into `_create_decoder()` and update calls to it, which means overriding much of `AspuruGuzikAutoEncoder`'s call to its superclass `SeqToSeq`'s init.

### To do:
- next step mentioned above, also continue in teacher forcing attempt Colab 
- check input/output shapes
- train and compare to our previous results
'

Title: b"I'm Working On Generalizing OneHotFeaturizer to Work With Arbitrary Strings"
Body:
b"##  Feature

I'm working on generalizing OneHotFeaturizer to work with arbitrary strings. This is part of my upcoming GSoC proposal to improve protein sequence support in DeepChem.

This roughly entailed the following changes:
- Changing the parent class for OneHotFeaturizer from MoleculeFeaturizer to Featurizer
- Rewriting _featurize() to take in a string instead of a mol (BREAKING)
- Adding a new method to handle RDKit mol objects (and call _featurize())
- Renaming methods, variables, and changing comments/documentation as appropriate to reflect the above changes

## Motivation

So far, DeepChem only has rudimentary support for training on protein sequences. A first step to solving this problem may be to make our featurizers support protein sequences. 

By making the onehotfeaturizer support arbitrary strings, it will not only be able to encode amino acid or codon sequences but also other potential future applications. 

This change was initially suggested by @rbharath  in #2150 .

@nissy-dev 

## Additional context

A draft PR for this will be submitted in very short order."

Title: b'Excessive on-disk size of DiskDataset objects?'
Body:
b"##  Questions & Help

Hi everyone,

Thanks as always to the developers of Deepchem for your work building a great tool!

I have a question about on-disk storage size of `DiskDataset` objects.  For a use case involving a multi-task dataset of hundreds of thousands of samples and tens of tasks, where the data is sparse across tasks (not every sample has a measurement for each task), I find Deepchem using 10s of GBs of `/tmp/` storage. I believe this is being allocated to `DiskDataset` objects.  The source data these `DiskDataset`s are constructed from is orders of magnitude smaller than that.  In addition to the storage size, constructing the `DiskDataset` objects is also very slow.

I'm wondering if this level of disk usage is typical, or may be peculiar to my data types, data structures, or usage patterns?  Are there ways to mitigate this by e.g. using a sparse representation for on-disk storage for the `DiskDataset`s?

Let me note that my experience is mostly with Deepchem 2.3.x, so I apologize if this has been addressed in some way in more recent versions."

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"It's an interesting question: could we make DiskDataset automatically detect when an array is sparse, and save it to disk in a compressed format?  How would that affect both disk space and speed?  We would presumably need to convert it to a dense array on loading, but that's easy.  For a very sparse array, it might even end up being faster.

How sparse is your data?  What fraction of elements are nonzero?

You said the files are appearing in `/tmp`.  Do you know what those files are?  When you create a dataset, or load one of the MoleculeNet datasets, and don't specify a save directory, then it puts it in tmp.  Is that what we're talking about?  Or are these just temporary files that are created during the process of creating the DiskDataset?  How big is the final dataset on disk once it's done creating it?"

Title: b'nesanders'
Body:
b'Thank you @peastman , I really appreciate your attention and reply.

Yes, these files are appearing in the tmp directory as specified by the `data_dir` parameter when instantiating the `DiskDataset`.  

Yes, I think the questions you pose in your first paragraph are the kinds of things I was wondering. This particular dataset has density ~20%.  But as I take a closer look, I think I may have been wrong that the `y` sparsity is the main issue here.  

I see that `shard-0-X.npy` is taking ~11GB.   `shard-0-y.npy` is only 26MB and others are smaller.  This is for use with a `GraphConv` model, so X is storing an array of `deepchem.feat.mol_graphs.ConvMol` objects.  Are those filesizes typical for this use case, and are there options to compress?'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"Possibly that could be optimized.  It's just writing out pickled ConvMol objects.  Each object has some arrays that are passed to its constructor, and a bunch of other arrays that are calculated from them to provide faster access to certain information.  All of that gets written out to the file.  We should look into whether it would be better to recalculate some of those arrays instead of saving them."

Title: b'nesanders'
Body: b'@peastman that makes a lot of sense.  It could be interesting to have a utility for the DiskDataset class to estimate 1) the total disk space usage and 2) the featurization calculation time for a dataset to help the user decide whether they want to write the smiles string or the `ConvMol` object to disk.'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"I wouldn't go as far as SMILES strings.  That would involve repeating the whole featurization.  Take a look at the constructor for ConvMol.  It only takes a few arguments, then computes a lot of other quantities from them.  So the choice is whether to write out all those quantities, or only the values passed to the constructor.  We should see how that affects both file size and loading time."
