b'> Firstly, still about gc_model_builder(model_params , model_dir), do I need to pass anything to model_params at all? In my implementation, I'm not passing anything to model_params and it works

No, you don't need to pass anything to the `model_params`.

> Secondly, how can I change the epoch number and batch size of this model? I tried adding them to the params_dict but it seems like to be not working, since np_epoch=1 and np_epoch =100 gave almost same scores. I think this is because epoch number and batch size are not the parameters defined in GrapgConvModel's init(). Also, you can notice that I added "invalidaparam!!!":[50] in params_dict. I was thinking this should lead to some kind of error, but it just ran successfully. How to understand this behavior?

`batch_size` is definitely a parameter you can specify while defining the model (The basic TensorGraph model accepts a `batch_size` argument). For the epoch, I think you should use `nb_epochs` and not `nb_epoch`. About the invalidparam, I would think it just gets ignored since its not really a parameter and hence no errors raised. There must be a check somewhere to ignore it, I'd have to check where.

> Thirdly, I notice that this grid_search.py is returning the model having the highest score returned from evaluation based on the user-provided metric. However, if I want to use RMSE (rooted mean squared error) as metric, the best model should be the model with the lowest RMSE score instead of the highest score.

The code I'm running is below, but there are 30k+ CIF files it relies on so it might be hard to reproduce independently without sharing those somehow... (though they're all on Materials Project and I can share the code to download them yourself if you like, or, I imagine you'd see the same thing with whatever CIFs you use...)

```

# X = output of featurize
# y = formation energy
# w = 1.0

# TODO: this should yield a tuple of lists
def get_data(cif_dir, csv_path, chunk_size=8192):
  featurizer = dc.feat.CGCNNFeaturizer()
  cifs = glob(cif_dir+"*.cif")
  # shuffle list

    print("finished a chunk!")

Title: b'Changes to ButinaSplitter'
Body:
b"cc @rbharath @proteneer 

This is a followup to https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/issues/2112#issuecomment-700942341 and the discussion following it.  ButinaSplitter is currently not very useful, but could be made more useful with a few changes.

As discussed there I modified it to use the same code for building datasets as ScaffoldSplitter.  I then tested it with the following code.

```python
splitters = ['random', 'scaffold', 'butina']
metric = dc.metrics.Metric(dc.metrics.roc_auc_score)
for splitter in splitters:
    tasks, datasets, transformers = dc.molnet.load_tox21(featurizer='ECFP', split=splitter)
    train_dataset, valid_dataset, test_dataset = datasets
    model = dc.models.MultitaskClassifier(n_tasks=len(tasks), n_features=1024, layer_sizes=[1000])
    model.fit(train_dataset, nb_epoch=10)
    print('splitter:', splitter)
    print('training set score:', model.evaluate(train_dataset, [metric], transformers))
    print('test set score:', model.evaluate(test_dataset, [metric], transformers))
    print()
```

RandomSplitter gives a test set score of 0.78, and ScaffoldSplitter gives 0.68, which shows how random splitting doesn't produce a truly independent test set.  Scaffold splitting does much better.  ButinaSplitter gives a test set score of 0.78, exactly the same as RandomSplitter!

ButinaSplitter has an adjustable cutoff.  The above was with the default value of 0.18.  So I repeated the test with different values of the cutoff.  Here are the test set scores.

0.18: 0.78
0.3: 0.74
0.4: 0.73
0.5: 0.66
0.6: 0.61
0.7: 0.65
0.8: 0.61

At least on this dataset, 0.18 is much too small.  It works no better than random splitting.  It gets better as you increase the cutoff, and by 0.6 it's significantly better than ScaffoldSplitter.  Further increases make little difference.

I looked up the original paper on the clustering method (http://www.l4patterns.com/uploads/dbclus-paper.pdf), and they used a cutoff of 0.8.  How was the value 0.18 selected?  Would it be reasonable to increase the default to 0.6?  Is this value likely to be universal, or will it vary a lot between datasets?"

Title: b'proteneer'

Title: b'rbharath'

```
for dataset in [train_dataset, valid_dataset, test_dataset]:
   for transformer in transformers:
       dataset = transformer.transform(dataset)
```

only overwrite the `dataset` variable and don't actually replace the train/valid/test datasets. For that you'll want

```
transformer = dc.trans.NormalizationTransformer(transform_X=True, dataset=train_dataset)
train_dataset = transformer.transform(train_dataset)
valid_dataset = transformer.transform(valid_dataset)
test_dataset = transformer.transform(test_dataset)
```

The second bug is that `SklearnModel` requires an instantiated sklearn model as input. So you'll want

```
sklearn_model = RandomForestClassifier()
model = dc.models.SklearnModel(sklearn_model)
```

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b'I believe you're trying to evaluate a multiclass dataset using precision and are running into the issue details in this scikit-learn stackoverflow issue: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/52269187/facing-valueerror-target-is-multiclass-but-average-binary

This is a bit of a hack, but I think you can fix it by wrapping the metric:

```
def precision_average(y_test, y_pred):
  return precision_score(y_test, y_pred, average='micro') # or any other average you like. See sklearn docs
metric_precision_average = dc.metrics.Metric(precision_average, mode="classification")
model.evaluate(train_dataset, [metric_precision_average])
```

Can you give this a try adn see if it works for you?'

Title: b'Recommended splitters are not the defaults'
Body: b"I've noticed that molnet loaders often have default splitting methods that are different from the recommended method.  For example tox21 has the default `split='index'`, but the documentation recommends random splitting.  BACE has the default `split='random'`, but the documentation recommends scaffold splitting.  Others probably have the same problem.  We should fix all of them so the recommended method is the default."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"One thought here I've had for overhauling MoleculeNet is that we should make `ScaffoldSplitter` the default for all molecular datasets. `RandomSplitter` is often really bad for benchmarking, and causes variation across runs while `ScaffoldSplitter` makes apples-to-apples comparisons possible across methods, and provides a better estimate of generalizability due the the better separation between train/valid/test"

Title: b'Support for DGL Modeling'
Body:
b"Hi DeepChem team,

This is Mufei from the [DGL](https://github.com/dmlc/dgl) team. I've also spent some time developing [DGL-LifeSci](https://github.com/awslabs/dgl-lifesci) -- a DGL-based package for working with graphs in chemistry and biology. It seems that DeepChem has started supporting DGL-based modeling with PyTorch (e.g. #2089 by @nd-02110114 ), which is rather exciting! I've had some chats with @rbharath before about contributing to this effort. Below are some observations & proposals and I'd like to know your thoughts.

Compared with pure PyTorch-based modeling, DGL-based modeling additionally requires:
- Converting graph data into DGL's data structure `DGLGraph` and storing node/edge features in `DGLGraph.ndata` and `DGLGraph.edata`
- Using APIs like `DGLGraph.update_all` for invoking message passing over graphs in NN modules

For the first point, DeepChem employs [`GraphData`](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/master/deepchem/feat/graph_data.py) as an intermediate graph representation across different frameworks (DGL, PyTorch Geometric, etc.). It allows graph creation from a COO format along with pre-processed features and exposes a `to_dgl_graph` API for converting a `GraphData` instance into a `DGLGraph` instance. For the second point, DeepChem implements DGL-based PyTorch models under `deepchem/deepchem/models/torch_models`.

For a better support of DGL-based modeling and more generally, graph-based modeling, there are several possible points:
- Support for APIs like `from_dgl_graph` and `from_pyg_graph`, which can be helpful for users familiar with DGL/PyG before.
- A simple interface for custom dataset. This can be something like a variant of [CSVLoader](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/master/deepchem/data/data_loader.py), which directly constructs a graph dataset from files of a standard data format like `CSV`. It allows users to specify the type of graph to construct as well as the way to featurize their nodes/edges. DGL-LifeSci's [MoleculeCSVDataset](https://github.com/awslabs/dgl-lifesci/blob/master/python/dgllife/data/csv_dataset.py#L19) can be an example for this.
- Functions for constructing standard types of graphs (molecular graphs, complete graphs, KNN graphs, distance-based graphs) from raw data like SMILES strings. While graph creation from a COO format maximizes the flexibility, it can be convenient to have such functions for users who only want to try existing modeling approaches on their own datasets. I think the design of [Protein Graph Library](https://github.com/a-r-j/graphein) follows a similar idea. 
- Support for heterogeneous graphs, i.e. graphs of typed nodes and edges. I have the impression that DeepChem is mainly for molecular property prediction and a bit protein-ligand binding affinity prediction, so maybe this is less an issue. However, this can still be helpful even for molecular property prediction when one wants to combine information from different graph structures. [Molecule Attention Transformer](https://github.com/ardigen/MAT) is an example for this.
- Examples for model training and evaluation on MoleculeNet
- Additionally, DGL-LifeSci has implemented some graph neural networks [here](https://github.com/awslabs/dgl-lifesci/tree/master/python/dgllife/model) and I'd like to know if you are open to directly import them in DeepChem."

DeepChem's dataset architecture is generic (graph datasets are simply stored within numpy object arrays either in memory or on disk in `.npy` files) so `InMemoryLoader` can generate graph datasets. Our usual flow would be something as follows (in pseudocode)

```
feat = dc.feat.SomeGraphFeaturizer(feat_args=...)
loader = dc.data.InMemoryLoader(feat)
dataset = loader.create_dataset(pandas_column_with_smiles)
```
You can pass in different arguments for featurization by changing the choice of featurizer or the constructor arguments for the featurizer. For biological networks or biomedical knowledge graphs, there can be a large number of node types (e.g. drugs, proteins, diseases) and edge types (drug-drug interaction, drug-protein interaction, protein-protein interaction, etc.). There seems to be an increasing interest in applying GNNs to proteins. With biological networks containing compounds and proteins, there can be more things to play with in modeling.
> 

These are really nice examples! I think I'm more sold on the idea of supporting heterogenous graphs. Are there any DGL datastructures/featurizers for heterogeneous graphs that we could leverage?


> > Examples for model training and evaluation on MoleculeNet
> > This is definitely on our priorities! @nd-02110114 is actively working on this already, and I'd love to see more MoleculeNet benchmarks for all DGL models be put up.

As a suggestion for a starting point, it would be great to expose more DGL models within deepchem. Title: b'nissy-dev'

b'Sorry for slow response :bowing_man:
Currently, I face the issues about crystal graph convolutional model built with DGL, so I'm a little busy for debugging it. (The detail issue is here https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/issues/2160)

>I think doing this would be straightforward and would simply involve making a wrapper class (check out our tutorial on making custom PyTorch models in DeepChem).

Yes! I seem we just implement the wrapper model If the input graph for model is a bi-directed graph (graph made by `smile_to_bigraph` method). The following is sample codes.  (I can not check this code work correcly, but the main implementation flow is the following)

```python

from dgllife.model import MPNNPredictor

# 1st: Define the PyTorch model for fixing output dimension of DGL original model
class DGLMPNN(nn.Module):

  def __init__(self, n_tasks, n_classes, mode, ......):
    super(DGLMPNN, self).__init__()
    self.mode = mode
    self.n_tasks = n_tasks
    self.n_classes = n_classes

    if self.mode == 'regression':
      out = n_tasks
    else:
      out = n_tasks * n_classes
     self.mpnn = MPNNPredictor(n_tasks=out, .....)

  def forward(self, dgl_graph, node_feat, edge_feat):
    out = self.mpnn(dgl_graph, node_feat, edge_feat)
    if self.mode == 'regression':
      return out
    else:
      logits = out.view(-1, self.n_tasks, self.n_classes)
      # for n_tasks == 1 case
      logits = torch.squeeze(logits)
      proba = F.softmax(logits)
      return proba, logits

# 2nd: Define the model which inherits TorchModel
class DGLMPNNModel(TorchModel):

  def __init__(self, arg1, arg2, ...., kwargs):
    model = DGLMPNN(arg1, arg2, ...)
    if mode == "regression":
      loss: Loss = L2Loss()
      output_types = ['prediction']
    else:
      loss = SparseSoftmaxCrossEntropy()
      output_types = ['prediction', 'loss']
    super(DGLMPNNModel, self).__init__(model, loss=loss, output_types=output_types, **kwargs)

  def _prepare_batch(self, batch):
    # we override `_prepare_batch` to prepare for each model inputs
    inputs, labels, weights = batch
    
    # prepare for model inputs
    dgl_graphs = [graph.to_dgl_graph() for graph in inputs[0]]
    batch_graph = dgl.batch(dgl_graphs).to(self.device)
    node_feats = batch_graph.ndata['h'].pop()
    edge_feats = batch_graph.edata['edge_attr'].pop()

    # prepare for other data
    _, labels, weights = super(DGLMPNNModel, self)._prepare_batch(([], labels, weights))

    # 1st element is the model inputs
    return (batch_graph, node_feats, edge_feats), labels, weights
```'

For biological networks or biomedical knowledge graphs, there can be a large number of node types (e.g. drugs, proteins, diseases) and edge types (drug-drug interaction, drug-protein interaction, protein-protein interaction, etc.). There seems to be an increasing interest in applying GNNs to proteins. With biological networks containing compounds and proteins, there can be more things to play with in modeling.
> 
> These are really nice examples! I think I'm more sold on the idea of supporting heterogenous graphs. Are there any DGL datastructures/featurizers for heterogeneous graphs that we could leverage?
> 

DGL's graph data structure `DGLGraph` naturally supports heterogeneous graphs. For featurization, it shall not be difficult to extend featurization for homogeneous graphs to featurization for heterogeneous graphs.

> In general, lots to do here, and any work you can contribute would be much appreciated! If you're interested, let me know if you'd be willing to attend one of the developer calls. It might be easiest to just discuss there :)

Do you have a developer call next week? I can attend that call."

Title: b'Pretty Print for Featurizers, Splitters, and Transformers'
Body:
b"In #1816, I recently suggested adding a pretty print utility for `Dataset` objects. I think we should do the same for featurizers, splitters, and transformers. The biggest reason for this is that given a featurizer object, it's not clear what precisely it does. Here's the current print

```
>>> dc.feat.CircularFingerprint(size=1024, radius=4)               
<deepchem.feat.fingerprints.CircularFingerprint at 0x1a3d84fac8>
```
Here's the proposed printout
```
>>> dc.feat.CircularFingerprint(size=1024, radius=4)               
CircularFingerprint[size=1024, radius=4]
```
Representations for Transformers and Splitters could be handled similarly. It would also be useful to have a string form for these objects. Here's my proposed format
```
>>> str(dc.feat.CircularFingerprint(size=1024, radius=4)
CircularFingerprint_size_1024_radius_4
```
This looks a little janky, but this is easy to use as a directory name on the filesystem. So you can easily track how a given dataset on disk was featurized."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b'Writing some notes here to document the AWS infrastructure. This should be migrated to the docs in a future PR:

DeepChem's website infrastructure is all managed on AWS through different AWS services. All DeepChem developers have access to these services through the deepchem-developers IAM role. At present, @rbharath is the only admin with access to the IAM role, but longer term we should migrate this so other folks have access to the roles.

There are two core deepchem S3 buckets:
- deepchemdata: This bucket hosts the deepchem.io website, MoleculeNet datasets, pre-featurized datasets, and pretrained models. This bucket is set up to host a static website (at https://deepchemdata.s3-us-west-1.amazonaws.com/index.html). 
- deepchemforum: This bucket hosts backups for the forums. The bucket is private for security reasons. The forums themselves are hosted on a digital ocean instance that only @rbharath currently has access to. Longer term, we should migrate the forums onto AWS so all DeepChem developers can access the forums. The forums themselves are a discord instance. The forums upload their backups to this S3 bucket once a day. If the forums crash, they can be restored from the backups in this bucket

DeepChem also makes use of some other AWS infrastructure:

- Route 53: DNS for the deepchem.io website is handled by Route 53. The "hosted zone" deepchem.io holds all DNS information for the website. 
- Certificate Manager: The AWS certificate manager issues the SSL/TLS certificate for the *.deepchem.io and deepchem.io domains. (Our recent certificate issues were due to these certificates expiring)
- Cloudfront: We make use of a cloudfront distribution to serve our static website. The cloudfront distribution connects to the certificate in Certificate Manager and uses the deepchemdata bucket as the origin domain. We set CNAME for www.deepchem.io and deepchem.io

Non AWS resources:

Title: b'Making Predictions on Large Datasets'
Body:
b"A common task users will want to do with DeepChem is make predictions on a large dataset of molecules. For example, users might want to take a model and run it against a large database like [ZINC15](https://zinc.docking.org/). One issue to note here is that a featurized library of molecules could get quite large. A million molecules featurized with `ConvMolFeaturizer` takes up roughly 15-20 GB of space on disk. Featurizing the full dataset of 200M ZINC15 compounds could come out to a 3-4 TB dataset.

At present we don't have a good way to run predictions across a large dataset. The `KerasModel.predict` and `TorchModel.predict` methods build up numpy arrays in memory. I've also noticed that garbage collection tends not to work well within a loop of this type. That is, iterating across a large dataset, I see a growth in memory usage which indicates that loaded shards/batches aren't being released even after we've crossed them in the for-loop of `predict`. I propose that we create a good API to make predictions on large datasets. Here are a couple first options for creating this sort of API:

- We could add a `Dataset.map` function which maps a given function across a dataset and creates a new `Dataset`. Then to make predictions on a large dataset, we would call `predictions = dataset.map(lambda (x, _, _, _): model.predict(x))`.
- We could add a flag to `Model.predict` called `write_to_disk`. If this is set, a generator will be used to write predictions to disk instead of running predictions entirely in memory.

We also need a standard reference dataset to test our implementation's memory usage with. I propose that we add ZINC15 to MoleculeNet. It's a standard database used widely in the community and having a MoleculeNet loader will make it easier for our users to screen their models against a diverse database of molecules.

CC @peastman @seyonechithrananda "

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"I think there are two distinct issues here.  If garbage collection really isn't working properly, that's a bug.  We need to track it down and fix it.

The other issue is creating a new API for predictions on large datasets.  This really depends on what the use cases are.  It already is very easy to do prediction on large datasets without needing to load everything into memory:

```python
for x, y, w, ids in dataset.iterbatches():
  prediction = model.predict_on_batch(x)
  # Do whatever you want with it here
```

That code is trivial.  Any complexity will come from what you do with the predictions.  If creating a new DiskDataset from the predictions is a common use case, that could certainly make sense to simplify.  For example,

```python
predicted_dataset = model.create_predicted_dataset(dataset, data_dir='predictions')
```"

Title: b'Design of PyTorch models'
Body:
b"Now that we're considering adding models based on PyTorch, it seems like a good time to consider the design for them.  We'll want to minimize code duplication, and also ensure the API is as consistent as possible (both between PyTorch based models, and between them and other DeepChem models).  At the same time, we should maintain lots of flexibility and make it easy to use existing PyTorch models from outside.

To get the discussion going, let me offer a design proposal.  This is intended just as a starting point for discussion, so please feel free to suggest changes or alternate designs.

We will create a TorchModel class whose API and feature set are as close as possible to KerasModel.  In place of a `tf.keras.Model`, the constructor will take a `torch.nn.Module`.  Aside from that one difference, the API will be nearly identical.  It will use the same Optimizer, Loss, and Callback objects.  I'm not sure whether all features of KerasModel can be supported, but as far as possible we'll try to do it.

Would that work?  Are there any serious problems we would run into with that approach?"

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'I really like this design! It allows for carry-over of design sense between Keras and PyTorch and should allow for clean docs'

Title: b'Error during model evaluation with dataset with empty list of task names'
Body:
b'During evaluation of a model with some metric and using a dataset with empty `dataset.task` the following error occurs:

```python
>>> metric = dc.metrics.Metric(dc.metrics.rms_score, np.mean)
>>> valid_score = model.evaluate(dataset, [metric])['mean-rms_score']
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "~/deepchem/deepchem/models/models.py", line 248, in evaluate
    n_classes=n_classes)
  File "~/deepchem/deepchem/utils/evaluate.py", line 306, in compute_model_performance
    use_sample_weights=use_sample_weights)
  File "~/deepchem/deepchem/metrics/__init__.py", line 772, in compute_metric
    y_true, mode=self.mode, n_tasks=n_tasks, n_classes=n_classes)
  File "~/deepchem/deepchem/metrics/__init__.py", line 169, in normalize_labels_shape
    "Shape of input doesn't match expected n_tasks=%d" % n_tasks)
ValueError: Shape of input doesn't match expected n_tasks=0
```

A possible workaround is to assign `dataset.task` some list of appropriate length.  This also means the error can be reproduced from a standard molnet set by assigning `dataset.task` to an empty list:

```python
import deepchem as dc
import numpy as np
from deepchem.models.graph_models import GraphConvModel

qm9_tasks, qm9_datasets, transformers = dc.molnet.load_qm9(featurizer='GraphConv')
train_dataset, valid_dataset, test_dataset = qm9_datasets
n_tasks = len(qm9_tasks)

test_dataset.tasks = []

metric = dc.metrics.Metric(dc.metrics.rms_score, np.mean)
model = GraphConvModel(n_tasks, batch_size=100, mode='regression')
loss = model.fit(train_dataset, nb_epoch=1)
test_score = model.evaluate(test_dataset, [metric])['mean-rms_score']
```

This error occurs since b399a20d.

On a related note: The different dataset classes (`NumpyDataset`, `DiskDataset`) do not have a consistent interfaces to handle the task names. 
1. There is `dataset.get_task_names()` but no `dataset.set_task_names()`.
2. If a new dataset is created without explicity setting the task names, then `NumpyDataset.get_task_names()` automatically returns an array with indices of appropriate length. `DiskDataset.get_task_names()` on the other hand returns an empty list. (Which is how I found this issue.)

I suggest to add a method `dataset.set_task_names()` and some way to pass the task names during construction of a new dataset.
'

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"Datasets are generally immutable once created, so a `set_task_names()` method wouldn't be appropriate.  I agree we should make the different classes more consistent.  Currently:

- NumpyDataset and ImageDataset do not allow you to specify task names.  They hardcode that the task names are integers.
- DiskDataset allows you to specify task names.  If you don't, it returns an empty list.

How about if all of them let you specify a list of task names, and automatically use integers if you don't?

> This also means the error can be reproduced from a standard molnet set by assigning dataset.task to an empty list

Don't do that!  Like I said, Datasets are supposed to be immutable, so if you start modifying their internal fields Bad Things could happen.  We should probably discourage this by renaming the field to `_tasks` and making `tasks` into a property."

Ah, here is the problem: I missed that because NumpyDataset does not and I assumed all datasets work similar.

> We should probably discourage this by renaming the field to _tasks and making tasks into a property.

Yes, absolutely! Although just renaming it might be fine as well.

"

Body: b"> Although just renaming it might be fine as well.\r\n\r\nAgreed!  There's already `get_task_names()` after all."

Title: b'Converting GraphData into RDKit Mol'
Body:
b"One common question that comes up is how to convert back from a featurized molecular graph into a RDKit Mol object. (This is a very useful utility for generative model design). Now that we're moving towards the unified graph representation with `GraphData`, I think we should consider adding a standard conversion function from `GraphData` to RDKit mol. One thing to note is that this function won't always be well defined (`GraphData` can be used for non-molecular graphs). But if we can define a standard conversion, we can make sure that out existing graph convolutional featurizers, once converted to use `GraphData`, can easily be converted back into RDKit Mols.

This stackoverflow post provides a nice bit of code to do a conversion between a networkx graph and RDKit mol which we can adapt: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/51195392/smiles-from-graph

CC @Draghohmmar"

Title: b'output_types is handled incorrectly'
Body:
b"KerasModel.predict() has an argument called `output_types`.  If this is specified, it is supposed to return all outputs whose types are included in `output_types`.  But it doesn't actually do that.  Instead it just treats it like a boolean flag.  If you pass any value for `output_types` that evaluates to True, it returns all outputs that have any non-standard type regardless of what the exact types are.

The error is in this code:

https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/8217de5ab76a7cd62d0524471b8b3569601f109a/deepchem/models/keras_model.py#L622-L623
"

Title: b'Tensorflow callbacks: EarlyStopping needs implementing'
Body:
b'I have tried to utilize early stopping from tensorflow framework but I get an error saying that: "TypeError: 'EarlyStopping' object is not callable"

```
import tensorflow as tf
early_stopping = tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(
    monitor='val_loss',
    min_delta=0,
    patience=10,
    verbose=0,
    mode='auto',
    baseline=None, restore_best_weights=False
)
model = dc.models.GraphConvModel(1,mode='regression')
model.fit(train_data, callbacks=[early_stopping])
```

Error message:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/47124775/89155808-77ff8580-d561-11ea-8845-1df716e038ce.png)

I think the issue is that DeepChem tries to run Callback itself rather then its specific methods e.g. on_epoch_start and on_epoch_end.
EarlyStopping has three relevant methods specified: on_traning_start, on_epoch_end, on_training_end
```
  def on_train_begin(self, logs=None):
    # Allow instances to be re-used
    self.wait = 0
    self.stopped_epoch = 0
    if self.baseline is not None:
      self.best = self.baseline
    else:
      self.best = np.Inf if self.monitor_op == np.less else -np.Inf

  def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs=None):
    current = self.get_monitor_value(logs)
    if current is None:
      return
    if self.monitor_op(current - self.min_delta, self.best):
      self.best = current
      self.wait = 0
      if self.restore_best_weights:
        self.best_weights = self.model.get_weights()
    else:
      self.wait += 1
      if self.wait >= self.patience:
        self.stopped_epoch = epoch
        self.model.stop_training = True
        if self.restore_best_weights:
          if self.verbose > 0:
            print('Restoring model weights from the end of the best epoch.')
          self.model.set_weights(self.best_weights)

  def on_train_end(self, logs=None):
    if self.stopped_epoch > 0 and self.verbose > 0:
      print('Epoch %05d: early stopping' % (self.stopped_epoch + 1))
```

Given that your method is invoked using the same parameters:  c(self, current_step) == on_epoch_end(self, epoch), I have tried to hack it and use on_epoch_end directly, but did not due to type mismatch: int vs dict, not sure from where Int comes from though:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/47124775/89157449-73889c00-d564-11ea-94b6-53f0e247d71d.png)

```
  def get_monitor_value(self, logs):
    logs = logs or {}
    monitor_value = logs.get(self.monitor)
    if monitor_value is None:
      logging.warning('Early stopping conditioned on metric `%s` '
                      'which is not available. Available metrics are: %s',
                      self.monitor, ','.join(list(logs.keys())))
    return monitor_value
```


'

Title: b'peastman'

b"Here's the description of the `callbacks` argument in the API documentation:

>     callbacks: function or list of functions
>      one or more functions of the form f(model, step) that will be invoked after
>      every step.  This can be used to perform validation, logging, etc.

You're trying to pass it a Keras callback object, which is something totally different.  If you want to do early stopping, you can use `dc.models.callbacks.ValidationCallback`."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"This isn't a fix, but here's a code snippet invoking a graph conv layer that works for deepchem-nightly:
```
import numpy as np
import deepchem as dc
from rdkit import Chem
n_atoms = 4  # In CCC and C, there are 4 atoms                             
smiles = ['CCC', 'C']
import rdkit
featurizer = dc.feat.graph_features.ConvMolFeaturizer()
mols = featurizer.featurize(smiles)
multi_mol = dc.feat.mol_graphs.ConvMol.agglomerate_mols(mols)
atom_features = multi_mol.get_atom_features().astype(np.float32)
degree_slice = multi_mol.deg_slice
membership = multi_mol.membership
deg_adjs = multi_mol.get_deg_adjacency_lists()[1:]
args = [atom_features, degree_slice, membership] + deg_adjs
layer = dc.models.layers.GraphConv(64)
result = layer(args)
assert result.shape == (n_atoms, 64)
num_deg = 2 * layer.max_degree + (1 - layer.min_degree)
assert len(layer.trainable_variables) == 2 * num_deg
```

I think what happened here is that GraphConv models are now defined in the Keras subclassing style since they do a non-standard batching in their inputs. This means the old `Input` definitions which worked in TF 1.x don't work for TF2.x and `GraphConv` layers have to be invoked in eager mode as the above shows"

    WARNING:tensorflow:Inconsistent references when loading the checkpoint into this object graph. Either the Trackable object references in the Python program have changed in an incompatible way, or the checkpoint was generated in an incompatible program.

Next it prints the kernel and bias arrays of the graph convolution layers and it looks like the weights of these layers are not loaded. The dense layer weights however are correctly loaded. Could this be related to the eager mode execution?'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"Hmm, this looks like it could be a bug in our reloading code... Would you have a short code snippet I could use to debug? I'll take a look at this and see if I can figure out what's happening here"

Title: b'chstem'
Body:
b'Sure, this is based on Tutorial 4:

### Preparation
Create and fit some `GraphConvModel`

```
import numpy as np
import deepchem as dc
from deepchem.models.graph_models import GraphConvModel

tox21_tasks, tox21_datasets, transformers = dc.molnet.load_tox21(featurizer='GraphConv', reload=False)
train_dataset, valid_dataset, test_dataset = tox21_datasets

n_tasks = len(tox21_tasks)
model = GraphConvModel(n_tasks, batch_size=50, mode='classification')

num_epochs = 10
losses = []
for i in range(num_epochs):
    loss = model.fit(train_dataset, nb_epoch=1)
    print("Epoch %d loss: %f" % (i, loss))
    losses.append(loss)
predictions = model.predict(test_dataset) 
```

### The Problem 
Simulate reloading the model and check if predictions agree. **This will print the mentioned warnings.**

```
model2 = GraphConvModel(n_tasks, batch_size=50, mode='classification', model_dir=model.model_dir)
model2.restore()
predictions2 = model2.predict(test_dataset)
print(np.allclose(predictions, predictions2))  # False
```

### Workaround
A possible workaround is to set the weights of the `GraphConv` layers explicitly. (I currently export them to a separate `.npz` file, but there should be some way to get them from the checkpoint file directly. I just did not want to start digging there. Here I just copy them from the original model which is still available in memory.)
This also requires `model2.model.call()` to be triggered at least once before, but here we already did that with the above `model2.predict(test_dataset)`.

```
gc_weights = [l.get_weights() for l in model.model.graph_convs]
for l, w in zip(model2.model.graph_convs, gc_weights):
    l.set_weights(w)
predictions2 = model2.predict(test_dataset)
print(np.allclose(predictions, predictions2))  # True
```'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"I think what's going on is that this is the same bug as https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/issues/1943. If you save and reload a model within the same script, I think there's a namespace collision that messes up restoration.\r\n\r\nWe need to fix this issue though. I like your workaround! We should figure out how to get a more general reloading fix in place..."

Title: b'chstem'
Body: b'This is the same bug, yes. But this **not** about saving and reloading within the same script! Here I just did this for simple demonstration. But actually I ran into this problem trying to reload the model on a different machine than storing it.'

Body:

```

predictions2 = model2.predict(test_dataset)
print(np.allclose(predictions, predictions2))  # True
```"

Title: b'Unify molecule graph data'
Body:
b'Currently, I seem that there are two data classes, `ConvMol` and `WeaveMol` for a molecule graph and these classes are designed for each specific model (like `ConvMol` <- `GraphConvModel`) 

I think that this situation is not good and we should unify one data class for molecule graph. Generally, all models receive the same graph data class like DGL or PyG. This design leads to make codes more readable and maintainable. 

I recommend DeepChem has only one molecule graph data and all GNN/GCN models receive it. And, current graph data is too complicated, so I also recommend the graph data is simpler like PyG. The PyG design is from [here](https://pytorch-geometric.readthedocs.io/en/latest/notes/introduction.html?highlight=data#data-handling-of-graphs).

For molecule graph, I imagine the data class which holds the following attributes.

- `data.x`: Node feature matrix with shape [num_nodes, num_node_features]
- `data.edge_index`: Graph connectivity in COO format with shape [2, num_edges] and type torch.long
- `data.edge_attr`: Edge feature matrix with shape [num_edges, num_edge_features]
- `data.graph_attr`:Graph feature with shape [1, num_graph_features]
- `data.y`: Target to train against  graph-level targets of shape [1, *]
'

Title: b'Cosine similarity calculation'
Body:
b'I believe the function computing cosine similarity, found in layers.py, does not compute the denominator correctly if y is a matrix instead of a single vector:

** Current code **

```
def _cosine_dist(x, y):
  denom = (backend.sqrt(backend.sum(tf.square(x)) * backend.sum(tf.square(y))) + backend.epsilon())
  return backend.dot(x, tf.transpose(y)) / denom
```

** Possible fix **

```
def _cosine_dist(x, y):
  denom = backend.sqrt(backend.dot(tf.reshape(backend.sum(tf.square(x), axis=1), (-1, 1)), tf.reshape(backend.sum(tf.square(y), axis=1), (1, -1))) + backend.epsilon())
  
  return tf.math.divide(backend.dot(x, tf.transpose(y)), denom)
```

The denominator should not be equal for every computed similarity value. It should be specific for each pair of vectors for which we wish to compute similarity.

Edit by @rbharath: Fixed formatting on code samples'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'@gvisani Thanks for the bugcatch! I think the original function was written assuming `x` and `y` were single vectors and not batched correctly. We should add some unit tests, improve the documentation, and incorporate the above fix. '

Title: b'Parallelizing Transformers'
Body:
b'At present the `Transformer` classes transform datasets as follows. Each `Transformer` defines a `transform_array(X, y, w)` method that transforms one batch of data. The full dataset is transformed by iterating over the dataset shards (for `DiskDataset`) and transforming one shard at a time.

This transformation technique should be easy to parallelize (although we might become IO bound with loading shards from disk perhaps). We should consider parallelizing Transformers. At present, transforming a large dataset is still quite slow.

CC @peastman '

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"Good idea.  Currently `DiskDataset.transform()` works by creating a generator that loads each shard and transforms it.  Then it passes that generator to `create_dataset()`.

https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/3ce0aeebb7ec7fd03765fbcd4ce80b5de3712523/deepchem/data/datasets.py#L1346-L1353

`create_dataset()` iterates over the data provided by the generator and writes each shard to disk.

https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/3ce0aeebb7ec7fd03765fbcd4ce80b5de3712523/deepchem/data/datasets.py#L975-L979

Since Python doesn't let multiple threads run at the same time, we have to use multiple processes instead.  And we don't want to be passing lots of data back and forth between processes, because that's slow.  So we really want all the processing for each shard to be done in a single process: load the current shard, apply the transform, and write the new shard to disk.  It may take a little bit of rearchitecting to make that happen."

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'Do you have any examples where transforming is slow?  I think I have this working, but when I test on various examples I find that transforming never takes more than about a second to begin with, and only a tiny fraction of the time required to load and featurize the dataset.  And in most cases the parallel version is actually slower, because the overhead of spawning processes is greater than the very tiny benefit of doing the transforming in parallel.'

Title: b'Remove verbose kwarg from DeepChem classes and make sure all prints are converted to logging statements'
Body:
b'Earlier versions of DeepChem relied on print statements to log. In particular, we used the following utility function:

```
def log(string, verbose=True):                                  
  """Print string if verbose."""                                
  if verbose:
    print(string)                  
```

And attached the `verbose=True/False` keyword argument to the constructor of classes. This is essentially a rudimentary logging system. I propose we remove the `verbose` flag and swap all instances of this over to using python's `logging` module. This is much friendlier for production use cases since it's possible to control the amount of logging output produced by DeepChem much more easily.

Title: b'Transform multiple fields'

https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/88d8bd25180909ca589bfa7fb0bfbb28b7fc9b3e/deepchem/trans/transformers.py#L108-L111

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"Some transformers only make sense for some fields (`BalancingTransformer` is only defined for `w` for example) so I think this was to fail fast so users didn't try to transform `X` with `BalancingTransformer` (for example). At present, this doesn't take `X, y, w` into account, so a transformer that transformed multiple fields would have an ill-defined `untransform`.\r\n\r\nI think we could fix this easily but making `untransform` have a keyword argument for `X, y, w`. Title: b'Inconsistent method definitions'
Body:
b"As I've started trying to add type annotations, it's uncovered that we've been inconsistent about how we override methods.  A subclass is supposed to always override methods in a way that's consistent with the parent class.  If you don't know the exact type of an object, you should be able to invoke methods using the API defined by the superclass and it should work for any subclass.

For example, Model defines the method `fit(self, dataset, nb_epoch=10, batch_size=50, **kwargs)`.  KerasModel overrides that method and adds a lot of other arguments.  That's ok: the parent class allows for arbitrary extra keyword arguments.  But those first three arguments that are explicitly specified need to be the same, and they aren't.  For KerasModel, the third argument is `max_checkpoints_to_keep` instead of `batch_size`, and in fact there's no `batch_size` argument at all.  That is set by the constructor.  The same is true for `predict()`, and I'll likely encounter others as I go along.

Somehow we need to make these consistent.  I suggest removing the `batch_size` argument from the base class methods.   The default implementations could either rely on `kwargs` to get the batch size, or we could just get rid of the default implementations altogether.  At present we only have three subclasses of Model: KerasModel, SklearnModel, and SingletaskToMultitask.  All three of them already provide their own implementations of `fit()` and `predict()`, and in fact none of them takes a `batch_size` argument, which is a pretty strong indication that it shouldn't be there in the base class. "

Title: b'Improve the flexiblity of molnet function'
Body:
b'Currently, The `load_xxxx` functions in `deepchem.molnet` don't have the flexiblitiy about featurizers and transforms. This sometimes leads to problems.

In my case, I couldn't use the `load_qm9` with `AdjacencyFingerprint ` , so I redefined the load_qm9 function by myself 

https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/82cb9075f16243bbb6c916f52a5ebbd5020b911d/deepchem/molnet/load_function/qm9_datasets.py#L64-L90

In addition to this, currently we can't change the argument values when instantiating `featurizer `.  I wanted to change `max_n_atoms` about `AdjacencyFingerprint` of `load_tox21`, but I couldn't. 

https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/82cb9075f16243bbb6c916f52a5ebbd5020b911d/deepchem/molnet/load_function/tox21_datasets.py#L59-L60

I think the same issues also happened about `transforms`.  Curently, many `load_xxxx` functions standardize the objective values. However, we sometimes want to normalize them, but we can't.


Therefore, I think the arguments of `load_xxxx` functions should accept `deepchem.feat.Featurizer` instances and `deepchem.feat.Transformer` instances. The following code is my thinking.


```python

"""
Tox21 dataset loader.
"""
import os
import logging
import deepchem

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

TOX21_URL = 'http://deepchem.io.s3-website-us-west-1.amazonaws.com/datasets/tox21.csv.gz'
DEFAULT_DIR = deepchem.utils.get_data_dir()

DEFAULT_FEATURIZERS = {
  'Raw': deepchem.feat.RawFeaturizer(),
  'ECFP': deepchem.feat.CircularFingerprint(size=1024),
  'GraphConv': deepchem.feat.ConvMolFeaturizer(),
  'AdjacencyConv': deepchem.feat.AdjacencyFingerprint(max_n_atoms=150, max_valence=6),
  'Weave': deepchem.feat.WeaveFeaturizer(),
  'smiles2img': deepchem.feat.SmilesToImage(img_size=80, img_spec='std'),
}


def load_tox21(featurizer=DEFAULT_FEATURIZERS['ECFP'],
               split='index',
               reload=True,
               K=4,
               data_dir=None,
               save_dir=None,
               **kwargs):
  """Load Tox21 datasets. Does not do train/test split"""
  # Featurize Tox21 dataset

  tox21_tasks = [
      'NR-AR', 'NR-AR-LBD', 'NR-AhR', 'NR-Aromatase', 'NR-ER', 'NR-ER-LBD',
      'NR-PPAR-gamma', 'SR-ARE', 'SR-ATAD5', 'SR-HSE', 'SR-MMP', 'SR-p53'
  ]

  if data_dir is None:
    data_dir = DEFAULT_DIR
  if save_dir is None:
    save_dir = DEFAULT_DIR

  # this is backward compatibility
  if isinstance(featurizer, str):
    featurizer = DEFAULT_FEATURIZERS[featurizer]

    featurizer_name = featurizer.__class__.__name__
    save_folder = os.path.join(save_dir, "tox21-featurized", str(featurizer_name))
    save_folder = os.path.join(save_folder, str(split))

    loaded, all_dataset, transformers = deepchem.utils.save.load_dataset_from_disk(

  dataset_file = os.path.join(data_dir, "tox21.csv.gz")
  if not os.path.exists(dataset_file):
    deepchem.utils.download_url(url=TOX21_URL, dest_dir=data_dir)

  loader = deepchem.data.CSVLoader(
      tasks=tox21_tasks, smiles_field="smiles", featurizer=featurizer)
  dataset = loader.featurize(dataset_file, shard_size=8192)
  ...

Title: b'DeepChem Serving'
Body:
b"At present, there isn't a good way to serve predictions with DeepChem. As DeepChem matures as a codebase, users will want to use it in more production settings. For example, imagine that you've trained a high quality DeepChem solubility model. You might want to deploy this trained model somewhere where it can be queried by users.

I want to kick off a discussion about how we can improve our support for serving DeepChem models. At present, the gold standard for ML serving seems to be TF serving: https://www.tensorflow.org/tfx/serving/architecture. For `KerasModel` we could integrate with TF serving to allow for serving models. However for `SklearnModel` and `XgboostModel` (and eventual `TorchModel`), we'd want to support a uniform serving API.

I don't currently have well formed ideas on what an API could look like, but I'll do more research and report back on this thread once I've thought about it further. In the meanwhile, if you've thought about this, would love input on good API design here.
"

Title: b"Let's remove dc.hyper"

b"The DeepChem hyperpameter module `dc.hyper` is very simple, featuring only simple algorithms for hyper parameter searching. I propose that we remove the `dc.hyper` module and replace all tutorial usages with Ray tune or Keras tuner examples:

Title: b'Distributed KerasModel'
Body:
b"TensorFlow's support for distributed training has improved a lot in the last few releases. The integration with Keras is pretty slick. You simply have to define a strategy as follows:

```
strategy = tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy()
```
and then define the model within the scope of the strategy
```
with strategy.scope():
  model = tf.keras.Sequential([
      tf.keras.layers.Conv2D(32, 3, activation='relu', input_shape=(28, 28, 1)),
      tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(),
      tf.keras.layers.Flatten(),
      tf.keras.layers.Dense(64, activation='relu'),
      tf.keras.layers.Dense(10)
  ])

  model.compile(loss=tf.keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True),
                optimizer=tf.keras.optimizers.Adam(),
                metrics=['accuracy'])
```
I think we could do this in KerasModel. In particular, we could add a `strategy` argument to `KerasModel` and automatically build models within that strategy. This could help us scale to large dataset with multi-GPU training.

What do folks think about this as a proposed feature? CC @peastman "

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"That would be really nice.  I haven't looked into how strategies work.  If we could reuse them, that would be great."

Title: b'Adding DaskDataset'
Body:
b"At present, `DiskDataset` is our workhorse class for large datasets. This class is pretty nicely optimized with a cache and everything, and I've been able to use it on 50GB datasets without too much trouble. However, I'm not sure if it can scale to 1TB+ datasets in its current form.

Luckily for us, the [dask](https://github.com/dask/dask) project has been working to create a distributed python library along with a distributed [dask dataframes](https://tutorial.dask.org/04_dataframe.html). 

I propose that we add a new `DaskDataset` class backed by Dask dataframes. This class would obey the usual Dataset paradigm but should have the ability to scale to larger datasets (potentially at the 1TB+ range). If we want to apply DeepChem on truly large datasets (say those generated from MD simulations, or ultra high throughput combinatorial chemistry assay datasets), this could provide a powerful tool in our users toolboxes. "

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'Maybe create some benchmarks?  Create a very large dataset to see how DiskDataset scales.  Also we should decide exactly what types of scalability we care about.  For applications involving such large amounts of data, will training on a single computer be too slow?  Do we need to be thinking about distributed training at the same time?'

Title: b'Add pysmiles support for loading'
Body: b"Now that deepchem-nightly pip is mostly functional, we face the challenge that deepchem is very functionality limited on a pip install. The reason is that there look to be severe structural issues that mean rdkit can't get a pip install in the foreseeable future (http://rdkit.blogspot.com/2019/11/why-rdkit-isnt-available-on-pypi.html).\r\n\r\nI propose that we use [pysmiles](https://pypi.org/project/pysmiles/) as a back-up loader if rdkit isn't available. Most of our featurizers depend on RDKit, but a user will be able to us models like `TextCNNModel` which don't depend on RDKit featurizers to still do some work."

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'This makes me nervous.  Having two different libraries that can be used to perform the same function is a great way to get inconsistencies in behavior.  At the very least we would need to run the full test suite twice on every PR, once with rdkit and once with pysmiles.  But even then it would be really easy for bugs to get missed.  If all the developers had rdkit installed, they would never encounter problems that come up when using pysmiles instead.'

Title: b'Create abstract superclasses for deep models'
Body: b"We have a number of classes such as `GAN`, `SeqToSeq` that define different types of models with different `fit/predict` methods (`fit_gan` and `fit_sequences`). At present, these classes are defined as inheriting from `KerasModel`. We're now transitioning DeepChem to allow for multiple deep learning frameworks. Given this, we might want to define Torch GANs or SeqToSeq models.\r\n\r\nI propose that we create abstract superclasses which define the DeepChem API for GANs/SeqToSeq/NormalizingFlows/etc. These abstract superclasses will help us enforce a uniform API across different deep learning frameworks."

Title: b'Adding Type Annotations to DeepChem'
Body:
b"The `mypy` toolchain for static annotations has matured a good bit and become a powerful tool for improving the quality of Python codebases. I propose that we start adding type annotations onto the DeepChem codebase. This would involve the following steps:

- Adding a checker to travis for type correctness
- Incrementally adding type signatures to the DeepChem codebase over a series of pull requests.

Luckily, `mypy` is incremental so we don't need to make a transition all at once. I think the best way might be to pick isolated modules or components of DeepChem, add annotations, then proceed outwards as we gain confidence."

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'Sounds like a great idea!'

Title: b'Allow KerasModel to accept tf.keras.optimizers objects directly'
Body: b"At present, `KerasModel` expects specified optimizers to be instances of `dc.models.optimizers.Optimizer`. These are wrappers around `tf.keras.optimizers` optimizers that provide the nice ability to be able to define a `LearningRateSchedule` for your learning rate. \r\n\r\nAt present `KerasModel` throws an error if you try to use it with a `tf.keras.optimizers` optimizer out of the box. I propose that we allow `KerasModel` to direclty accept `tf.keras.optimizers` objects. This is an easier default for beginners who can later define their own `Optimizer` objects if they'd like something more customizable."

Title: b'Inconsistency between Model.reload()/SklearnModel.reload()/KerasModel.restore()'
Body: b"There's an inconsistency between the various reloading methods in DeepChem. `KerasModel` uses `restore()` while `Model` and `SklearnModel` use `reload()`. I propose we settle on a common name for this. I think it would be easier to swap `Model.reload()` to `Model.restore()` since `KerasModel` is the most commonly used DeepChem model."

Title: b'Speed up printing for datasets'
Body: b'For very large datasets, printing the dataset in IPython can be very slow since `dataset.ids` is loaded by using `get_shard()` for all shards. For large datasets, this means features/labels/weights will be unnecessarily loaded which could take a long time. We could speed up this method by providing a facility to load only `dataset.ids` from disk (`X`, `y`, `w`, `ids` are written to disk as separate files for each shard so this should be straightforward to do).\r\n\r\n'

Title: b'Adding PyTorch Models and Layers'
Body:
b'I am going to open a PR for setting up equivalents of our models in PyTorch, under `dc.models.pytorch_models`, with suitable import guards (#1907). 

Before starting the PR, I just wanted to open a general discussion for more feedback and comments. A couple of initial comments:

- I plan to start with the graph models and associated layers, then move to ChemCeption and Transformer based models. These models are more widely used, and also allow us to extend transfer learning support to them. 

- The API of the layers / model should mostly remain unchanged since the main workhorse across `tf.keras` and `torch` is a `model(inputs)` statement. There will be some rewrite around the optimizers since they accept parameters as an initialization argument unlike `tf.keras`. 

I wil keep updating the list with any interesting workarounds or issues as I run into them. I am sure there are functions which behave differently between `tf.keras` and `torch` (an example would be the lack of a `gather_nd` function in `torch`), and one would need wrapper functions to make arguments similar.

@rbharath @peastman @seyonechithrananda @nd-02110114'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'I think we need to decide on an important question: is our goal to have a collection of TensorFlow models *and also* a collection of PyTorch models?  Or is our goal to have one single collection of models, some of which happen to be implemented in TensorFlow and others in PyTorch?\r\n\r\nIf the latter (which is what I would vote for), we should avoid duplication between them.'

Title: b'vsomnath'
Body: b'For the more used models, like `GraphConv` or `Transformers`, it would be useful to have it across both, but for the others, TensorFlow should be more than enough. '

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'What would be the benefit of having two different versions of GraphConvModel?'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"@vsomnath Great, thanks for taking this on! I think this will be really valuable infrastructure to have in place. As an extra addition, I'd suggest ChemProp as another PyTorch model to add. Their work seems to be getting a lot of attention recently.\r\n\r\nI think if there are different features that the PyTorch implementation will have (like better transfer learning support), it might be worth a duplicate implementation. I know there are a lot of graph conv variants available in PyTorch, so it would be really interesting to have some of the variants in PyTorch Geometric that we don't currently support added. I'd also generally prefer avoiding duplication when possible, but perhaps some duplication is unavoidable as needed PyTorch infrastructure."

No problem with that.  What I wouldn't want to see is separate TensorFlowGraphConvModel and PyTorchGraphConvModel classes that implement identical graph structures and differ only in how they're implemented."

Title: b'vsomnath'
Body:
b"Thanks, I'll include the ChemProp model too!

Coming back to variants spread out across TensorFlow and PyTorch, it would be kinda strange to have the newer variants in PyTorch, and the original 4-5 graph models in TensorFlow. Anyone wanting to run them would have to install both PyTorch and TensorFlow for example. To retain backward compatability, it would be useful to keep the existing graph model implementations. But having all graph models in PyTorch would be easier from an installation and usage perspective. Whether the old ones get phased out or not can be decided later.
"

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b'As much as possible, the user shouldn't need to know or care what library a particular model is implemented with.  Nothing appears in their APIs that's TensorFlow specific.  A user should be able to just create a GraphConvModel and have it work.

This does mean users will need to install both TensorFlow and PyTorch, or else some models won't be available.  But that's unavoidable if we choose to use both of them.

We might consider having the import guards provide stub classes that just throw an exception.  First define a class

```python
class TensorFlowStub(object):
  def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
    raise ModuleNotFoundError("The class '%s' cannot be used because TensorFlow is not installed" % type(self).__name__)
```

And then we could write

```python
try:
  import tensorflow
  from deepchem.models.graph_models import GraphConvModel
except:
  class GraphConvModel(TensorFlowStub):
    pass
```'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"I like the idea of stub classes! It helps pin down what class needs TF/PyTorch and makes it easier on users.

+1 for the idea that a user shouldn't need to know what library a model is implemented in. It would be really nice if we had a unifying DeepChem aesthetic that meant users could get pretty far (until they want to implement their own models) without knowing the underlying infrastructure for a particular model class.

My two cents is that we're likely to have both TensorFlow and PyTorch support long-term. I think there are differences in the frameworks which mean that somethings will just be easier in the one or the other."

Title: b'Inconsistent behavior in Dataset.iterbatches()'
Body:
b'`Dataset.iterbatches()` has an argument called `epoch` (note that's singular).  The definition of it is inconsistent between classes.

- The abstract Dataset class defines it as, "Number of epochs to walk over dataset."
- NumpyDataset defines it the same way, but totally ignores it.
- DiskDataset defines it as "Not used" and ignores it.
- ImageDataset doesn't provide documentation on the parameters.  It ignores that one.
- The corresponding method in DataBag defines it as, "Number of times to loop through the datasets," but ignores it.  However, it also checks for an argument called `epochs` (plural) in `kwargs`, and if it finds it, uses that as the number of epochs.

Clearly this is a mess.  I suggest renaming the argument to `epochs` and having all classes actually use it.'

Title: b'Improving Featurization for Large Datasets'
Body:
b"DeepChem has some limitations at present when featurizing large datasets. In particular, here are a couple issues that crop out:

- There's no out-of-the-box way to featurize a large collection of objects that are already in memory. The `DataLoader` classes allow for featurization of large files by walking over them and writing shards to disk with a generator. However, suppose you have say a large collection of smiles strings in a pandas dataframe that you've loaded into memory already. Right now, you'd either need to write these smiles to disk again or write a custom generator for use with `DiskDataset.create_dataset`.
- Large featurization jobs can often fail midway. This can be due to running of memory, timeouts, or many other reasons. There isn't a good way to recover from a partial featurization failure.

Fixing both these issues would make it easier to apply DeepChem to large problems. Here are a couple of suggested changes:

- Let's add an `InMemoryLoader`. This loader accepts raw inputs for featurization (smiles, filenames) directly from in-memory. This will enable easier interoperability with user data processing pipelines. This would work like the other `DataLoader` objects, but instead of loading from a specific filetype, just directly accepts inputs from memory.
- Let's add a `restart` option to `DataLoader` classes. This gets a little complicated to do right, so I have some first thoughts on design:
  - We add a new keyword argument `checkpoint_interval` to the `DataLoader`. Every `checkpoint_interval` inputs, the loader writes a checkpoint `DiskDataset` to disk. This is stored in `dc.utils.get_data_dir()` and is something like `DATADIR/checkpoint_1` (we can add a `checkpoint_name` keyword argument to customize this). 
  - If the featurization job fails midway, you can just run the loader with the same arguments. The loader on starting will check for checkpoints. If checkpoint are available, it will continue from where the last checkpoint left off.

Having this capability would make it much easier to run large structural featurizations on things like PDBBind or process large datasets in general. I'd love any feedback folks have on this design.

CC @peastman @vsomnath "

Title: b'vsomnath'
Body: b'I have to give some thought to the first issue suggestion, but for the second one, I was doing something similar during GSOC last year. The ChEMBL dataset had 1M inputs, and I was checkpointing every `checkpoint_interval` to have something done even if there were memory issues, and could only featurize the remainder incase of an incomplete job.\r\n'

Title: b'AWS S3 for DeepChem'
Body:
b'After speaking to the infrastructure expert at Materials Project, here are some notes I gathered about running an AWS S3 service for an open source project.

- By estimating the storage and traffic requirements, we can ask for promotional credits on an annual basis that may cover the costs: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/opensource/aws-promotional-credits-open-source-projects/
- The owner of the bucket should make an Identity and Access Management (IAM) role to give read/write access to other specific AWS accounts.
- All files should be gzipped, because costs accrue based on the file sizes being stored and transferred.
- Enable "lifecycle management policy," which automatically downgrades objects that aren't accessed frequently and decreases costs.
- AWS includes automatic versioning of datasets.
- Key advantage of AWS S3 is ability to scale if needed.'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'Thanks for the notes! These are great. Setting up IAM roles for access to the DeepChem S3 bucket sounds very doable. Applying for AWS credits would also be very useful.'

Title: b'Multiple Objective Optimization Module'
Body:
b'A common task for DeepChem users is to design a molecule that satisfies a number of different objectives. For example, a user might want to design a molecule that is within a given solubility range, binds tightly to a given target, and does not bind to an antitarget. This isn't straightforward to do since there are multiple objectives. This is an example of the broader class of [multiple objective optimization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-objective_optimization). 

I propose that we add a new `dc.moo` module that provides a general framework for multiparameter optimization in DeepChem. The core of this module would be a new abstract class `MultipleObjectiveOptimizer` that provides an abstract superclass specifying an API for multiple objective optimization problems. The core method for this class would have the following API

```
class MultipleObjectiveOptimizer:
  """Abstract superclass for multiple objective optimization.

  This class contains no implementations but rather specifies the API that must be satisfied by 

  def optimize(objectives, constraints, dataset):
    """The optimize method provides a generic API to frame a multiple objective optimization task.

    Parameters
    ------------
    objectives: list
      Each element of objectives should be a function that that accepts as argument datapoints in `dataset`. The function should return either a binary True/False value or a continuous readout.
    constraints: list
      Each element of `constraints` must be a string that is one of the following values `[True, False, "max", "min"]`. The `constraints` list is processed in order with `objectives`. That is, `constraints[i]` is the constraint for the function `objectives[i]`. If `constraints[i]` is `True` or `False`, this means that `objectives[i]` must be a function that returns binary values and that a solution to the multiple objective optimization problem must take on the corresponding binary value. If `constraints[i]` is "max" or "min", then this means that `objectives[i]` must be real valued and the goal is to either maximize or minimize this objective.
  dataset: dc.data.Dataset (optional, default=None)
      If specified, the dataset to optimize the multiple objectives over. `dataset.X` should contain these elements. `dataset.y`, `dataset.w`, `dataset.ids` don't need to be specified. If `dataset` is specified, `generator` should be `None`.
  generator: `Generator` (optional, default=None)
    If specified, a generator which on each invocation returns a new datapoint. This argument should be specified instead of `dataset` when there is a very large set which is to be optimized over and you don't necessarily want to store the optimized set of disk.

  Returns
  --------
  solutions: list[Tuple]
    Each entry in this list is a pareto optimal point in `dataset`. If no such points exist, `solutions == []`. Each point is a tuple of `(datapoint, values)` where `values` is a list containing the value of `datapoint` on `obectives`.
  """
  raise NotImplementedError
```
There are a few existing python packages for multiple objective optimization such as [platypus](https://platypus.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html). We can wrap `platypus` and other solvers under this API so we have access to the best available tools. However these packages still appear to be relatively immature so we might also have to implement our own mutiple objective solvers. 

One very simpler optimizer could just walk over `dataset` and look for pareto optimal points, where a point is pareto optimal if it's not possible to improve any one objective function without worsening another [wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_efficiency)). (If `generator` is specified, all points up to a given budget `N` could be walked). Note that there are often multiple pareto optimal points, which form a set called the pareto frontier, which is why a list of solutions rather than a single solution is returned.

I'd love any feedback folks have on this proposed design. My hope is that it can become a powerful tool for molecular design when combined with DeepChem modules for solubility, potency, etc. I can take the lead on implementing this feature, but before I get started I want to make sure the design for this module is sensible.
  
CC @peastman @vsomnath @nd-02110114 @seyonechithrananda @lilleswing '

Title: b'Removing SklearnModel'
Body:
b"At present the `SklearnModel` is a simple wrapper around Scikit-learn's API ([file](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/master/deepchem/models/sklearn_models/__init__.py)). We added this wrapper in to make scikit-learn models fit into DeepChem's standard API so we could invoke models the same way regardless of whether they used Scikit-Learn or DeepChem's custom modeling capabilities.

After doing some thought, I'm starting to think we got this original design backwards. Scikit-learn's community is much larger than DeepChem's. It makes more sense that we defer to Scikit-learn's established API when using scikit-learn models. This would mean that users of DeepChem wouldn't have to learn a custom set of classes for using scikit-learn with MoleculeNet classes. 

I'm proposing we make the following changes:

1. Remove `SklearnModel` from DeepChem. This would entail deprecating `SklearnModel` in DeepChem 2.4 and removing it outright from DeepChem 2.5.
2. Swap over all examples and tutorials to use scikit-learn directly instead of using `SklearnModel`. This will require a bit of rewriting of some examples, but should be a limited amount of work and will reduce the cognitive overhead for our users. 

Does this plan make sense to folks? I'd love thoughts and feedback before we make any actual changes

CC @peastman @VIGS25 "

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'That sounds reasonable.'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"Adding a comment here following up on discussion in #1916 

I've been doing a good amount of thinking and I'm less enthusiastic about removing `SklearnModel`. It's a thin wrapper that's straightforward to maintain and it's quite useful in practice. I've been making heavy use of `SklearnModel` recently in a few projects, and the nice thing is that it gives me apples-to-apples metric evaluation with GraphConvModel or other models.

I propose that we instead clean up `SklearnModel` to have clear documentation and just maintain it as a part of the library."

Title: b'Indexing into Datasets for Random Access'
Body:
b'At present, there's no good API to access a random element of a dataset. For example, suppose I have a large `DiskDataset` with 100 million entries, a shard size of 10,000 and I'd like to access the 50 millionth entry. I'd currently have to walk through the full dataset with `iterbatches()` until I reached this element. Here's an alternative proposed API that would be much nicer.

```
>>> dataset = dc.data.DiskDataset.create_dataset(...)
>>> len(dataset)
100000000
>>> dataset[50000000] # Yes this is actually the 50,000,001-th entry
(array([....]), 1.0, 1.0, "50 millionth element label")
```
This can be extended to support slices as well.
```
>>> dataset[50000000:51000000]
(array([...]), array([...]), array([...]), array([...]))
```
One design question here is whether slicing should return a new `Dataset` or numpy arrays. This could potentially be controlled by a user set flag.

I'd love some feedback on this design/idea. CC @peastman @vsomnath '

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'I think this is a good idea.  I suggest the return values should exactly match what you get from `itersamples()`.'

Title: b'Structuring Transfer Learning'
Body:
b"Starting off from Peter's Transfer Learning comments Peter's in #1834, 
> For the transfer learning code, I wonder if we want to make it a bit more generic? As currently written, it feels more like an example than a feature. For example, it's hardcoded to pretrain on one specific dataset. 

The PR included only the ChemNet specific protocol for transfer learning, but it would be useful to have a more general framework. To the best of my knowledge, transfer learning for molecules/chemistry falls along three axes:

1. ChemNet Transfer Learning protocol (https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.02734): Supervised with auxiliary labels
2. BERT Style pretraining using SMILES strings (https://huggingface.co/seyonec/ChemBERTa-zinc-base-v1) : Self-supervised
3. Graph-Based Pretraining (https://openreview.net/forum?id=HJlWWJSFDH) - Self-supervised 

Using this issue to kickoff discussions on this.
"

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"Thanks for kicking off this discussion! I think a couple other variants to consider are 

4. Doing contrastive learning on ChemNet style images. That is, using standard image constrastive learning with chemnet style encoding of images.
5. Using multiple conformations as a data augmentation technique for self-supervised learning as suggested in this forum post (https://forum.deepchem.io/t/molecular-attention-transformers/91/5?u=bharath)

I'm not sure yet what a generic pretraining/transfer learning API should look like. One challenge is that different pretraining methods are tied to different models. ChemNet Transfer is tied to ChemNet (although you can imagine RDKit property pretraining as a general variant), BERT pretraining is tied to transformers, graph-based pretraining to graph convolutions, etc.

Perhaps we can add `pretrain()` as a non-implemented method to the abstract superclass `Model`. Then different subclasses can override this with their own custom pretraining method. This allows different models to support different pretraining modes.

"

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"What exactly would `pretrain()` do?  It would be useful to define the scope of this feature, and what problems it's intended to solve.  What do we really mean by pretraining, beyond simply calling `fit()` twice with two different datasets?"

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b'I think the main difference would be that `pretrain()` could have a different objective function than `fit()`. I think for ChemBERTa style models for example, the `pretrain()` objective would be masked language modeling, while the `fit()` object function would be a standard L2loss or Cross-entropy loss.

Perhaps one way of implementing this would be to allow a model to have multiple objective functions and allow `fit()` to select between them. Then `pretrain()` could just be a convenience wrapper around a suitable `fit()` call.
'

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b'> Perhaps one way of implementing this would be to allow a model to have multiple objective functions and allow fit() to select between them.

`fit()` already allows you to provide an alternate loss function, so that would be very easy.

Is that the only difference?'

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"> This method would be akin to the dc.molnet.load_X methods in that it would query S3 for a set of pretrained weights for this model class and see if there's a set of weights that corresponds to the hyperparameters specified for the class.

I would do it a little differently.  That puts the burden on the user to know the exact values of all hyperparameters for the pretrained model they want, then create a model with exactly those values.  Instead let's have a function that constructs and returns a new model object.

It could even be a single function for all models.  You provide an identifier that specifies the model you want.  It looks up that identifier online and retrieves the information needed to create it.  That would include the name of the model class to create; the values of all arguments to pass to the constructor; and a checkpoint to load the parameters from."

That would include the name of the model class to create; the values of all arguments to pass to the constructor; and a checkpoint to load the parameters from.

I think this is a really good idea. It functions well in practice and has the added ease of use, similar to how Huggingface does it. They allow users to get the config (which contains hyperparameters), tokenizer and model all from the same identifier:

```
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('distilgpt2')   # Initialize tokenizer
model = AutoModelWithLMHead.from_pretrained('distilgpt2')    # Download model and configuration from S3 and cache.

```
