Title: b'Make Jenkins CI Build Server on AWS'
Body:
b"We've had a recurring issue with failing slow tests (as #1902) notes. The main reason for these failures is that we can't run the full test suite regularly. To solve this issue, we need a way to automatically run the full test suite on a regular basis. Here are a couple thoughts on how we could do this:

1) We can upgrade to a paid plan on Travis-CI. This starts at $69/month. This caps builds at 2 hours.
2) Set up a custom Jenkins build server on AWS (https://aws.amazon.com/getting-started/hands-on/setup-jenkins-build-server/). Amazon estimates this will cost $89/month, but in return we get unlimited build times and control over the environment. We could trigger a build on this server upon each PR using a webhook.

I'm willing to cover the bill for either of these options. Given that, which one should we go for? I'm leaning towards the Jenkins build server since that will give us more control over the process. I think that while we're setting up the build-server, we can configure it so we get nightly pip/conda/docker builds for deepchem which we can push up to AWS. I can also set up a jenkins build server to run MoleculeNet benchmarks. This will have to run less often due to the cost, but we can start to track benchmark numbers on a weekly basis at least.

What do folks think? CC @peastman @lilleswing "

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"What about just running them by hand once every month or so?  It only takes about an hour, maybe less, so it's not hard.  We just have to remember to do it.  We also should establish that running the full test suite on all supported operating systems is part of creating a release."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"Running by hand is a good start for sure! The only concern I have there is forgetting to run the tests. We'd need some system to track the runs (or just be careful to keep track of it ourselves)\r\n\r\nAnother alternative might be to set up a cron job on AWS as a scheduled task (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/scheduled_tasks.html). If this is done once a month, then cost should be quite low since we're not using that much compute."

Title: b'Adding User Defined Graph Features'
Body:
b"One feature request that has come up a couple times is the ability to add user defined graph features. That is, the user has some method of defining per-atom (or per-bond) features for a molecule and they would like to combine this with one of the existing graph convolutional featurizers. Perhaps this could be called `UserDefinedGraphFeaturizer` or something like that.

One road-block to doing this is that different graph convolutions don't have a common API. Ideally, there would be a clear way to great a generic `UserDefinedGraphFeaturizer` that works for both `GraphConvModel` and `WeaveModel`.

CC @peastman @Jiang-Lu-CAS"

Title: b'Make TensorFlow an optional dependency'

b"Current TensorFlow is a hard dependency for DeepChem. I think we should swap TensorFlow to a soft dependency like RDKit. The main reason for this is that as repos like [torchchem](https://github.com/deepchem/torchchem) and [jaxchem](https://github.com/deepchem/jaxchem) mature, they will likely use deepchem's core features (datasets, splitters, featurizers, transformers, hyperparameter optimization). Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"I thought the plan was that we would split out everything that isn't specific to TensorFlow (datasets, featurizures, transformers, etc.) into the molnet repo, and DeepChem would be left with all the TensorFlow specific parts."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"Right now, the code is pretty tightly coupled, so it's hard to do a split like that cleanly. I tried in https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/pull/1780 / https://github.com/deepchem/moleculenet/pull/4 to split out moleculenet but the set of changes got really gnarly and I backtracked from it. 

I've been doing a bit of thinking about design in the last few weeks and I have a couple of thoughts on possible directions:

- ***Original Plan:*** Move (datasets, featurizers, transformers, etc.) to molnet repo, and keep TensorFlow specific parts in deepchem.
  - ***Pros:*** By our original design, MoleculeNet becomes the shared resource that multiple downstream packages like deepchem/torchchem/jaxchem use.
  - ***Cons:*** This looks like it will be a very gnarly change that will be a ton of work. Plus, lots of people use DeepChem for things like splitters/featurizers already. These people will need to all shift to using molnet instead. Even if we phase in this change gradually, it's a large effort.
-  ***Alternative Plan:*** Keep (datasets, featurizers, transformers, etc.) in DeepChem repo. Make TensorFlow a soft dependency for 2.4 release, and possibly move TensorFlow codebase to a new tensorchem repo in 2.5+. The idea is that the core deepchem repo becomes ML framework agnostic and other repos like jaxchem/torchchem/tensorchem provide models in different frameworks. The molnet repo will only contain actual dataset loaders and not (datasets, featurizers, transformers, etc.) in this framing.
    - ***Pros:*** Less code has to move since most of DeepChem's modules stay where they are. This is also more or less the same as the original molnet plan, with the difference that the framework-agnostic repo is deepchem instead of molnet.
    - ***Cons:*** This will require some effort now to make TF a soft dependency and eventually to factor out TF parts into separate repo. Users will need to get used to using tensorchem/torchchem/etc for models. 

What do you folks think? I think the gnarliness of my first attempted refactoring pushed me a bit away from the original design to this alternate framing, but I'm pretty open to whatever design direction ends up making the most sense."

Body:
b'- DeepChem Version: 2.3
- Platform: Linux

I ran across some issues discussed in this issues, regarding the smiles environments of size 1 and was wondering, if it should be implemented in deepchem
https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/issues/897

I commented there, but I think it probably is going to get lost, since the issue is already closed.
The problem is that environments with radius 0 don't create smiles, but they might be relevant for interpretation purposes nonetheless. My propose solution would be:

>   def _featurize(self, mol):
    """
    Calculate circular fingerprint.

    Parameters
    ----------
    mol : RDKit Mol
        Molecule.
    """
    from rdkit import Chem
    from rdkit.Chem import rdMolDescriptors
    if self.sparse:
      info = {}
      fp = rdMolDescriptors.GetMorganFingerprint(
          mol,
          self.radius,
          useChirality=self.chiral,
          useBondTypes=self.bonds,
          useFeatures=self.features,
          bitInfo=info)
      fp = fp.GetNonzeroElements()  # convert to a dict

      # generate SMILES for fragments
      if self.smiles:
        fp_smiles = {}
        for fragment_id, count in fp.items():
          root, radius = info[fragment_id][0]
          if radius == 0:
            atom = mol.GetAtomWithIdx(root)
            aromatic = atom.GetIsAromatic()
            symbol = atom.GetSymbol()
            if aromatic:
                symbol = symbol.lower()
            smiles = "[" + symbol + "]"
          else:
            env = Chem.FindAtomEnvironmentOfRadiusN(mol, radius, root)
            frag = Chem.PathToSubmol(mol, env)
            smiles = Chem.MolToSmiles(frag)
          fp_smiles[fragment_id] = {'smiles': smiles, 'count': count}
        fp = fp_smiles
    else:
      fp = rdMolDescriptors.GetMorganFingerprintAsBitVect(
          mol,
          self.radius,
          nBits=self.size,
          useChirality=self.chiral,
          useBondTypes=self.bonds,
          useFeatures=self.features)
    return fp


In addition I would be interested in extracting fragments associated with bits in the neural fingerprint layer of graph conv networks. (In the Duvenaud Neural Fingerprint paper they extracted the features, but I wasn't able to identify how that worked) Do you have an idea how that could be done?


best regards
Tobias'

    for fp_ix in range(params['fp_length']):

        combined_list = []
        for radius in all_radii:

        for fig_ix in range(num_figs_per_fp):

Title: b'KacperKubara'
Body:
b'Ah, I think I have figured it out (more or less). I need this stuff for my undergrad dissertation so I could spend some time on it :) The key to understand what's happening here are `atom_activations` and how do they relate to the paper. Before that though, let's have a look at the following part of the code:
``` Python
   # For each fingerprint bit
    for fp_ix in range(params['fp_length']):
        print "FP {0} has linear regression coefficient {1}".format(fp_ix, last_layer_weights[fp_ix][0])
        combined_list = []
        # For each radius counted from the most-activating atom
        # all_radii is defined as params['fp_depth'] + 1 where fp_depth is a layer depth
        for radius in all_radii:
            # Take atom activations for the specifc radius and fingerpint bit
            # Why do we take radius like it? -> Because the layer depth is related to the neighbourhood radius (look at the paper)
            # if the layer is deeper that means that we take information from a neighbourhood with a bigger radius
            fp_activations = atom_activations[radius][:, fp_ix] 
            # Create a list of activations for each radius
            combined_list += [(fp_activation, atom_ix, radius) for atom_ix, fp_activation in enumerate(fp_activations)]

        unique_list = remove_duplicates(combined_list, key_lambda=lambda x: x[0])
        # Sort by decreasing activation
        combined_list = sorted(unique_list, key=lambda x: -x[0])

        for fig_ix in range(num_figs_per_fp):
            # Find the most-activating atoms for specific fingerprint bit, across all molecules and depths (radius).
            activation, most_active_atom_ix, cur_radius = combined_list[fig_ix]
            # Take a molecule to which the most_active_atom_ix ID belongs
            most_activating_mol_ix = parent_molecule_dict[most_active_atom_ix]
            # Get the neighbouring atom within a certain radius to most_active_atom_ix 
            highlight_list_our_ixs = get_neighborhood_ixs(array_rep, most_active_atom_ix, cur_radius)
            # Just some conversion for RDKit
            highlight_list_rdkit = [array_rep['rdkit_ix'][our_ix] for our_ix in highlight_list_our_ixs]

            print "radius:", cur_radius, "atom list:", highlight_list_rdkit, "activation", activation
            # fp_ix is a fingerprint bit
            # fig_ix controls how many molecule substructures we want to find for fp_ix
            # fig_ix=0 has the biggest activation value, fig_ix=num_figs_per_fp the smallest activation value
            draw_molecule_with_highlights(
                "figures/fp_{0}_highlight_{1}.jpg".format(fp_ix, fig_ix),
                train_smiles[most_activating_mol_ix],
                highlight_atoms=highlight_list_rdkit)
```
#### General understanding of the code above
I've added some comments here to understand what's going on. Basically what I think is happening here:

1. For each fingerprint bit:

- We take `atom_activations` for the specifc _fp_ bit and for varying radius which defines the neighbourhood of the most activated atom. Radius is basically a layer depth of the network which is also explained in the paper: 

> The size of the substructures represented by each index depends on the depth of the network. Thus the number of layers is referred to as the radius of the fingerprints.

In other words, we take activations for specific _fp_ bit across all network layers.

- Then is just a matter of transforming the data to plot it (more details in the comments). We basically take top _k_ molecule substructures with the highest activations for specific fingerprint bit.

### Now, what the  is the `atom_activations` ?!
Code below is responsible for generating those enigmatic `atom_activations`:
``` Python
    def output_layer_fun_and_atom_activations(weights, smiles):
        """Computes layer-wise convolution, and returns a fixed-size output."""
        # This code will compute these activations for all molecules that were passed at once
        # Handy function to generate all  molecular features for us
        array_rep = array_rep_from_smiles(tuple(smiles))
        atom_features = array_rep['atom_features']
        bond_features = array_rep['bond_features']

        all_layer_fps = []
        atom_activations = []
        def write_to_fingerprint(atom_features, layer):
            # Output weights for specific layer
            cur_out_weights = parser.get(weights, ('layer output weights', layer))
            # Output bias for specific layer
            cur_out_bias    = parser.get(weights, ('layer output bias', layer))
            # Apply softmax after a linear layer - im not certain what are the dimensions
            atom_outputs = softmax(cur_out_bias + np.dot(atom_features, cur_out_weights), axis=1)
            # We get activations for specifc layer for all molecules
            # I think we got activations that have fp size for a certain radius (layer depth)
            atom_activations.append(atom_outputs)
            # We are not interested in this stuff below -> we dont use that in the code for plotting
            # Sum over all atoms within a moleclue:
            layer_output = sum_and_stack(atom_outputs, array_rep['atom_list'])
            all_layer_fps.append(layer_output)

        num_layers = len(num_hidden_features)
        # For layer depth (radius of neighbourhood)
        for layer in xrange(num_layers):
            # Get the atom_activations for specific radius for all molecules
            write_to_fingerprint(atom_features, layer)
            # Propagate the results to another layer (???)
            atom_features = update_layer(weights, layer, atom_features, bond_features, array_rep,
                                         normalize=normalize)
        write_to_fingerprint(atom_features, num_layers)
        return sum(all_layer_fps), atom_activations, array_rep
```
#### General understanding of the code above

1. Get atom features for molecules that we passed as an argument
1. For each layer (neighbourhood radius):
- Get bias and weight for layer
- Apply linear layer and then softmax function to get atom_outputs (I believe that size should be (fp_size, molecule_count) but I might be wrong)
- Append the output to `atom_activations`
- Use `update_layer()` to pass the values to another layer
3. Return the atom_activations

So hopefully my small essay will make the code more clear. The code is quite difficult to understand so please bear in mind that is possible that I've made a mistake somewhere.'

Title: b'Compute Atomic Convolutions only on Contact Regions'
Body:
b"The atomic convolutions currently take in an entire protein-ligand complex. This makes working with them very gnarly since proteins get large (tens of thousands of atoms easily). Since the coordinates of the entire protein are handled, the tensors we need to handle in GPU memory get really large really quickly. This means that in practice, training an atomic convolution isn't really feasible unless you pre-restrict to binding pockets. This is feasible on PDBBind where binding pocket PDBs are available, but isn't easy for general structures.

I've been experimenting with a few different ideas for improving this situation and think I've come up with a fairly simple hack. Start by computing the pairwise distance matrix between the protein and the ligand. Prune out all protein atoms which aren't within some contact radius of the ligand (say 4.5 Angstroms, but this can be set by the user). This drastically reduces the number of atoms which need to be handled in featurization numpy arrays and tensorflow tensors. The advantage of this hack is that we no longer need to manually specify a binding pocket since the contact region implicitly delineates a contact region. We also can handle much larger proteins since the only computation that considers the full protein is the pairwise distance computation which can be done with `scipy`

I've implemented this within `AtomicConvFeaturizer` in #1792. I'm still experimenting with it. So far featurization seems to be a good bit faster in addition to saving memory."

Title: b'Generalize AtomicConvModel to handle a list of fragments'
Body:
b"At present, the code for `AtomicConvModel` and its associated `ComplexNeighborListFragmentAtomicCoordinates` featurizer is really messy. A big part of this has to do with the explicit handling of protein/ligand atoms. This leads to a lot of explicit handling of quantities such as `frag1_coords`, `frag2_coords`, `frag1_neighbor_list`, `frag2_neighbor_list` etc.

I propose we clean this by generalizing `AtomicConvModel` and `ComplexNeighborListFragmentAtomicCoordinates` to just take in a list of fragments. Then we can clean up the code by just using a list.

In addition, the ability to handle a list of `N` coordinates means we gain some powerful new biophysical capabilities since we can run atomic convolutions on larger complexes with multiple molecules rather than the restricted protein-ligand case that we handle now.

What do folks think? This is a companion proposal to #1798. I'm currently working on creating some good examples for `AtomicConvModel` and finding it hard because the code is messy and not ergonomic. Some refactoring along the lines of this PR and #1798 could make it much nicer.

CC @peastman @vsomnath "

Title: b'Refactor RdkitGridFeaturizer Implementation'
Body:
b'`RdkitGridFeaturizer` is a very complicated class. It has a whole range of options which allow for the computation of different features on macromolecular input data (such as PDBBind data). However, the many options are poorly documented and the current implementation is very hard to work with. It's a giant jumble of code that isn't modular or easily modifiable.

I propose that the constituent features of `RdkitGridFeaturizer` be factored out into their own featurizer classes. Here are the new featurizer classes that would result

- `ContactCircularFingerprint`: Computes a concatenated ECFP fingerprint of the regions of two molecules that are in close contact. So for a ligand and its binding pocket on a protein, it computes a ligand circular fingerprint, a protein binding pocket circular fingerprint and concatenates them. This corresponds to the 'ecfp_hashed' feature current computed by `RdkitGridFeaturizer`. The output for a complex is a vector of length `2*size` where `size` is the circular fingerprint size.
- `ContactCircularVoxelizer`: Computes a tensor of shape `(voxels_per_edge, voxels_per_edge, voxels_per_edge, size)` where `voxels_per_edge=int(box_width/voxel_width)` is the number of voxels per edge of the box around the macromolecular complex which is featurized. This corresponds to the 'ecfp' feature current computed by `RdkitGridFeaturizer`.
- `SplifFingerprint`: Compute a "SPLIF" fingerprint of a protein-ligand complex. This corresponds to feature 'splif_hashed' computed currently by `RdkitGridFeaturizer`. This produces a vector of length `2*size` for a macromolecular complex. This is conceptually pretty similar to `ContactCircularFingerprint` but computes ECFP fragments only for direct contacts instead of the entire contact region.
- `SplifVoxelizer`: Compute a "SPLIF" voxel grid of shape `(voxels_per_edge, voxels_per_edge, voxels_per_edge, size)`.  Corrresponds to 'splif' feature for current `RdkitGridFeaturizer`.
- `ChargeVoxelizer`: Computes the gasteiger partial charges for atoms in the provided macromolecular complex. Produces a tensor of shape `(voxels_per_edge, voxels_per_edge, voxels_per_edge, 1)` which computes the local partial charge at each voxel. Corresponds to 'charge' feature of `RdkitGridFeaturizer`
- `HydrogenBondCounter`: Counts the number of hydrogen bond interactions. Produces a scalar count of shape `(1,)` which computes the total number of hydrogen interactions in the complex. Corresponds to 'hbond_count' feature of `RdkitGridFeaturizer`.
- `SaltBridgeVoxelizer`: Counts salt-bridge interactions. Produces a tensor of shape `(voxels_per_edge, voxels_per_edge, voxels_per_edge, 1)` which computes the number of salt bridges in each voxel. Corresponds to 'salt_bridge' feature of `RdkitGridFeaturizer`.
- `CationPiVoxelizer`: Counts the number of cation-Pi interactions. Produces a tensor of shape `(voxels_per_edge, voxels_per_edge, voxels_per_edge, 1)` which computes the number of cation-Pi in each voxel. Corresponds to 'cation_pi' feature of `RdkitGridFeaturizer`.
- `PiStackVoxelizer`: Counts the number of Pi-Pi/Pi-T interactions. Produces a tensor of shape `(voxels_per_edge, voxels_per_edge, voxels_per_edge, 2)` which computes the number of Pi-Pi /Pi-T interactions in each voxel. Corresponds to 'pi_stack' feature of `RdkitGridFeaturizer`.
- `HydrogenBondVoxelizer`: Counts the number of hydrogen bonds interactions. Produces a tensor of shape `(voxels_per_edge, voxels_per_edge, voxels_per_edge, 1)` which computes the number of hydrogen interactions in each voxel. Corresponds to 'hbond' feature of `RdkitGridFeaturizer`.

I've implemented most of these changes in #1792. The resulting code is much cleaner and much easier to reason about. In this model the external API for `RdkitGridFeaturizer` is unchanged, but it's possible to invoke the substituent featurizers independently. Under the hood, `RdkitGridFeaturizer` now just invokes the correct combination of substituent featurizers to do its work. 

Access to these featurizers as first class objects may be of its own scientific value since it will be possible to experiment with different featurizers and use combinations for different problems. Exposing the voxelizers explicitly will also make it easier to experiment with 3D convnets for analyzing macromolecular complexes.'

Title: b'Fixing Seed Handling in Splitters'
Body:
b"At present, the `Splitter` classes don't do a clean job of handling seeds. All functions accept a `seed` argument. This should be used to control the sources of randomness (which is `np.random`). However in many places, the seed isn't set. In addition, having every function accept the seed means that there are strange possibilities for error if one call includes a seed and another doesn't.

I propose that instead of function-level seed handling, we pass the seed into the constructor. Here's an example under this API:

```
splitter = dc.splits.ScaffoldSplitter(seed=123)                        
train, valid, test = splitter.train_valid_test_split(dataset)
```

This matches the seed handling in `dc.models.KerasModel` which also controls seeds in the constructor. I've implemented this change in #1792. It nicely cleans up a lot of the seed handling code since you can basically handle it once in the superclass constructor and have it be handled correctly throughout. I'm hoping this also fixes some of our reproducibility issues with MoleculeNet benchmarks. I think bad seed handling was causing splits that didn't reproduce  "

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"Can you point to the particular changes in #1792?  It's a huge PR affecting hundreds of files, and I can't find them."

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"To correctly handle different seeds in different places, it's important that we have separate random generators for them.  If you create a splitter with a particular seed, it should always produce the same results regardless of what unrelated functions you call in between.  If everything shares the same default generator that won't be the case.  So each splitter that uses random numbers should create a new generator with `np.random.RandomState(seed)` in its constructor, then use it instead of the default generator."

Title: b'Pretty Print for Dataset Objects'
Body:
b'Beginners have trouble working with our `Dataset` objects in part because they're opaque. Here's how a `Dataset` object prints on the REPL:

```
>>> dc.data.NumpyDataset(np.random.rand(5,5))
<deepchem.data.datasets.NumpyDataset at 0x1a454f3a20>
```

I propose that we add pretty printers for dataset objects. Here's my proposed simple pretty printer:

```
  def __repr__(self):
      return "<%s X.shape: %s, y.shape: %s, w.shape: %s, ids: %s, task_names: %s>" % (self.__class__.__name__, str(self.X.shape), str(self.y.sh
ape), str(self.w.shape), self.ids.__repr__(), self.get_task_names())
 
  def __str__(self):                                                   
      return "<%s X.shape: %s, y.shape: %s, w.shape: %s, ids: %s, task_names: %s>" % (self.__class__.__name__, str(self.X.shape), str(self.y.sh
ape), str(self.w.shape), self.ids.__repr__(), self.get_task_names())
```

It prints shapes for the features, but prints the id arrays outright. This makes things like splitters work very nicely. Here's the output of a simple scaffold splitting script:

```
Original set of molecules
['C1=CC2=C(C=C1)C1=CC=CC=C21', 'O=C1C=CC(=O)C2=C1OC=CO2', 'C1=C[N]C=C1', 'C1=CC=CC=C[C+]1', 'C1=[C]NC=C1', 'N[C@@H](C)C(=O)O', 'N[C@H](C)C(=O)O', 'CC', 'O=C=O', 'C#N', 'CCN(CC)CC', 'CC(=O)O', 'C1CCCCC1', 'c1ccccc1']
Training set

       'CCN(CC)CC', 'CC(=O)O', 'c1ccccc1', 'C1CCCCC1', 'C1=[C]NC=C1',
       'C1=CC=CC=C[C+]1'], dtype=object), task_names: [0]>
Valid set
<NumpyDataset X.shape: (1,), y.shape: (1, 1), w.shape: (1, 1), ids: array(['C1=C[N]C=C1'], dtype=object), task_names: [0]>
Test set
<NumpyDataset X.shape: (2,), y.shape: (2, 1), w.shape: (2, 1), ids: array(['O=C1C=CC(=O)C2=C1OC=CO2', 'C1=CC2=C(C=C1)C1=CC=CC=C21'],
      dtype=object), task_names: [0]>
```

Notice how it's very clear which compounds are in which split with the pretty print enabled. The downside of this printer is that printing a large dataset can get unwieldy with all the ids printed.

I'd like some feedback on this proposed pretty print design. Are there ways we can make this print more robust or configurable? Are there other things we might want to add to have a well featured pretty-printer? 

CC @peastman @vsomnath '

Body:
b'I see, it should be a part of the next release. Meanwhile, you can just subclass `GraphConvModel` and add an extra function that mimics this (example below): 

https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/51f426b3b6acb876703e49d24ef4f16cb0b44b43/deepchem/models/graph_models.py#L617

```
class UpdatedGraphConv(GraphConvModel):
     def get_graph_feature(self, inputs, training=False):
           atom_features = inputs[0]
           degree_slice = tf.cast(inputs[1], dtype=tf.int32)
           membership = tf.cast(inputs[2], dtype=tf.int32)
           n_samples = tf.cast(inputs[3], dtype=tf.int32)
           deg_adjs = [tf.cast(deg_adj, dtype=tf.int32) for deg_adj in inputs[4:]]

           in_layer = atom_features
           for i in range(len(self.model.graph_convs)):
             gc_in = [in_layer, degree_slice, membership] + deg_adjs
             gc1 = self.model.graph_convs[i](gc_in)
             if self.model.batch_norms[i] is not None:
               gc1 = self.model.batch_norms[i](gc1, training=training)
            if training and self.model.dropouts[i] is not None:
               gc1 = self.model.dropouts[i](gc1, training=training)
            gp_in = [gc1, degree_slice, membership] + deg_adjs
            in_layer = self.model.graph_pools[i](gp_in)
          dense = self.model.dense(in_layer)
          if self.model.batch_norms[-1] is not None:
            dense = self.model.batch_norms[-1](dense, training=training)
          if training and self.model.dropouts[-1] is not None:
            dense = self.model.dropouts[1](dense, training=training)
          neural_fingerprint = self.model.graph_gather([dense, degree_slice, membership] +
                                           deg_adjs)
          return neural_fingerprint
```

```python

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body:
b'So the way I am reading your code you are storing y_pred and y_true over and over in a loop
Toxcast has 8598 molecules over 618 tasks.  It is a categorical task so each task is one hot encoded to 2 integers.  An integer is 24 bytes in pure python.

```python
8598 * 618 * 24 * 2 * 2 / (1042* 1042) # ~487
# molecules * tasks * bytes per int * one_hot_encoding * y_pred, y_true / (bytes in megabyte)
```
So each loop you are loading ~ 500mb into RAM.
Flush y_pred and y_true to disk on each run.'

Title: b'zealseeker'
Body:
b'Hi @lilleswing .  It is not caused by `y_trues` and `y_preds` I think. In each loop I just save the predictions of one compound. The final `y_preds` and `y_trues` should only occupy `1000 * 617 * 24 * 2` bytes, where 1000 is the number of compounds in "validation set".
Even if I tried removing the "y_true" and "y_pred" sentences, the issue still existed.

I'll try to use multiprocessing module to run each loop. (I still doubt that the model leads to memory leak)'

Title: b'Optimizing loading datasets'
Body:
b"As part of my efforts to improve the speed of GraphConvModel, I've been profiling some of our example scripts.  I discovered that nearly half the time is actually spent loading shards, not in anything to do with the model.  I'd like to see if we can improve this.

One obvious solution is to cache shards in memory rather than reloading them every time.  DiskDataset is designed to let you work with datasets that are too big to fit in memory.  But in practice a lot of datasets are quite small and could easily fit in memory.  The challenge, though, is figuring out how much we can safely cache.  It's too bad Python doesn't support soft references, since they'd be perfect for this.  Any thoughts about this?

Digging a little deeper, I see that almost all the loading time is actually spent in numpy_pickle.py.  We store shards in `.joblib` files, which store data in pickled format.  Pickling is really slow.  Would it be possible to switch to `.npy` files instead?  I haven't tested yet, but I suspect that would be a lot faster.  What was the reason for choosing this format?"

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'Based on some preliminary testing, loading a shard stored in a .npy file seems to be about 2-3 times faster than loading one stored in a .joblib file.'

Title: b'vsomnath'
Body: b'Do you think h5py provides a neat way to do soft referencing? - http://docs.h5py.org/en/stable/refs.html'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"I don't think that's the same thing.  That appears to be a way of referencing data stored in a file.  We want references to data in memorywe can always reload it if necessary.  The goal is to keep it in memory as long as possible and only garbage collect it if absolutely necessary."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"I'm not sure why we chose `joblib`. I think the reason might have been that the first version of the `DiskDataset` class used pickling directly and we swapped to `joblib` since it was more robust.\r\n\r\nI think swapping to `.npy` files could be quite sensible for the speed improvements. If we can keep backwards compatible support for loading old `.joblib` files but move to `.npy` as the new default, this could be a pretty smooth transition. I'd be in favor of the shift if it helps speed things up!"

from __future__ import division
from __future__ import print_function
from __future__ import unicode_literals

import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf
import deepchem as dc
from deepchem.models import GraphConvModel

from deepchem.models.tensorgraph.layers import Feature
from deepchem.models.tensorgraph.tensor_graph import TensorGraph
from deepchem.models.tensorgraph.layers import Dense, GraphConv, BatchNorm
from deepchem.models.tensorgraph.layers import GraphPool, GraphGather
from deepchem.models.tensorgraph.layers import Dense, SoftMax, SoftMaxCrossEntropy, WeightedError, Stack
from deepchem.models.tensorgraph.layers import Label, Weights
from deepchem.metrics import to_one_hot
from deepchem.feat.mol_graphs import ConvMol

tox21_tasks, tox21_datasets, transformers = dc.molnet.load_tox21(featurizer='GraphConv')
train_dataset, valid_dataset, test_dataset = tox21_datasets
tg = TensorGraph(use_queue=False)

atom_features = Feature(shape=(None, 75))
degree_slice = Feature(shape=(None, 2), dtype=tf.int32)
membership = Feature(shape=(None,), dtype=tf.int32)

deg_adjs = []
for i in range(0, 10 + 1):
    deg_adj = Feature(shape=(None, i + 1), dtype=tf.int32)
    deg_adjs.append(deg_adj)

batch_size = 50

gc1 = GraphConv(64,activation_fn=tf.nn.relu,in_layers=[atom_features, degree_slice, membership] + deg_adjs)
batch_norm1 = BatchNorm(in_layers=[gc1])
gp1 = GraphPool(in_layers=[batch_norm1, degree_slice, membership] + deg_adjs)
gc2 = GraphConv(64,activation_fn=tf.nn.relu,in_layers=[gp1, degree_slice, membership] + deg_adjs)
batch_norm2 = BatchNorm(in_layers=[gc2])
gp2 = GraphPool(in_layers=[batch_norm2, degree_slice, membership] + deg_adjs)
dense = Dense(out_channels=128, activation_fn=tf.nn.relu, in_layers=[gp2])
batch_norm3 = BatchNorm(in_layers=[dense])
readout = GraphGather(batch_size=batch_size,
                      activation_fn=tf.nn.tanh,
                      in_layers=[batch_norm3, degree_slice, membership] + deg_adjs)

costs = []
labels = []
for task in range(len(tox21_tasks)):
    classification = Dense(out_channels=2, activation_fn=None, in_layers=[readout])

    softmax = SoftMax(in_layers=[classification])
    tg.add_output(softmax)

    label = Label(shape=(None, 2))
    labels.append(label)
    cost = SoftMaxCrossEntropy(in_layers=[label, classification])
    costs.append(cost)
    
all_cost = Stack(in_layers=costs, axis=1)
weights = Weights(shape=(None, len(tox21_tasks)))
loss = WeightedError(in_layers=[all_cost, weights])
tg.set_loss(loss)

def data_generator(dataset, epochs=1, predict=False, pad_batches=True):
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        if not predict:
            print('Starting epoch %i' % epoch)
        for ind, (X_b, y_b, w_b, ids_b) in enumerate(dataset.iterbatches(
                batch_size, pad_batches=pad_batches, deterministic=True)):
            d = {}
            for index, label in enumerate(labels):
                d[label] = to_one_hot(y_b[:, index])
            d[weights] = w_b
            multiConvMol = ConvMol.agglomerate_mols(X_b)
            d[atom_features] = multiConvMol.get_atom_features()
            d[degree_slice] = multiConvMol.deg_slice
            d[membership] = multiConvMol.membership
            for i in range(1, len(multiConvMol.get_deg_adjacency_lists())):
                d[deg_adjs[i - 1]] = multiConvMol.get_deg_adjacency_lists()[i]
            yield d
            
tg.fit_generator(data_generator(train_dataset, epochs=5))

```

Title: b'Cleanup DataLoader Public API'
Body:
b"The `dc.data.data_loader` module has a number of helper functions which it uses in the various `DataLoader` subclasses. These functions are currently public, but they were never really designed to be used outside this module. I propose we change these to be private helper functions. Here are the functions in particular I propose making private:

- `convert_df_to_numpy` -> `_convert_df_to_numpy`
- `featurize_smiles_df` -> `_featurize_smiles_df`
- `featurize_smiles_np` -> `_featurize_smiles_np`
- `featurize_mol_df` -> `_featurize_mol_df`

I'm working towards getting nice DeepChem docs generated, so cleaning up the names and making it clear these are helper methods and not part of the external API would be good."

Title: b'Enable MoleculeNet Loaders to use arbitrary Featurizers and Splitters'
Body:
b"One of the limitations of MoleculeNet loaders is that `featurizer` and `split` are provided as strings. This means that users can't use a MoleculeNet loader function to featurize a MoleculeNet dataset with a different featurization if desired. I propose that we allow `featurizer` and `split` to be `Featurizer` and `Splitter` objects. These will be used to featurize the dataset if specified.

MoleculeNet loaders also store featurized datasets in `DEEPCHEM_DATA_DIR`. To get an easy directory name for a dataset with a custom featurizer/splitter, I propose we use the string representation proposed in https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/issues/1829. For example, this could create directories like
```
Delauney_CircularFingerprint_size_1024_radius_4_RandomSplitter_train_80_valid_10_test_10/
```
The advantage of this is that even years later it will be very clear how this MoleculeNet dataset was featurized."

tox21_tasks, tox21_datasets, transformers = dc.molnet.load_tox21()

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body:
b'@zalperst yes a zero weight indicates that the given y value does not have an experimental result.

As regards to duplicates all I can say is "this is the data we have".
There are many reasons why duplicate smiles may happen in a dataset.
* multiple tautomers
* race-mixes
* undefined stereo
* multiple experimental runs on the same compound

Cleaning a dataset in this world still takes domain knowledge and best practices are limited.
'

Title: b'zalperst'
Body: b"It is also worth emphasizing that many of these duplicate molecules have **inconsistent** labels. In investigating some of these I didn't find many chiral centres (infact i didn't seen any, but I didn't go through all of them), neither could I find tautomers. This also sheds light on the results of the 'molecule net' paper where it was consistently found that a random split of the dataset worked better than a more principled scaffold split. You could imagine that this can cause major problems, especially if one is using oversampling techniques to balance the data. I believe this runs counter to the goals that moleculenet was seeking to achieve, i.e. the standardization and benchmarking of chemoinformatic dataset. I urge you to fix these problems, it is essential to gain the trust of the machine learning community who work on rigorously well curated datasets (at least the most famous of them) and allow for reproducibility. Furthermore it is extremely easy to deal with this sort of problem: just take out the inconsistent molecules, it doesn't require much domain knowledge, also isn't deepchem supposed to have that domain knowledge in the first place? "

Title: b'How to get an molnet dataset as pandas dataframe?'
Body:
b"### Pandas dataframes from molnet datasets

I am new to deepchem and use the following code snippet to get pandas dataframe for a molnet dataset.

- Is there a simpler way to get the dataset as Pandas dataframe and to export the full dataset in CSV format with column labels?
- How to get the column labels of the features to the dataframe?
---
```python
import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from deepchem.molnet import load_delaney

delaney_tasks, delaney_datasets, transformers = load_delaney(featurizer='ECFP', split='random')
train_dataset, valid_dataset, test_dataset = delaney_datasets

def convert_dataset_to_df(dataset):
    col_y = dataset.tasks
    num_col_w = dataset.w.shape[1]
    col_w = [f'task_weight_{i:03}' for i in range(1, num_col_w + 1)]
    num_col_x = dataset.X.shape[1]
    col_x = [f'ECFP4_{i:04}' for i in range(1, num_col_x + 1)]
    columns = col_y + col_w + col_x
    df = pd.DataFrame(np.concatenate((dataset.y, dataset.w, dataset.X),
                                     axis=1),
                      index=dataset.ids,
                      columns=columns)
    df.index.name = 'ID'
    # Downcast fingerprint floats to integer
    df[col_x] = df[col_x].apply(pd.to_numeric, downcast='integer')
    return df
	
train_df = convert_dataset_to_df(train_dataset)
valid_df = convert_dataset_to_df(valid_dataset)
test_df = convert_dataset_to_df(test_dataset)

path = './datasets-prepared'
train_df.to_csv(os.path.join(path, 'delaney-ECFP4-train.csv'), index_label='ID')
valid_df.to_csv(os.path.join(path, 'delaney-ECFP4-valid.csv'), index_label='ID')
test_df.to_csv(os.path.join(path, 'delaney-ECFP4-test.csv'), index_label='ID')
```

Thanks"

Title: b'vsomnath'
Body:
b"Hi, 

> Is there a simpler way to get the dataset as Pandas dataframe and to export the full dataset in CSV format with column labels?

To the best of my knowledge, there is no functionality within DeepChem to turn `deepchem.Dataset` to a `pandas.DataFrame`, just because all models are designed to work with `deepchem.Dataset`, and it offers other benefits while writing and reading from disk. Most datasets in their raw form are available as `.csv` files so you should be able to download them and then just featurize the `SMILES` string and do the splits on that. 

> How to get the column labels of the features to the dataframe?

Title: b'KacperKubara'
Body:
b'Hey marcabrus,
I have the same issue as you: I am trying to find explainability methods for GCNs. From what I understand LIME cannot be directly used with GCNs as it requires a fixed input size. The graph, especially molecules, usually vary in size so the input won't be fixed.

Having said so, I have found a few papers regarding explainability methods for GCNs. One of the methods to circumvent this problem is to generate fixed-size neural fingerprints using GCNs and then apply LIME. Actually, the GraphConvTensor seems to be an implementation of circular fingerprints combined with CNNs (architecture is based on this [paper](MoleculeNet: a benchmark for molecular machine learning) according to this issue: https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/issues/1723). 

Another approach might be to "convert" the standard CNN explanation methods to graph domain.
This field of research is quite new and there is v. small number of papers discussing this topic and I was not able to find their code implementation yet! If you are interested in these methods, have a look at the links below.

[http://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_CVPR_2019/papers/Pope_Explainability_Methods_for_Graph_Convolutional_Neural_Networks_CVPR_2019_paper.pdf](http://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_CVPR_2019/papers/Pope_Explainability_Methods_for_Graph_Convolutional_Neural_Networks_CVPR_2019_paper.pdf)

Title: b'Change model.fit() to accept Numpy arrays X, y,... as default.'
Body:
b'Currently, model.fit() requires a dc.data object as input. This contrasts with sklearn and keras which have defaults model.fit(X, y). I propose that we change our fit() method to follow the same API.

The main advantage of this change is that we could onboard new users more gently and remove a common gotcha. We also get better interoperability with the broader python ML ecosystem.

For backwards compatibility, we can add a check in the next version that looks for the old input style and issues a warning. Eventually, in case users want to pass in a dc.data object, they will need to set a keyword argument.'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"TensorGraph already has a `fit_on_batch()` method that takes numpy arrays.  Contrary to its name, it does *not* require the arrays to be a single batch.  It just constructs a NumpyDataset from them and passes it on to the regular `fit()` method.  The only hardcoded assumption in that method is that there's only a single epoch, and that could easily be changed.\r\n\r\nThis seems like part of the discussion about long term architecture, harmonizing dc.data with tf.data and TensorGraph layers with Keras layers.  Do we ultimately want to have a single `fit()` method that can accept any sort of object, whether numpy arrays or a DeepChem dataset or a Tensorflow dataset?"

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'Agreed this is part of the longer term architecture discussion. My instinct is that we should optimize for interoperability with the ecosystem. This will enable us to gain more users and be more useful in general.\r\n\r\nI think supporting a single comprehensive fit() might work well since it will "just work" for most people.'

Title: b'Support make_estimator() for all models'
Body:
b"Most subclasses of TensorGraph will need changes before `make_estimator()` will work with them.  Anything that overrides `default_generator()` definitely will.  I already made the necessary changes to `MultiTaskRegressor` and `MultiTaskClassifier`.  I also looked at `MultiTaskFitTransformRegressor`, but concluded it probably can't be supported without significant changes to how transformers work.

Here is a list of all TensorGraph subclasses.  (If I missed anything, let me know.)  We can check off each one once we've either modified it to work, or concluded it isn't practical to do that.

- [x] MultiTaskRegressor
- [x] MultiTaskClassifier
- [x] MultiTaskFitTransformRegressor
- [ ] TensorflowMultiTaskIRVClassifier
- [x] GAN
- [ ] WeaveTensorGraph
- [ ] DTNNTensorGraph
- [ ] DAGTensorGraph
- [ ] PetroskiSuchTensorGraph
- [ ] GraphConvTensorGraph
- [ ] MPNNTensorGraph
- [x] SeqToSeq
- [ ] BPSymmetryFunctionRegression
- [ ] ANIRegression
- [ ] TextCNNTensorGraph
- [x] ProgressiveMultitaskRegressor
- [x] RobustMultitaskClassifier
- [x] RobustMultitaskRegressor
- [x] Sequential

To support a class, here's what needs to be done.  First, add a test case for it in test_estimators.py.  You may be able to adapt code from one of the other test cases.  The tutorial from #1136 may also be helpful.

In most cases the test will fail with an error saying the class overrides `default_generator()` but not `create_estimator_inputs()`.  So now you need to override `create_estimator_inputs()` to do whatever special manipulations `default_generator()` is doing, only with Tensorflow operators instead of numpy.

The job of `create_estimator_inputs()` is to create a dict where the keys are all of the model's input layers, and the values are the tensors to use for them.  Here is what the default implementation looks like.  Notice that it supports an arbitrary number of `Feature` layers, but only one `Weights` and one `Label` layer.  That's because of limitations in how estimators work.

```python
    tensors = {}
    for layer, column in zip(self.features, feature_columns):
      tensors[layer] = tf.feature_column.input_layer(features, [column])
    if weight_column is not None:
      tensors[self.task_weights[0]] = tf.feature_column.input_layer(
          features, [weight_column])
    if labels is not None:
      tensors[self.labels[0]] = tf.cast(labels, self.labels[0].dtype)
    return tensors
```

Consider `MultiTaskClassifier`.  It overrides `default_generator()` to convert the labels from class indices into one-hot encoded values:

```python
feed_dict[self.labels[0]] = to_one_hot(y_b.flatten(),
                                       self.n_classes).reshape(
                                           -1, self.n_tasks,
                                           self.n_classes)
```

It therefore overrides `create_estimator_inputs()` and modifies it to likewise convert the labels to one-hot:

```python
tensors[self.labels[0]] = tf.one_hot(
    tf.cast(labels, tf.int32), self.n_classes)
```"

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"Sequential is complicated because the model isn't fully defined until you call `fit()` on it.  The main reason that was done is so that you don't have to define the sizes of the inputs in advance.  That isn't a problem here, since they'll be defined by the arguments to `create_estimator()`.  But it also has the strange feature that the loss is defined by an argument to `fit()`.  Is there a reason for that?  Could we make the loss be an argument to the constructor instead?\r\n\r\nNote that the current API allows you to call `fit()` twice and specify a different loss each timebut the second time, it silently ignores the value you pass and uses the loss from the first call instead.  I'd call that a bug."

How about making the loss something that's added explicitly via an `add_loss()` call? Adding in the constructor seems awkward since the loss would be added before all the layers.

Agree that the behavior of `fit()` is a bug that should be fixed."

```
import numpy as np
import tensorflow as tf

import deepchem as dc
from deepchem.data import NumpyDataset
from deepchem.models import TensorGraph
from deepchem.molnet import load_bace_classification, load_delaney
from deepchem.models.tensorgraph.layers import ReduceSum, L2Loss, Dense, BatchNorm
from deepchem.models.tensorgraph.layers import Reshape, Label, Feature, Weights
from deepchem.models.tensorgraph.layers import SoftMaxCrossEntropy, SoftMax, WeightedError
from deepchem.models.tensorgraph.graph_layers import WeaveLayerFactory, WeaveGather
from deepchem.metrics import to_one_hot


class WeaveModel(TensorGraph):

  def __init__(self,
               n_tasks,
               n_atom_feat=75,
               n_pair_feat=14,
               n_hidden=50,
               n_graph_feat=128,
               mode="classification",
               n_classes=2,
               **kwargs):
    """
    Parameters
    ----------
    n_tasks: int
      Number of tasks
    n_atom_feat: int, optional
      Number of features per atom.
    n_pair_feat: int, optional

    n_hidden: int, optional

    n_graph_feat: int, optional
      Number of output features for each molecule(graph)
    mode: str
      Either "classification" or "regression" for type of model.
    n_classes: int
      Number of classes to predict (only used in classification mode)
    """
    if mode not in ['classification', 'regression']:
      raise ValueError("mode must be either 'classification' or 'regression'")
    self.n_tasks = n_tasks
    self.n_atom_feat = n_atom_feat
    self.n_pair_feat = n_pair_feat
    self.n_hidden = n_hidden
    self.n_graph_feat = n_graph_feat
    self.mode = mode
    self.n_classes = n_classes
    super(WeaveModel, self).__init__(**kwargs)
    self.build_graph()

  def build_graph(self):
    """Building graph structures:
                Features => WeaveLayer => WeaveLayer => Dense => WeaveGather => Classification or Regression
                """
    self.atom_features = Feature(shape=(None, self.n_atom_feat))
    self.pair_features = Feature(shape=(None, self.n_pair_feat))
    self.pair_split = Feature(shape=(None,), dtype=tf.int32)
    self.atom_split = Feature(shape=(None,), dtype=tf.int32)
    self.atom_to_pair = Feature(shape=(None, 2), dtype=tf.int32)
    weave_layer1A, weave_layer1P = WeaveLayerFactory(
        n_atom_input_feat=self.n_atom_feat,
        n_pair_input_feat=self.n_pair_feat,
        n_atom_output_feat=self.n_hidden,
        n_pair_output_feat=self.n_hidden,
        in_layers=[
            self.atom_features, self.pair_features, self.pair_split,
            self.atom_to_pair
        ])
    weave_layer2A, weave_layer2P = WeaveLayerFactory(
        n_atom_input_feat=self.n_hidden,
        n_pair_input_feat=self.n_hidden,
        n_atom_output_feat=self.n_hidden,
        n_pair_output_feat=self.n_hidden,
        update_pair=False,
        in_layers=[
            weave_layer1A, weave_layer1P, self.pair_split, self.atom_to_pair
        ])
    dense1 = Dense(
        out_channels=self.n_graph_feat,
        activation_fn=tf.nn.tanh,
        in_layers=weave_layer2A)
    batch_norm1 = BatchNorm(epsilon=1e-5, in_layers=[dense1])
    weave_gather = WeaveGather(
        self.batch_size,
        n_input=self.n_graph_feat,
        gaussian_expand=True,
        in_layers=[batch_norm1, self.atom_split])

    n_tasks = self.n_tasks
    weights = Weights(shape=(None, n_tasks))
    if self.mode == 'classification':
      n_classes = self.n_classes
      labels = Label(shape=(None, n_tasks, n_classes))
      logits = Reshape(
          shape=(None, n_tasks, n_classes),
          in_layers=[
              Dense(in_layers=weave_gather, out_channels=n_tasks * n_classes)
          ])
      output = SoftMax(logits)
      self.add_output(output)
      loss = SoftMaxCrossEntropy(in_layers=[labels, logits])
      weighted_loss = WeightedError(in_layers=[loss, weights])
      self.set_loss(weighted_loss)
    else:
      labels = Label(shape=(None, n_tasks))
      output = Reshape(
          shape=(None, n_tasks),
          in_layers=[Dense(in_layers=weave_gather, out_channels=n_tasks)])
      self.add_output(output)
      weighted_loss = ReduceSum(L2Loss(in_layers=[labels, output, weights]))
      self.set_loss(weighted_loss)

  def compute_features_on_batch(self, X_b):
    """Computes the features for feed_dict.

    A tf.py_func wrapper is written around this when using the input_fn for make_estimator
    """

    atom_feat = []
    pair_feat = []
    atom_split = []
    atom_to_pair = []
    pair_split = []
    start = 0
    for im, mol in enumerate(X_b):

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"This implementation is unfortunately pretty contorted (we first implemented in TF0.5 or something and had to do strange contortions to make operators work out)

`deg_slice` is one of the user inputs. It's generated by `dc.feat.ConvMolFeaturizer`. To see an example of usage of the raw layer, check out this test: https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/master/deepchem/models/tests/test_layers.py#L76. Here's an explanation of what `deg_slice` means: https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/master/deepchem/feat/mol_graphs.py#L217. Roughly speaking, it's an indexing tool to help us pull out different subsets of atoms.  `self_atoms` is pulling out the atom features for atoms of degree `deg` (that is, all the atoms which have `deg` number of bonds).

This implementation is based on https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.09292. It might be useful to read the pseudocode in that paper and compare side by side to get the idea for what we're doing."

Title: b'Protein/Ligand Preparation for Docking'
Body:
b"@bowenliu16 raised a number of interesting questions about protein preparation on the gitter which don't have great solutions within deepchem yet. I'm starting this thread to copy over the questions and discuss potential solutions:

1. What kind of protein preparation is done? Do we need to manually remove crystallized water and other ions? What about missing protein residues/loops?
    * `dc.feat.hydrogenate_and_compute_partial charges` is the current extent of protein cleanup. I don't believe we handle water/ion removal. Also, no handling of missing protein residues/loops. https://github.com/pandegroup/pdbfixer by @peastman handles many of these issues, so the right answer might be to use PDBFixer to handle these issues.
2. How many ligands can be in the .sdf file to be docked at the same time?
    * I think we only support one-ligand per .sdf file right now. Should probably generalize to support multiple ligands.
3. And what time of ligand processing do we need to do? Eg is any 3D conformation fine? We also have to manually specify the protonation states and any tautomers right?
    * `dc.feat.hydrogenate_and_compute_partial_charges` is the only ligand processing right now. It partially handles protonation, but I'd wager it doesn't do an excellent job. We don't handle tautomers yets.

I'd love to hear suggestions on good ways to handle pdb-cleanup, protonation, and tautomers with existing open source tools :-)

CC @peastman, @joegomes, @evanfeinberg "
Labels: Contribution Welcome,Good Intermediate Contribution,Scientific Knowledge Required

Title: b'joegomes'
Body:
b"These are good questions to consider and would make dc.dock more readily usable.

1. No water/ion removal.  I've used pdbfixer before and it works well for these tasks, it would be nice to incorporate it into file loading as an option.  Some PDBs in pdbbind contain waters near the binding pocket that aren't removed before model training (perhaps another point of discussion ..), so perhaps we don't want to remove all waters.  It will also be important to distinguish between solution ions and (possible) cations in the binding pocket.

2. Currently .sdf files are read by the `rdkit.mol.SDMolSupplier` iterator but we assume one ligand per file.  It would be easy to generalize the loading of multiple molecules.

3. I think for now any conformation is fine (Vina does conformation optimization) and we leave it to the user to enumerate protonation states and tautomers.  From some quick googling, it looks like MolVS, a python pkg built off rdkit, can enumerate tautomers given a rdkit mol object."

Title: b'proteneer'
Body:
b"
Expanding on 3)

3.1) Protonation states will require a pKa predictor of some form. Worse yet, you probably care about not just the solvent-phase protonation state but also the active-site protonation state (which requires a protein pKa predictor).

3.2) Tautomerization is really hard. Internally we have LigPrep (but obv it's a proprietary rule-based solution, which is less than ideal for an open-source package like DeepChem).

3.3) Another item to be aware of is different resonance structures of conjugated systems (which many tools probably doesn't do well on) that are not simple aromatic rings. @ptosco submitted a great PR to RDKit which can enumerate all resonance structures of a given mol, it can also rank them by stability using again, a rule-based heuristic: http://www.rdkit.org/Python_Docs/rdkit.Chem.rdchem.ResonanceMolSupplier-class.html

"

Title: b'Transformers should support tensors'

This would allow them to be used in Tensorflow's eager mode.  In #915 we discussed letting `predict_on_batch()` accept tensors, but right now the `transformers` argument wouldn't work. Title: b'Some questions about lime'
Body:
b'Hello everyone,
I am new here in deepchem.I found Lime is a great way to explain the molecular fingerprint.But I don't quite understand it. I do know the deeplearning NN separated the molecules into small segments like some functional groups and the Lime is a tool to show the fingerprint.
So my first question is that what is the relationship between the molecule and the fingerprint?
After running the code below,I tried to see 'my_fp'.And I saw some numbers explained by some chemical functional group,like,314: {'C=O'}, 594: {'CC(C)(O)CC[CH]'}.Somehow,I see one thing like'807: {''},',which is an empty column.What does that mean?
More important thing is that I really need to see which fingerprint contributes most in the whole trainingset.In other words,how to see the feature importance?For example,in tox21 database,after the DNN training,maybe some functional group can totally lead to the 'toxic' result,maybe some can lead to 80%'toxic'.How can I see the information like this?
Maybe what I wanna do make no sense in deepchem.More informations of Lime is really needed here.
Thanks for any kind of help.


'''
#!/usr/bin/env python
# coding: utf-8

# In[1]:


from rdkit import Chem
from rdkit.Chem.Draw import IPythonConsole
from IPython.display import SVG
from rdkit.Chem import rdDepictor
from rdkit.Chem.Draw import rdMolDraw2D


import numpy as np
import deepchem as dc
from deepchem.molnet import load_tox21

# Only for debug!
np.random.seed(123)

# Load Tox21 dataset
n_features = 1024
tox21_tasks, tox21_datasets, transformers = load_tox21()
train_dataset, valid_dataset, test_dataset = tox21_datasets


# In[2]:


# Fit models
metric = dc.metrics.Metric(
    dc.metrics.roc_auc_score, np.mean, mode="classification")

nb_epoch = 10
model = dc.models.tensorgraph.fcnet.MultitaskClassifier(
    len(tox21_tasks),
    train_dataset.get_data_shape()[0])

# Fit trained model
model.fit(train_dataset, nb_epoch=nb_epoch)
model.save()

print("Evaluating model")
train_scores = model.evaluate(train_dataset, [metric], transformers)
valid_scores = model.evaluate(valid_dataset, [metric], transformers)


# In[3]:


print("Train scores")
print(train_scores)

print("Validation scores")
print(valid_scores)


# In[4]:


#So LIME as is can work on any problem with a fixed size input vector. 
#It works by computing probability distributions for the individual features and covariance between the features.
#We are going to create an explainer for our data

from lime import lime_tabular
feature_names = ["fp_%s"  % x for x in range(1024)]
explainer = lime_tabular.LimeTabularExplainer(train_dataset.X,
                                              feature_names=feature_names,
                                              categorical_features=feature_names,
                                              class_names=['not toxic', 'toxic'],
                                              discretize_continuous=True)


# In[5]:


# We need a function which takes a 2d numpy array (samples, features) and returns predictions (samples,)
def eval_model(my_model, transformers):
    def eval_closure(x):
        ds = dc.data.NumpyDataset(x, None, None, None)
        # The 0th task is NR-AR
        predictions = model.predict(ds)[:, 0]
        return predictions
    return eval_closure
model_fn = eval_model(model, transformers)


# In[6]:


# We want to investigate a toxic compound
active_id = np.where(test_dataset.y[:,0]==1)[0][0]
print(active_id)
Chem.MolFromSmiles(test_dataset.ids[active_id])


# In[7]:


# this returns an Lime Explainer class
# The explainer contains details for why the model behaved the way it did
exp = explainer.explain_instance(test_dataset.X[active_id], model_fn, num_features=5, top_labels=1)
# If we are in an ipython notebook it can show it to us
exp.show_in_notebook(show_table=True, show_all=False)


# In[8]:


#So the model believes that fingerprint 118, 519 and 301 highly contribute to the molecules toxicity. 
#We can reverse our the hash function and look at the fragments that activated those fingerprints for this molecule.

from rdkit import Chem


def fp_mol(mol, fp_length=1024):
    """
    returns: dict of <int:list of string>
        dictionary mapping fingerprint index
        to list of smile string that activated that fingerprint
    """
    d = {}
    feat = dc.feat.CircularFingerprint(sparse=True, smiles=True, size=1024)
    retval = feat._featurize(mol)
    for k, v in retval.items():
        index = k % 1024
        if index not in d:
            d[index] = set()
        d[index].add(v['smiles'])
    return d
# What fragments activated what fingerprints in our active molecule?
my_fp=fp_mol(Chem.MolFromSmiles(test_dataset.ids[active_id]))


# In[9]:


# We can calculate which fragments activate all fingerprint
# indexes throughout our entire training set
all_train_fps = {}
X = train_dataset.X
ids = train_dataset.ids
for i in range(len(X)):
    d = fp_mol(Chem.MolFromSmiles(ids[i]))
    for k, v in d.items():
        if k not in all_train_fps:
            all_train_fps[k] = set()
        all_train_fps[k].update(v)


# In[10]:


# We can visualize which fingerprints our model declared toxic for the
# active molecule we are investigating
Chem.MolFromSmiles(list(my_fp[118])[0])


# In[11]:


Chem.MolFromSmiles(list(my_fp[519])[0])


# In[12]:


Chem.MolFromSmiles(list(my_fp[301])[0])


# In[13]:


# We can also see what fragments are missing by investigating the training set
# According to our explanation having one of these fragments would make our molecule more likely to be toxic
Chem.MolFromSmiles(list(all_train_fps[381])[0])


# In[14]:


Chem.MolFromSmiles(list(all_train_fps[381])[1])


# In[15]:


Chem.MolFromSmiles(list(all_train_fps[381])[4])


# In[16]:


Chem.MolFromSmiles(list(all_train_fps[875])[0])


# In[17]:


Chem.MolFromSmiles(list(all_train_fps[875])[2])


# In[18]:


Chem.MolFromSmiles(list(all_train_fps[875])[4])
#Using LIME on fragment based models can give you intuition over which fragments are contributing 
#to your response variable in a linear fashion.
'''


'

Title: b'Support residual blocks'
Body: b'Building models out of residual blocks is now a common practice, since they produce better results in many applications.  Classes like MultitaskRegressor, MultitaskClassifier, GraphConvModel, etc. could easily be modified to use residual blocks in place of simple dense or convolutional layers.  We should consider adding an option to do that.'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'This seems really useful!'

Title: b'patrickhop'
Body: b'I tried residual blocks on graphconvs a few times. Never had any luck.'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"I'm experimenting with it on MultitaskClassifier right now.  On my very simple tests so far, it works about as well as simple Dense layers.  But I haven't tried anything really challenging yet.  I'm also still figuring out how to deal with various subtleties.  For example, you can only use a residual block when two successive layers have the same width.  So depending on the layer widths, it may actually be a mix of residual and ordinary layers.  And then, pre-activation is supposed to work better than post-activation for residual blocks, but I need to make sure that gets handled correctly when switching back and forth between types of layers."

Title: b'patrickhop'
Body:
b'yeah, there are 3 cases to consider here:

(1) next layer is wider
=> pad or upsample using convs

(2) next layer is the same size
=> proceed with residual connection

(3) next layer is thinner
=> downsample using conv'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"Exactly.  Or more simply: if it's the same size, use a residual block.  Otherwise, use an ordinary dense layer.\r\n\r\nThe implementation in #1686 seems to work pretty well.  I wrote some simple tests that tried to overfit a small dataset.  With `residual=False` it started failing when the number of layers got beyond about 10, but with `residual=True` it had no problem with 30 layers."

There are several issues discussing the influence of samples with missing labels. As far as I can understand from the discussions, an overall technique is to assign the corresponding
weights to zero so that such samples won't affect learning. But does it mean that we simply
ignore a whole sample if at least one task label among multiple tasks is missing? If so, I
believe this is a notable problem for low data analysis, and I wonder if there are any solutions
considered (taking into account the correlation between tasks, semi-supervised learning, etc.).
If such solutions exist and are theoretically or empirically valid, do they consider regression
tasks?"

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'This is why DeepChem uses a 2D weight matrix of shape (samples, tasks).  That lets you mask out just the tasks that are missing for each sample.  You can also use BalancingTransformer to adjust the weights for the remaining tasks so the total weight of positive and negative samples is equal on each task.\r\n\r\nIn contrast, some frameworks (like Keras) only allow a single weight for each sample.  That makes them unsuitable for multitask models.'

``  def _featurize(self, mol):

    if self.sparse:

          useBondTypes=self.bonds,

      fp = fp.GetNonzeroElements()  # convert to a dict

          root, radius = info[fragment_id][0]
          if radius == 0:
            atom = mol.GetAtomWithIdx(root)
            aromatic = atom.GetIsAromatic()
            symbol = atom.GetSymbol()
            if aromatic:
                symbol = symbol.lower()
            smiles = "[" + symbol + "]"
          else:
            env = Chem.FindAtomEnvironmentOfRadiusN(mol, radius, root)
            frag = Chem.PathToSubmol(mol, env)
            smiles = Chem.MolToSmiles(frag)
          fp_smiles[fragment_id] = {'smiles': smiles, 'count': count}
        fp = fp_smiles
    else:

          mol,

          nBits=self.size,
          useChirality=self.chiral,
          useBondTypes=self.bonds,

Title: b'KacperKubara'
Body:
b'Hello, I have created a modified ScaffoldSplitter Class with an option to return the scaffolds. Any thoughts? Gist link below

Basically, I have moved part of `split()` functionality into a new function `generate_scaffolds()`. Code seems to be now a bit clearer too read and it can return only scaffolds if needed. I haven't tested it yet, but I will do it soon and will let you know. 

```python
class ScaffoldSplitter(Splitter):
    """
    Class for doing data splits based on the scaffold of small molecules.
    """

    def split(self,
              dataset,
              frac_train=.8,
              frac_valid=.1,
              frac_test=.1,
              log_every_n=1000):
        """
        Splits internal compounds into train/validation/test by scaffold.
        """
        np.testing.assert_almost_equal(frac_train + frac_valid + frac_test, 1.)
        scaffold_sets = self.generate_scaffolds(dataset)

        train_cutoff = frac_train * len(dataset)
        valid_cutoff = (frac_train + frac_valid) * len(dataset)
        train_inds, valid_inds, test_inds = [], [], []

        log("About to sort in scaffold sets", self.verbose)
        for scaffold_set in scaffold_sets:
            if len(train_inds) + len(scaffold_set) > train_cutoff:
                if len(train_inds) + len(valid_inds) + len(scaffold_set) > valid_cutoff:
                    test_inds += scaffold_set
                else:
                    valid_inds += scaffold_set
            else:
                train_inds += scaffold_set
        return train_inds, valid_inds, test_inds

    def generate_scaffolds(self, dataset, log_every_n=1000):
        """
        Returns all scaffolds from the dataset
        """
        scaffolds = {}
        data_len = len(dataset)

        log("About to generate scaffolds", self.verbose)
        for ind, smiles in enumerate(dataset.ids):
            if ind % log_every_n == 0:
                log(f"Generating scaffold {ind} {data_len}", self.verbose)
            scaffold = generate_scaffold(smiles)
            if scaffold not in scaffolds:
                scaffolds[scaffold] = [ind]
            else:
                scaffolds[scaffold].append(ind)

        # Sort from largest to smallest scaffold sets
        scaffolds = {key: sorted(value) for key, value in scaffolds.items()}
        scaffold_sets = [
            scaffold_set
            for (scaffold, scaffold_set) in sorted(scaffolds.items(),
                                                   key=lambda x: (len(x[1]), x[1][0]),
                                                   reverse=True)
        ]
        return scaffold_sets
```

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"Here's a recent paper on predicting relationships between genes based on expression data:

[Deep learning for inferring gene relationships from single-cell expression data](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1911536116)

The input to their model is a 2D histogram of the expression levels of two genes across a set of experiments.  The output is a prediction of, for example, whether one of the two genes directly regulates the other.  They train the model on a bunch of genes that are known to directly regulate each other.  Then they can pick any two genes, put the expression histogram into the model, and get a prediction of whether one regulates the other.

This same approach could potentially be used for other types of data as well."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"Here's an interesting recent research paper on using BERT to do biomedical text mining. 

[BioBERT: a pre-trained biomedical language representation model for biomedical text mining](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.08746)

There's been a longstanding dream in the biological community about using search engines to pull information out of the vast literature. This dream is starting to move a little closer with the advent of BERT-like models. BioBERT uses BERT weights then pre-trains on a corpus of biomedical literature. This pretrained model is then finetuned on specific tasks. The results show some solid improvements.

Adding these datasets and models could prove interesting to provide a base for future research"

Title: b'DeepChem Dataset Tutorial'
Body:
b"There have been a lot of questions recently about DeepChem datasets. This highlights the fact that we don't have a good introductory reference tutorial for datasets. I think it would be a great idea to put together a tutorial for `dc.data.Dataset`. This tutorial could cover:

- How to wrap `X, y, z` arrays as `NumpyDataset` objects
- How to extract `X, y, z` arrays from `Dataset` objects
- How to iterate over `(X, y, z)` tuples from a `Dataset`
- How to convert back and forth between `DiskDataset` and `NumpyDataset`
- How to load large datasets with `DiskDataset`. The meaning of shard-size and how to set it correctly.
- How to convert between `tf.data` and `Dataset`

There are a lot of topics here, but even covering some of them would be a great topic for a tutorial."

Title: b'Allow TensorGraph to use Keras layers'
Body:
b"We keep coming back to the question of how to better interoperate with Keras.  This will become even more important in TensorFlow 2.0, since it will eliminate the `tf.contrib` and `tf.layers` modules and standardize on `tf.keras` as the primary API for building models.

In #1038 we considered completely replacing TensorGraph and just using `tf.keras.Model` for everything, but we concluded that wasn't practical.  TensorGraph has a lot of features that Keras doesn't, including Transformers, 2D weight matrices for multitask models, more flexibility in the shapes of input and output tensors, and first class support for DeepChem Datasets.  We rely on those features.

I'd like to propose a different possibility: keep TensorGraph, but have it accept a `tf.keras.Model` as its model definition.  In this approach, model building would all be done with standard Keras classes, but you would never call `compile()` on it.  Instead, you would pass it to a TensorGraph and rely on its methods for training and prediction.

As part of this transition, we would convert our own Layer classes to extend `tf.keras.layers.Layer`.  We also would deprecate (but not remove) all the ones that are just equivalents of standard layers.  As much as possible, we would use standard Keras layers when building our models.  We would then focus on providing two main contributions.

1. A collection of non-standard layers that are important for chemistry, like graph convolutions and atomic convolutions.  These would extend `tf.keras.layers.Layer`, so they could be used directly in any Keras model.

2. TensorGraph, which provides important features not supported by Keras models, as well as better integration with the rest of DeepChem.  This would be optional for users.  If someone doesn't need these features, they would be free to stick to `tf.keras.Model` but could still use the layers we provide.

What do you think?  Does this sound like a plausible approach?  Do you see any problems with it?"

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"I like this proposal quite a bit! Our core value as a library is the large set of non-standard layers that we maintain. Making these layers available to all TensorFlow users would make us much more useful. Retaining TensorGraph as an optional feature will let us retain backwards compatibility and support complex custom models which need TensorGraph's flexibility.\r\n\r\nI think we'll add some additional code complexity on the backend with these changes. I think we can eventually remove deprecated layers (DeepChem 3.0 likely) which should mitigate these issues"

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'The new Keras model subclassing API might be relevant for this discussion: https://www.tensorflow.org/guide/keras#model_subclassing'

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"I'm getting close to starting on this.  Here is a more detailed proposal.  Tell me what you think of it.

We will create a new module called `dc.models.layers`.  All of the layers contained in it will directly subclass `tf.keras.layers.Layer`.  We will take all our existing *nontrivial* TensorGraph layers and convert them to Keras layers in this module.

`dc.models.tensorgraph.layers` will continue to exist and have the same classes it currently does, but the amount of code will get a lot smaller.  The existing nontrivial layers will just become thin wrappers around the classes in `dc.models.layers`.

We'll create a new class called `dc.models.KerasModel`.  It will act as a wrapper around a Keras model in the same way that `SklearnModel` acts as a wrapper around a scikit-learn model.  The constructor will take an instance of `tf.keras.Model` which will define the model.  It will provide support for the same features that TensorGraph does, like multitask weights, transformers, etc.

Over time, we will gradually convert all the standard models to be based on KerasModel instead of TensorGraph.

At some point in the distant future (maybe DeepChem 4.0?), we could consider eliminating TensorGraph.  That won't be happening any time soon though."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'I like this proposal quite a bit. It will let us keep backwards compatibility on `TensorGraph` for at least one major release to allow people time to transition.'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"@rbharath if you want to try converting some models, Unet and ResNet50 would be good ones to try.  They're both very straightforward, so they should be easy to convert.  Neither one has any meaningful tests, though (all they do is check the shape of the output), so you'll need to create tests first so you can verify it still works after converting it."
