Title: b'shntnu'
Body:
b'Our research focus is on assessing the impact of compounds and genetic perturbations on cells morphology, as imaged by microscopy, so I thought we'd chime in with some thoughts. 

We recently wrote a best practices [paper](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28858338) together with nearly 20 other labs on the computational/statistical workflow for this kind of experiment. Most of that is focussed on "classical" approaches, i.e., not deep learning, but it would still be a good starting point if you want to learn about challenges unique to imaging data.

Our own lab (Imaging Platform/Carpenter lab at the Broad Institute), and several others, [have](https://github.com/broadinstitute/keras-rcnn) [been](https://github.com/broadinstitute/keras-resnet) [heavily](https://github.com/broadinstitute/deepometry) [invested](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-018-02174-z) in deep learning for image analysis, including image-based  or morphological  profiling. Our initial experiments [have](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/early/2017/12/02/227645) [been](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/early/2016/11/02/085118) promising, and likewise for some of [our](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/early/2017/07/10/161422) colleagues who have take a similar approach. We've also been writing a Python [library](https://github.com/jccaicedo/DeepProfiler) to support this research, and will soon post a Jupyter notebook to reproduce results from our [CVPR 2018](http://cvpr2018.thecvf.com/) paper (in press) in case you are interested in testing out the library. 

Based on our experience, we believe that for an application such as the Cell Chem Bio [paper](http://www.cell.com/cell-chemical-biology/fulltext/S2451-9456(18)30037-0), where the matrix of ground truth is typically sparse, it could be challenging to use a simple strategy of directly training a CNN to predict the response, given the images. Instead, we believe one should either use pre-trained networks, then fine tune, or directly use features that were extracted from images using classical image analysis techniques (as was done in the  [paper](http://www.cell.com/cell-chemical-biology/fulltext/S2451-9456(18)30037-0)). Or, one could train using weak labels  which is what our CVPR paper is about (we will post the link here in a few weeks)  and use the learned representation for the prediction tasks.

I hope that perspective helps when making decisions about your API. 

[@jccaicedo](https://github.com/jccaicedo) and @shntnu
'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"`KerasModel` doesn't have a `save()` function, but Keras does provide a few different mechanisms that can be used to save and reconstruct  a `tf.keras.Model`.  So you could restore that, then create a new `KerasModel` wrapping it.  See https://www.tensorflow.org/guide/keras/save_and_serialize.\r\n\r\nI think it would be nice to have an equivalent of the TensorGraph `save()` method, but I haven't been able to figure out a general way of doing it.  First you have to save the internal Keras model, and different types of models require different mechanisms.  The `save()` function works with sequential and functional models, but not with subclassed ones.  And then the loss function is defined by an arbitrary callable Python object, which may not be saveable by any mechanism."

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b'I think this message is the key:

> (1) Failed precondition: Error while reading resource variable graph_conv/bias from Container: localhost. This could mean that the variable was uninitialized.

When you first create a model with Keras, a lot of the parameters are left in an uninitialized state.  They get initialized the first time you call `fit()`.  This is done so that you can create a model without having to specify the shapes of all the inputs, and it infers the shapes based on the values you pass on the first training step.  Try fitting your model before calling `save()`.  Does that work?'

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"You didn't give your code, so I can't be sure of all sources or nondeterminism you might have.  But generally there are a few of them:

- Most models initialize their parameters to random values.
- If you're using random splits for your dataset, that will be different every time.
- If you're explicitly using any random values (like from `np.random`), those will be diffferent every time.

Splitting methods generally offer a `seed` argument you can use to fix the random number seed.  Likewise Numpy and TensorFlow both have functions to set the random seed."

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"Try this.  Change

```python
model = sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier(len(tox21_tasks), train_dataset.get_data_shape()[0])

to

sklearn_model = sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifier(len(tox21_tasks), train_dataset.get_data_shape()[0])

Title: b'Organizing DeepChem Tutorials into a Cogent Sequence'

b"Thanks to great effort from our contributors, we have a good number of deepchem tutorials (https://deepchem.io/docs/notebooks/index.html) with more coming on the way. These tutorials provide a great resource for newcomers to DeepChem and to the field of molecular machine learning broadly. However, they're a bit dis-organized right now. How can we organize our tutorials to help newcomers on-board better? It might make sense to mark a few tutorials as beginner overviews, and the rest as advanced case-study or API reference material.

Title: b'pvskand'

b'@rbharath, @lilleswing,  this is a great idea indeed. Infact when I first saw the list of notebooks it was quite confusing for me.
Some thoughts on the current organization:
- In `Application Tutorials`, the first two tutorials i.e Graph Convs and Multitask Nets are good ones to start to know deepchem.
- Since we have few more Dataset tutorials (the splitters and the NumpyDataset) and few more coming soon like the DiskDataset Tutorial, I would suggest to have a separate section for Dataset Tutorials.
- The name `Machine Learning Methods Tutorials` is very vague or rather let me put it this way, some of the Application tutorials also do come under Machine Learning Methods. What we can do instead is have a separate column for Vision tasks, this way it would separate the core deepchem tasks from the vision tasks.
- Since there are few `TensorGraph` and `TensorBoard` tutorials we can have them in one separate section.
So summing up the above points we can have the following structure:

  - Dataset Tutorials
  - Beginner Tutorials for DeepChem [which include Graph Convs and Multitask Nets.]
  - Advance case-study with DeepChem
  - Vision Tutorials

Title: b'Aligning constructor arguments for TensorGraph Layers and Keras Layers'
Body:
b"Currently, our layer constructors differ from Keras layer constructors in a number of subtle ways. For example, consider 2d convolutions in TensorGraph:

```
Conv2D(num_outputs, kernel_size=5, stride=1, padding='SAME', activation_fn=<function relu>, normalizer_fn=None, biases_initializer=<class 'tensorflow.python.ops.init_ops.Zeros'>, weights_initializer=<function xavier_initializer>, scope_name=None, **kwargs)[source]
```

versus in Keras

```
Conv2D(filters, kernel_size, strides=(1, 1), padding='valid', data_format=None, dilation_rate=(1, 1), activation=None, use_bias=True, kernel_initializer='glorot_uniform', bias_initializer='zeros', kernel_regularizer=None, bias_regularizer=None, activity_regularizer=None, kernel_constraint=None, bias_constraint=None)
```

The arguments are almost identical, but there are a number of subtle differences that make things tricky. I'm running into this a lot in #979 where I'm porting the Keras Dragonn models into DeepChem. Since Keras layers have been adopted by `tf.keras`, I think they're starting to become a standard API. Aligning the APIs to share names, arguments, and argument ordering would make it easy for people to port code over. This would be very nice feature target for DeepChem 2.0."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'Digging into the code more, it looks like the `tensorgraph.layers.Conv2D` arguments match those for `tf.contrib.layers.conv2d`. This is also a semantically meaningful alignment. Do people have strong preferences for matching either the raw Tensorflow API or the Keras API?'

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body: b'tf.contrib.layers are just that -- contrib.\r\n\r\ntf.keras is a higher namespace'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"Agreed. In general, I'd be in favor of starting to use `tf.keras` to back our non-custom layers to the degree possible. We shouldn't be reinventing the wheel on basic layers.\r\n\r\nWould people be onboard with making `tf.keras` integration a 2.0 target?"

Title: b'TensorGraph implementation of Junction Tree Variational Autoencoders'
Body:
b'There's been a lot of progress in generating graph structures from deep networks. The latest paper, "Junction Tree Variational Autoencoders" devises a clever approach which treats a molecular graph as a junction tree of subgraphs. This paper appears to be a major qualitative advance which always generates valid subgraphs.

I'd love to see an implementation in DeepChem. In addition to being useful, I think it will be a nice test for `TensorGraph` since the training procedure is complex.

CC @lilleswing '

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body:
b'I'm not sure if this is a good first contribution as the paper is very complex IMO.

I started a different repo a week ago-ish for dev on the project.
https://github.com/lilleswing/jt-vae

So far I haven't even been able to do the junction tree decomposition to get the right number of fragments.  There are questions about how the author handles valences and attachment points to get the 780 number.

The DFS needed for the Junction Tree Decoder would be very hard to write in TensorGraph currently. 

After the reading the paper I am still not sure how the Graph Decoder works.

I agree that it is a major breakthrough -- but I don't think an implementation of this will be trivial.
If anyone wants to have a "fireside chat" over skype, or hangout about the paper let me know.  There are still many things I can't figure out and think it will require a team effort to reproduce.'

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body: b'Also I think the Junction Tree might have qsar reprocussions as a featurizer.  The paper shows how the latent space can contain more chemical information than previous latent spaces for molecules.'

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body: b'http://karlleswing.com/misc/dev_tree_decomp.html'

Title: b'miaecle'
Body: b'@lilleswing  Very interesting! My feeling is that the decomposition is not really chemistry based, but rather PGM based. A general tool used to decompose bayesian network and build junction tree might be helpful. Also this might be much more doable using pytorch, the tree decoder seems real complicated.'

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body:
b"It basically decomposes into 4 parts.
1. Junction Tree Encoder
* This uses the algorithm in the synopses to decompose a molecule into a tree.  Then it uses a modified GRU and MPNN to an latent space of 28.  I can't figure out valences to get a language of 780.  When you take into account valences you get ~2k.  When you replace all aromatic bonds with single bonds you get ~ 260.  
2. Graph Encoder
* This operates on the full molecule graph with atoms as vertexes and edges as nodes.  This uses standard MPNN to a latent space of 28
3. Junction Tree Decoder
* This is a DFS w/ MPNN.  First step is determining if there is an additional child from the current node, it also determines the node type.  They do a feasibility Check during the tree dfs to only sample from possible children nodes.  I'm not sure how they do this feasibility check. and on top of that I'm not sure how they would make this differentiable.
4. Graph Decoder
* This is where things get really murky for me.  Given the fragments and the junction tree there are supposedly many different molecules that could be created.  I suppose this is from rotations of the fragments? How do you do the enumeration of all possible graphs in a differentiable way? 

Finally after the graph is decoded they enumerate all possible stereo-isomers, encode all of them into the graph latent space, and pick  the one with the lowest cosine distance to the original latent space graph encoding.  Yet again how to do this in a differentiable way?

[single_bond_only.csv.txt](https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/files/1738171/single_bond_only.csv.txt)

Although I do find it interesting/cool using their decomposition and then removing aromaticity that there are only ~260 building blocks for 250k molecules."

Title: b'Change existing TensorGraph layers to match Keras2 API'
Body:
b"We've had a number of technical discussions about ways we can improve `TensorGraph` integration with mainstream TensorFlow. (https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/issues/1038, https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/issues/1076, https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/issues/988). These proposals inevitably run into some serious technical barriers. The main issue is that `TensorGraph` supports a lot of custom constructs (simple multitasking, submodels, serializiation, RNN support, etc) that we need in order to maintain the https://moleculenet.ai models and other advanced models that DeepChem supports. It looks like it's not going to be feasible to implement these models directly in Keras without significant pain.

However, it's interesting to note that Keras (and specifically Keras 2 https://blog.keras.io/introducing-keras-2.html) is more an API specification than a particular library. `tf.keras` is an implementation of this API. The main `keras` library is also an implementation, and I believe that there are others available. Given that `TensorGraph` is already pretty full-featured, I propose we go ahead and turn it into a Keras2 implementation. Here's what this conversion would entail:

- *Changing `TensorGraph` layers to match Keras2 specification*: We've already previously discussed doing this (https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/issues/988). In general, this will add lots of value since users can move over Keras2 models with set hyperparameters into DeepChem without trouble. This is currently an issue with Dragonn integration (https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/issues/1002), where it's tricky to port over the Keras2 Dragonn hyperparameters.
- *Add missing Keras2 layers*: This should be straightforward since we can just re-use `tf.keras` layers and need only add a little boilerplate.
- *Add support for functional API*: The Keras functional API (https://keras.io/getting-started/functional-api-guide/) is the blessed way to build complex Keras models. It would be nice to have a `TensorGraph` implementation. (Something like our `Sequential` class that builds the correct `TensorGraph` under the hood would work).

I think that the implementation complexity for these changes should be manage-able. Combined with the `tf.Estimator` support suggested by @peastman (https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/issues/1076#issuecomment-366386384), I think this set of API changes should be a solid path forward for the next few months.

I'd love feedback on this proposal. For users, does this seem like it would make DeepChem more useful to your day-to-day efforts? For developers, does the proposed implementation path sound feasible?"

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"I'm not convinced this is a good idea.  If we want to use Keras, there's already a full implementation in tf.keras.  Creating another complete implementation of the API would be a huge task, and wouldn't really benefit anyone.  And any faithful implementation of the Keras API would have exactly the same problems we ran into in #1038.  So instead we would end up with a halfhearted imitation of Keras that looked similar but worked in fundamentally different ways, and was incompatible with all other implementations.\r\n\r\nI think we're still searching for our long term architecture.  My instinct is that it will be either completely based on Keras (which is a nice API, but has limitations that may rule it out), or else Keras will have no part in it.  For example, if we decide to standardize around Estimator, then we should be basing the API for our layers on what's in tf.layers.  (Estimator, IMO, is a *much* less nice API than Keras, but also is unlikely to present fundamental roadblocks.  Sigh.)"

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"These are good points. We don't want to take on unnecessary development effort given that our development team is much smaller than the development teams for Keras/TensorFlow.

At the same time, I think we should at least implement part 1 (*Changing TensorGraph layers to match Keras2 specification*). We already have problems with duplicate layers (https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/issues/1092#issue-297972942 notes we have two BatchNorm layers). Making sure our standard layers (2d convolution, batch norm, 1d convolutions, etc.) match the Keras2 API will make it much easier for users to move code between DeepChem and Keras.

Agree that we're still looking for our long term architecture. Honestly, the whole field is looking for its long term architecture. My two cents is that pytorch/tf.eager style combined with Keras-like layers is probably the long term winner, but it's going to take years to settle. For now, comparing Keras and tf.Estimator, I agree that Keras has a much nicer API, and just implementing some type of `TensorGraph.make_estimator` function is probably good enough for our `tf.Estimator` integration needs."

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"Wouldn't it be better to change the TensorGraph layers to match the tf.layers specification?  If that's what we're standardizing on."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'I think the Keras2 API spec has a lot broader adoption than `tf.layer`. Matching Keras2 will let us move models back and forth between Keras and DeepChem easily.'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"I've changed the title of issue to match the discussion. If there are no objections, I think we can open this issue out to contributions."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"I'm opening this issue out to contributors. If you'd like to work on this issue, pick a layer that `TensorGraph` implements that's also a standard Keras2 layer. For example, a convolution layer or an LSTM layer or the like. Check against the Keras2 API spec, and modify the TensorGraph layer to accept the same arguments and in the same order. Use grep or a similar tool to verify that all uses of the layer in `examples/` or `contrib/` are modified accordingly.\r\n\r\nThis should be a good starter PR since it requires minimal, mostly mechanical code changes. Note that each contributed PR should target only one Layer in order to allow multiple people to tackle different parts of the task. If you'd like to contribute, please raise a comment on this thread mentioning the layer you'd like to convert and raise a pull request marked [WIP] tracking your work."

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"This won't always be mechanical, and we need to be very careful to avoid breaking things.  To give a simple example, compare the Keras and TensorGraph Dense layers.  Keras has a bunch of options that TensorGraph doesn't include (all the regularizers, for example), so we'll need to add those.  But TensorGraph also supports the `time_series` option that Keras doesn't, so what do we do with that?  Then they have options that do the same thing but with different names: `biases_initializer` and `weights_initializer` in TensorGraph, vs. `bias_initializer` and `kernel_initializer` in Keras.  But it's not just the names that are different: the TensorGraph versions take initializer functions while the Keras versions take strings for an enumerated list of supported initialization methods.  And then of course they have different defaults.  TensorGraph defaults to `variance_scaling_initializer` for the weights while Keras defaults to `'glorot_uniform'`.  So we're going to change the behavior of all existing models that use this layer!

Then there's the GRU and LSTM layers.  Recurrent layers work differently in Keras than in TensorGraph.  Some of the options like `stateful` and `return_state` simply don't make sense, because that isn't how recurrent networks are implemented in TensorGraph.

I'm still very skeptical about whether it's a good idea to make this change."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"These are good points. I'm removing the contribution welcome label for the time being. Let's discuss this at the next steering committee meeting to see if there's a reasonable implementation path."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"Closing this issue since we've mostly completed the transition to Keras layers."

Title: b'DeepChem extensibility issues'
Body:
b"I've heard from multiple teams that while they've found DeepChem very useful, they've often had to significantly modify the library in order to make use of it. This process usually takes them far enough from DeepChem's core structure that it's not even clear how they could merge their changes back into the main library without breaking large amounts of code.

It's worth asking why multiple users have run into this issue. I've proposed some changes in #1075 that I think will help a little. I think #1038 will help as well, but it looks like it's going to take a good chunk of development effort to make happen.

If you have thoughts on how we can improve the API to make it more extensible and useful, please chime in on this thread.

CC @evanfeinberg "

Title: b'ankitvgupta'
Body:
b'@rbharath Thanks so much for the great library - we are huge fans at Reverie Labs! 

We are building some production systems that involve using tf.Estimator with tf.data.Dataset, along with a few tf.Keras-based models for one-off cases here and there. As a result, incorporating TensorGraph layers seemed like reinventing the wheel a little bit. I think that your proposal for having more interoperability between TensorGraph and Keras, or moving to Keras entirely would address this challenge.

That said, we have found the models implemented in deepchem to be super useful, and very easy to port to tf.Estimators if needed. We are looking into making contributions into deepchem directly as well, and will definitely circle back about that in the coming weeks. 

Thanks again for all your efforts!
'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"@ankitvgupta Thanks for the detailed feedback! I'd love to hear your thoughts on tf.Estimator vs. tf.Keras. Are tf.Keras models interoperable with tf.Estimator? Do you think there would be gain from making DeepChem interoperate well with tf.Estimator?"

Title: b'ankitvgupta'
Body:
b"@rbharath Currently, the story around the intersection of tf.Keras and tf.Estimator is a little muddled. Estimator is essentially a wrapper around the vanilla Tensorflow which allows for convenient experimentation, as well as distributed multi-node training. It also integrates very closely with the tf.data.Dataset API, which has given us at Reverie various performance benefits.

tf.Keras supposedly works pretty well with Estimator, since the tf.keras library ships with a method to convert Keras models to Estimators (`tf.keras.estimator.model_to_estimator`), though I haven't tried that personally. That said, I believe that since you can use individual keras layers on tensorflow tensors, it'll work just fine in an Estimator, since an Estimator can wrap any valid tensorflow graph. We use it so that we get the full flexibility of all tensorflow ops.

The main reason we didn't want to depend too highly on DeepChem's TensorGraph is so that we could use as much of the automated experimentation tools that are now shipping with Tensorflow as possible. For example, `tf.contrib.learn.Experiment` can be used to further wrap an Estimator and manage all of the flow around training/validation/inference/checkpointing/logging, which has simplified our codebase quite a bit.

I do believe that Tensorflow is moving pretty strongly in the direction of making tf.Estimator central, especially since I see new tutorials written in that way. In my opinion, the best way to create interoperability is to have a really good separation of model functions. For example, if a model function can take input features and a dictionary of hyperparameters and return the final layer logits using any sequence of Tensorflow graph operations, that should be interoperable with any of the wrapper techniques like Estimator or the existing TensorGraph as well.





"

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"@ankitvgupta One possibility I'm looking into right now is adding a `TensorGraph.make_estimator()` method that would create an Estimator from any model, similar to how the Keras `model_to_estimator()` function works.  Does that sound like a good approach to you, or do you think something else would be better?  That would address the use case of integrating with tools designed to work with estimators.  But it wouldn't be able to support a lot of TensorGraph's more advanced capabilities like submodels, serialization, advanced support for recurrent layers, etc."

Title: b'ankitvgupta'
Body:
b'@peastman That seems like a reasonable starting point. The fundamental question that I think is more important is whether building that functionality is more useful in the long-term than building the Keras integration that @rbharath has discussed elsewhere. Intuitively speaking, I am generally a bit concerned about maintaining TensorGraph over the long term when packages like Keras exist and can do much of its functionality, especially with a large team of engineers maintaining them.

My guess is deepchem can be most useful if the contributors invest most of their time in what makes it unique - the chemistry - rather than dealing with all of the intricacies of writing/maintaining a Tensorflow wrapper long-term. That said, if you think that writing a `TensorGraph.make_estimator()` is relatively straightforward, I think that would be a nice stopgap solution to allow people to use new Tensorflow tooling while being able to keep their old models. Title: b'lilleswing'
Body:
b'You are right it is hard right now!  Thanks for bringing it up.  I generally use model performance on the validation set for monitoring the overfitting vs the loss function so the dev team hasn't noticed.

The easiest way right now is to run a fit on the valid_dataset and then restore the checkpoint from the fitting process.

```python
"""
Script that trains multitask models on Tox21 dataset.
"""
# Load Tox21 dataset
n_features = 1024
tox21_tasks, tox21_datasets, transformers = dc.molnet.load_tox21()
train_dataset, valid_dataset, test_dataset = tox21_datasets

# Fit models
metric = dc.metrics.Metric(dc.metrics.roc_auc_score, np.mean)

model = dc.models.MultiTaskClassifier(
    len(tox21_tasks),
    n_features,
    layer_sizes=[1000],
    dropouts=[.25],
    learning_rate=0.001,
    batch_size=50,
    use_queue=False)

# Fit trained model
model.fit(train_dataset, nb_epoch=1)

# checkpoint_interval causes the model not to save a checkpoint.
valid_loss = model.fit(valid_dataset, checkpoint_interval=0)
print(valid_loss)
# This will restore the model to the fit from the train dataset
model.restore()
```

This is not ideal.  The API we want to have is 
``` python
model.fit(train_dataset, nb_epoch=1)
valid_loss = model.predict(valid_dataset, outputs=model.loss)
print(np.mean(valid_loss))
```
However there are currently some assumptions on labels not existing for predict.  I can fix that in a PR.  The first code snippet should work for you right now.

'

Title: b'Combine ANITransformer into ANIRegression'
Body:
b'We are working to combine the ANITransformer into the ANIRegressor. The main goals are:

1. Allows for computation of the positional derivative of the potential
2. Allows for the weights of the transformer itself to be optimized
3. Slightly cleaner and easier to maintain code.

The major downside is that it would make it much harder to use the featurization with non ANIRegressor models. Maybe we should consider more generally allowing any transform to be integrated with downstream Tensorgraph layers?'

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body:
b'I think the ANI case is a weird one -- ANITransformer is really a featurizer and not a transformer IMO.

I would refactor ANITransformer to utilize a TensorGraph under the hood instead of using raw tensorflow.  Then we can re-use the layers created for other TensorGraphs.
'

Title: b'proteneer'
Body:
b"I've finally managed to get gradients, the easy one-liner is in the distance matrix computation, add a tf.nn.relu() before calling tf.sqrt(). Some of the diagonal elements of the distance matrix were extremely tiny negative numbers as a result of numerical instability of adding x with almost ~-x.

Having said that, there are lots of performance issues with the way the dist matrix and other angular components (by abusing the stacks). Notably there's an expansion where by (?, 23, 3) is expanded into (?, 23, 3, 23). We can probably drastically reduce the memory requires by doing a decomposition of the form r - 2AA' + r' where r is the squared norm of the rows. 

In any case, PR coming soonish."

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"#1176 makes this a bit more complicated, since we now want layers to work in both graph mode and eager mode.  And things may change a bit more as I work to get TensorGraph working in eager mode.  For now, here are the additional steps.

1. Add a test in test_layers_eager.py to verify the layer can be invoked in eager mode.
2. For layers that don't create variables (such as the x+2 example suggested above), no particular support is required by the layer.  Things should just work.
3. For layers that do create variables, they should create them the first time `create_tensor()` is called.  The field `_built` is predefined and set to `False` for tracking this.  They should also add all their variables to the `variables` field.  All of this applies *only* to eager mode.

Our mechanism for creating layers is a bit ad hoc.  It has kind of evolved as we've added new features, and is no longer as clean or consistent as it might be.  At some point we may want to think about refactoring it to make the process of defining new layers more consistent."

Title: b'dkoes'
Body: b'What split makes the most sense depends on what sort of generalization error you are trying to measure.  If you are interested in how well you will generalize to new targets, you should split by targets (which is what we do, with a significant difference in sequence identity).  If you are interested in how well you generalize to new chemotypes, a scaffold split makes sense (although this is a bit tricky; e.g. compounds with different scaffolds may still have the same "warheads").\r\n\r\nI don\'t find the time split or the non-core/core split particularly attractive, but to each their own.  They also aren\'t particularly amenable to cross-validation or bootstrapping.'

Title: b'Internal Vina and NNScore (Binana)'
Body:
b"Hello DeepChem team and conributors,

I'm planning to port/include the Numpy based implementation of Vina scoring function and Binana featurizer to DeepChem, as briefly discussed with @rbharath. It's based on my implementation which is currently included in [ODDT](https://github.com/oddt/oddt). In short, the Vina SF is operating purely with Numpy/Scipy which does not require additional IO nor the complicated PDBQT writer procedures. For detailed code see [oddt.docking.internal](https://github.com/oddt/oddt/blob/master/oddt/docking/internal.py) module.

The easiest way to go, would be add a `PoseScorer` or other featurizer API for both and build around ODDT, but will need it as dependency (BSD license). Additional advantage is that it could help phase out Pybel dependecies (#371) by switching them to RDKit backend with ODDT.

The other option is to port the code leaving the boilerplate behind, but it will be much more work and harder to maintain.

The only problem with DeepChem's Binana/NNscore is that it does not use the exact atom types definition on both sides of contacts (ligand and protein). This leads to much bigger (and probably sparse) vector of features. Do we wish to keep that?

Thoughts or suggestions? "

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body: b"@mwojcikowski can you comment on the PoseScorer API you want to propose?  I'm a  bit lost in how you would encapsulate the new atom typing with Rdkit molecules."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"@mwojcikowski Excited to see this moving forward! I think there's a lot of need for improved protein-ligand open source tooling.

In general, I'd be OK with adding on an ODDT dependency. There's no need to add on extra code into DeepChem if there's a good open-source implementation (with usable license) elsewhere. The one question I have is that it looks like ODDT has an openbabel (GPL code) backend. Does that conflict with ODDT's BSD license?

Seconding @lilleswing comment about the API. Would be good to post proposed PoseScorer API here to get feedback before PR."

Title: b'mwojcikowski'
Body:
b'@rbharath ODDT does not include any GPL code. We have `from pybel import *` and we extend base classes from openbabel to our needs. Both toolkits RDKit and OpenBabel are optional and are not required to function properly. Most of the functionality is toolkit independent. Main disadvantage of RDKit is limited format readers/writers, but for Vina and NNScore we're fine.

@lilleswing The atom typing is straightforward. ODDT generates structured Numpy array representing molecule (aka. `atom_dict`, see [docs](https://oddt.readthedocs.io/en/latest/#atom-dict)). It is standardized in both toolkits as much as possible. `atom_dict` is all Vina needs. NNscore on the other hand uses [additional translation](https://github.com/oddt/oddt/blob/master/oddt/scoring/descriptors/__init__.py#L13) from ADT to `atom_dict`.

I hope that clears things up.

Considering the API I will ping you back in a while, I need a moment to identify the best one. Basically we can replace every Vina "--score_only" call. Same goes with NNScore featurizer, which also does Vina scoring. The sampling algorithm for pose generation is under intensive work. '

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body:
b"@mwojcikowski openbabel is GPL :(.  I will begin chats with a legal team on whether incorporating it as an optional module in DeepChem breaks the MIT license (i.e. importing it from util.dependencies and failing if it does not exist and not having it in the ez install script).

How much of the base class logic do you use?  Do you use methods or just the interfaces?  Interfaces are not copy writable, so if we fulfill the interfaces but don't use implementation we are safe.  If we are only using a little simple logic we can rewrite it.
https://www.gnu.org/prep/standards/standards.html#Reading-Non_002dFree-Code

Also I'm excited for a stable PoseScoring API.  Are we going for a regressor?  Are we going for a classifier with various thresholds (hit finding, hit to lead, lead opt)?  Are we going for a rank ordering (most useful for deciding which molecules to synthesize)?
"

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"Great, I think we should be good license wise for now.\r\n\r\n@mwojcikowski the ODDT docs look very nice! We would greatly appreciate any help with the DeepChem docs. They're all in github, but have been languishing for want to attention :-)"

Title: b'mwojcikowski'
Body:
b"@lilleswing It's not the Pybel you were looking for ;) The actual pybel (`pip install openbabel`) is [GPL](https://pypi.python.org/pypi/openbabel). I will underline once again: ODDT does not contain GPL code. 

The ODDT backend for openbabel in question is [here](https://github.com/oddt/oddt/blob/master/oddt/toolkits/ob.py). Feel free to compare its content with the [Pybel module](https://github.com/openbabel/openbabel/blob/master/scripts/python/pybel.py). I use the common interfaces/API for classes, which as you said are not copy writable. If the has no underlying changes it is absent in ODDT code, and inherited from external pybel, eg. `class Molecule(pybel.Molecule)`.

Side note: toolkits are not forced to be installed neither from conda nor from pip. If there are none then ODDT reises exception. If there is just one (RDKit either Openbabel) it keeps using the one throughout.

The only real part you can find identical is the `Residue` class, which I have [authored](https://github.com/openbabel/openbabel/commit/7c8a9b63279cee7cdab0635af218f8165b2fa90f) in between 2.3 and 2.4 so I keep it for backward compability.

Legally there is nothing wrong if MIT code uses GPL code from outside the codebase (hey, you all probably use kernel somewhere). It probably might be forbidden in the company legal guideline to use GPL libraries for any internal use, which as I understand, is what worries you. But in the RDKit + DeepChem + ODDT trio does not violate that rules in any ways (no copyleft code there).  

I hope this calcifies the licensing for now.  

@rbharath Thanks, I try to document as much as I can, although I'd say its rather under-documented at best ;) It's fine that you have tutorials in notebooks but we could maybe move parts of them to straightforward RST and let Sphinx do its magic. I have no idea if google indexes the content of .ipynb on Github."

Title: b'thomasklau'

b'Since you're running the PDB grid featurizer code, I think it would be helpful to say that I found a bug that occurs when hashing ECFP pairs. The string needed to be converted to unicode first. I fixed it to be:

def hash_ecfp_pair(ecfp_pair, power):
  """
  Returns an int of size 2^power representing that
  ECFP pair. Input must be a tuple of strings.
  """
  ecfp = "%s,%s" % (ecfp_pair[0], ecfp_pair[1])
  ecfp = ecfp.encode('utf-8')
  md5 = hashlib.md5()
  md5.update(ecfp)
  digest = md5.hexdigest()
  ecfp_hash = int(digest, 16) % (2**power)
  return (ecfp_hash)

I believe that this makes the code simply not add the ECFP features to the grid.'

Note that this is with tox_siamese_one_fold with n_pos and n_neg = 10. Again, nvidia-smi is just a heuristic, but I'm quite curious to know what are the reasons for the low utilization.

Given that the memory usage is about 11.8GB out of 12GB, maybe we're memory bound?

Edit: This is with Titan X Pascal*"

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"@proteneer That's really interesting. The memory usage is much higher than I would have expected, but I'm not that surprised about the low GPU utilization. The one-shot models do a lot of CPU processing (they sample a task to train on, sample a random support set and query set from the data associated from that task, and then do a gradient descent step). My current guess would be that caching some of the CPU computation could possibly improve GPU utilization."

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"I've been profiling the `tox_res_one_fold.py` example, and the main problem is that it's launching huge numbers of tiny kernels that each run for only a few microseconds. Title: b'rbharath'

2. I'd suggest first optimizing for the case of multiple GPUs on the same server. This is the simplest distributed setup and many teams are actually likely to be able to afford this cluster. The TensorFlow team also has a nice tutorial on doing this for vanilla conv-nets https://www.tensorflow.org/tutorials/deep_cnn#training_a_model_using_multiple_gpu_cards

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"`compute_saliency()` doesn't work with GraphConvModel.  It's designed for models that take a simple numpy array as input and produce one or more arrays as output. Title: b'Oversampling for Multitask Classification'
Body:
b'In the ChemNet fine-tuning (and also the original models trained on MolNet datasets), the authors mention they carry out versampling of the minority class. 

For a single-task classification, this is trivial - you just sample indices of actives, and append them to the original dataset to generate the new dataset, to achieve the desired active / inactive ratio. 

For multi-task classification, how does one go about this? - Being active in one task does not necessarily mean being active in another task, and this can mess up the imbalance when trying to oversample. Also, if we go oversampling task by task, how do we combine the results of the different tasks to get the final dataset? '

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"One way of handling cases like this is to do it with weights: give more weight to the underrepresented class on each task.  That's what BalancingTransformer does.  But since you're trying to reproduce a particular paper, you presumably want to do the same thing they did in the paper.  Do they not explain how they handled this?"

Title: b'vsomnath'
Body:
b"Yes, with the Balancing Transformer already present, I was unsure whether to just stick to that or carry out the oversampling technique mentioned. 

In the paper, they unfortunately don't mention how it is done. This is the only text that talks about this.
> The remaining 5/6th or 9/10th of the dataset was then used in the
random 5-fold cross validation approach for training Chemception, and stratification was enforced
for the classification tasks (Tox21, HIV), which meant that the training, validation and test set had
approximately the same ratio of classes. In addition, we noted that the ratio of the classes for
classification tasks were imbalanced, ranging from 1:5 to 1:34. To address this skewed
distribution, we oversampled the minority class; in the construction of the training/validation/test
set, we computed the imbalance ratio and appended additional data from the minority class by that
imbalance ratio. It should be noted that this oversampling step was performed after stratification 
which means that while the same data may be repeated in a particular training/validation/test set,
the data across different training/validation/test sets are unique and do not overlap. 
"

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'That makes it sound like they trained each task independently, rather than training them together as a multitask model.  Maybe write to them to ask?'

Title: b'vsomnath'
Body: b"So `get_params` works by first getting the init signature and then the parameter names from the signature. Next it iterates through the parameter names and does a `getattr(self, param_name, None)`.\r\nI checked the attributes of `fcnet.MultitaskRegressor` and except `n_features` and `n_tasks` (which don't have any default values assigned), all others don't feature in the list."

Title: b'vsomnath'

Title: b'Upgrade to TF 1.14'
Body:
b"The developers at TensorFlow addressed #1642, saying that this issue has been fixed in TF 1.14, and indeed it has been.

After upgrading to TF 1.14 on a local branch and running tests - most tests passed. The ones which were failing have been fixed except for one, which tries to fit a GAN with multiple generators and discriminators.

I isolated the reason for the failure, and this is a Keras issue and not a DeepChem one.

TF 1.13.1
https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/6612da89516247503f03ef76e974b51a434fb52e/tensorflow/python/keras/engine/network.py#L960

TF 1.14
https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/a5120db4d6917f943176ef3c5bb938064604c761/tensorflow/python/keras/engine/network.py#L849

If you see, there's an extra line `depth_keys = depth_keys[1:]` which was not there in TF 1.13.1
This is preventing some tensors from being computed and hence throwing up an issue with multiple generator-discriminator GAN.

If we should upgrade to TF 1.14, then for now, the GAN test can be marked with `attr('slow')`.

"

Title: b'peastman'

Then we need to make the appropriate changes to our code to work correctly with the new behavior.\r\n\r\nPossibly we'll need to check the TF version at runtime and use a different behavior depending on whether the version is <1.14.  Hopefully that won't be necessary, but we can do it if needed."

Title: b'Population Based Training'
Body:
b'https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.09846
https://dl.acm.org/citation.cfm?doid=3292500.3330649

This is an interesting approach to hyperparameter optimization I just came across.  An implementation in DeepChem could be really useful.  It involves running many optimizations in parallel, each starting with different hyperparameters.  Each process periodically does three things: 1) evaluate it's current performance; 2) if it's one of the worst performing members, replace its parameters and hyperparameters with ones from one of the best performing members, and 3) make small random changes to its hyperparameters.  It's a very efficient way to parallelize training, since it only needs minimal communication between processes.  Since everything happens in parallel, the total clock time for training is the same as for a single optimization on one computer.  And it produces not just a single set of "best" hyperparameters, but a complete schedule for varying them over training.'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'This could be really interesting to have in DeepChem. I think practical hyperparameter optimization is still a major pain point for our users.'

For `fit_generator()` that isn't necessarily possible.  After all, one of the purposes of that method is to support models that take multiple inputs and therefore require more than just the `X` array from a dataset.\r\n\r\nYou also mentioned the possibility of tracking other metrics, which would also be useful. > What do you think the main issues would be?

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"I've been thinking about ways to support this.  There are lots of things someone might want to do.  They might want to compute the average loss over the validation set.  Or some other metric over the validation set.  Or they might have some other way of evaluating the model that doesn't specifically involve a validation set.  Once they've done that there are a lot of things they might want to do.  Examples include:

- Write the evaluation metric to the console.
- Log it to Tensorboard.
- End fitting (early stopping).
- Adjust the learning rate.
- Save a copy of the model parameters to disk.

It would be good to create a mechanism that can support all of these and others.  I'm thinking along the lines of some sort of callback mechanism.  The code might look something like this:

```python
callback = ValidationCallback(validation_dataset, interval=10000)
model.fit(..., callback=callback)
```

We could provide a variety of standard callbacks, and users could also write their own.

Note that Keras also supports a callback mechanism for model fitting, but I don't like some parts of how it's designed.  I think we can do better."

Title: b'vsomnath'
Body:
b'So the current PR does the following things:

- Write the evaluation metric to TensorBoard
- Log it to TensorBoard
- Compute average loss over the validation set
- Compute metrics on the validation set, if metrics are supplied
- Save a copy of model parameters to disk

But a more general setup would definitely be great!

'

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"I'm getting ready to start on this.  Here's the API I'm thinking of.

You can pass an arbitrary list of callbacks to any of the fitting methods.  A callback can be any callable object.  It gets invoked after each step, with the KerasModel being passed as the only argument.  (Possibly the index of the current step will also be passed.  I'm still thinking about that.)  A callback can raise an exception to signal the model to end fitting.

There will be a class called ValidationCallback to handle validation.  When you create it you'll specify a Dataset and an interval at which to perform validation (measured in training steps).  It will only support models that can be directly applied to a Dataset.  For other models, you need to write your own callback.  You can optionally specify one or more Metrics which will be logged along with the loss.

I'm still thinking about how best to handle two other features: early stopping, and saving a copy of the best model parameters so far to a particular directory.  You might potentially want to do all of these things at once, and you don't want several callbacks to each independently repeat the validation.  Should all these be features of a single class?  Or do we allow dependencies between callbacks, so one of them computes the loss and then others make decisions based on it?  Perhaps one callback could wrap another one?  I'm still thinking about it."

Title: b'vsomnath'
Body:
b"So from what I understand, there is a class (BaseLogger), would be invoked at every step and handle loss computation at every step, and logs the training loss periodically. There is a ValidationCallBack, that is setup if `validation_dataset` is not None, and that handles metrics and losses for validation dataset. Is this correct?

I think saving a copy of the best model parameters to directory can be a property of the BaseLogger.
Can't we have EarlyStopping inherit from ValidationCallBack? - It does most things similar to ValidationCallBack, but just has an additional stopping criteria.
"

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"What is BaseLogger?  That wasn't part of my proposal.  Is that something you're suggesting?  If so, could you describe in more detail what it would do?

> Can't we have EarlyStopping inherit from ValidationCallBack?

I considered that, but what if you want both early stopping (when the validation score stops improving) and also saving a copy of the model whenever you get a new best validation score?  If those were separate classes, and each of them extended ValidationCallback, that would mean running the validation twice."

Title: b'vsomnath'
Body:
b'I borrowed the `BaseLogger` term from Keras Callbacks, but it was motivated by your invoked "after every step" statement: 
> A callback can be any callable object. It gets invoked after each step, with the KerasModel being passed as the only argument.

Using the same idea as Keras, this CallBack would compute the loss at every step, and then display every certain iterations. This is used by default in every model. It can slso compute some metrics on the training set, if needed. 

In case of Keras (https://github.com/keras-team/keras/blob/master/keras/callbacks.py), the EarlyStoppingCallback keeps track of the best weights if a toggle is turned on. So having one class should be sufficient.

'

Title: b'MAML and architecture changes'
Body:
b"I'm trying to figure out how to keep MAML (model agnostic metalearning) working with all the architectural changes we're making.  My changes in #1567 have broken it.  I've verified that this is caused by the change to keras layers.  Simply changing one line to replace `tf.layers.Dense` with `tf.keras.layers.Dense` causes it to stop working.

 MAML is an unusual algorithm.  Most models are defined by a series of layers, with each layer defining both a set of variables and a calculation to do.  You might call the layer several times with different inputs, but it always applies the came calculation with the same variables to them.

MAML is different.  You need to apply the model several times using the *same* inputs but *different* variables.  Except sometimes they aren't really variables.  They're the output of a calculation, which you need the layer to use in its calculation where it would normally use variables.  Standard layer classes just aren't written to work that way.

I solved this problem by using the `tf.contrib.graph_editor` module.  You define a model using layers, and it builds a graph from them in the normal way.  Then it clones pieces of the graph, replacing the variables with the outputs of calculations.  This works nicely but has several problems.

First, it apparently doesn't work with keras layers.  I don't know why.  I could try to figure out what they're doing differently that interferes with the graph editor.  Possibly I could get it working again.  But there are other serious problems that will also need to be dealt with very soon.

The second problem is that this approach can never work in eager mode.  It's inherently graph based.  Given that TensorFlow is moving to eager mode as the default approach for everything, that's not very satisfactory.

But a much bigger problem is that `tf.contrib.graph_editor` is going away in TensorFlow 2.  As far as I can tell, it isn't being migrated to its own project or anything like that.  It's just being abandoned and there will no longer be any supported way of doing this sort of graph manipulation.

I've tried to think of an alternate API that could be supported with TensorFlow 2, but I haven't found anything satisfactory.  This algorithm requires you to separate the definition of the variables from the definition of the computation.  You need to define the model using functions of the form `f(inputs, variables)`, where the algorithm can pass in arbitrary tensors to use as the variables.  That isn't how keras layers work, which means you wouldn't be able to use layers in defining your model.

I'm kind of stuck on this.  Any suggestions about what to do?"

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"@rbharath any thoughts on this?  It's blocking #1567, which in turn is blocking lots of other things, so I'd like to reach a decision as quickly as possible."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'There seem to be a couple PyTorch MAML implementations out there (https://github.com/dragen1860/MAML-Pytorch). Perhaps it might be worth seeing how they got MAML to work in eager mode and seeing if a TF eager port would be possible?'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'They define the model with a function of the form `f(inputs, variables)`.  See https://github.com/dragen1860/MAML-Pytorch/blob/master/learner.py#L121.  Then they implement the calculation using the functions in `torch.nn.functional`, which is pretty similar to `tensorflow.nn`.'

Title: b'Updating set of initialized variables under restore '
Body:
b'https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/87410a5e475a043bf68e4f16e57ba8305356153a/deepchem/models/keras_model.py#L326

This is just more of a doubt I have about the ordering of operations, and about where to place restore. 

With the current setup, if `restore` is set to True in `fit_generator()`, the variable values are restored but the set of initialized variables is not updated. The problem is that `_create_training_ops` follows after `restore()`. `_create_training_ops` initializes all the variables again, and hence the restore functionality is overridden by the `session.run(variables_intializer)`. 

I also checked TensorGraph (https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/87410a5e475a043bf68e4f16e57ba8305356153a/deepchem/models/tensorgraph/tensor_graph.py#L217), and there `restore()` is invoked after everything has been initialized. 



'

Title: b'Would it be possible to add the MLQSAR dataset? [moleculenet]'
Body:
b"Hello,

We should have realistic sized datasets to benchmark classification methods
on HTS datasets.

How about integrating the one from:
---
Butkiewicz, M., Lowe, E., Mueller, R., Mendenhall, J., Teixeira, P., Weaver, C., & Meiler, J. (2013). Benchmarking ligand-based virtual high-throughput screening with the PubChem database. Molecules, 18(1), 735-756.
---

Here is a textual description for it:
---
 2. Results and Discussion
2.1. Compilation of Validated PubChem HTS Screens Provides Benchmark Data Sets for Training QSAR Models
PubChem provides publically available libraries of small organic molecules that have been tested in a diverse set of HTS experiments. Primary screens often include many false-positive hit compounds which display a response in initial assay experiments but are inactive in confirmatory experiments. We focus on HTS experiments with a single well-defined biological target protein. With respect to the desired target, these hit compounds may include non-binders that act on a different component of the assay or binders that are non-specific to the target and recognize other biological molecules. To minimize the number of false-positive hit compounds we compiled nine data sets applying the following criteria: the HTS experiment must target one specific protein and contain a minimum of 150 confirmed active compounds. Further, we chose a diverse set of PubChem assays focused on pharmaceutically relevant small molecule protein targets such as GPCRs, ion channels, transporters, kinase inhibitors, and enzymes. All PubChem assays are identified by PubChem summary id (SAID) of the primary protein target and describe a collection of confirmatory screens for active compounds given by PubChem assay ids (AID). It proved critical to go through a detailed manual verification of the HTS experiments performed and collate PubChem raw data to arrive at high-quality data sets.
---

So, nine protein targets, with between 60k to 300k molecules per target.

I have a version somewhere where all molecules have been standardized and separated per target. I could turn it into some CSV files, if that's what you need.

Note that the paper should be cited when people use the dataset, as a courtesy for the people who did the work.

Regards,
F.
"

Title: b'ReduceMean raises assertion error in TensorGraph.build shape check'
Body:
b'**Description:**

<!-- Please provide information about your setup -->
<!-- To get the DeepChem version use the following commands:
>> import deepchem
>> deepchem.__version__ 

If you installed by source please give us the git hash as well
>> git log | head -n 1
-->
- DeepChem Version: 2.2.1.dev49
- Platform: Ubuntu 16.04

<!-- Please describe your problem as detailed as necessary -->
I find the `ReduceMean` layer (and presumably also `ReduceMax` and `ReduceSum` layers) to raise an `AssertionError` when `TensorGraph.build` is called on a model containing these, if the `axis` keyword argument is anything other than `None`. 
<!-- If applicable, please provide working code that can reproduce your issue 
We are much more likely to address a bug with a working reproduction quickly
-->
```
from deepchem.models import TensorGraph
from deepchem.models.tensorgraph.layers import Feature, ReduceMean

class DummyModel(TensorGraph):
  def __init__(self, **kwargs):
    super(DummyModel, self).__init__(**kwargs)
    feature1 = Feature(shape=(None, 2))
    feature2 = Feature(shape=(None, 2))
    output = ReduceMean(in_layers=[feature1, feature2], axis=0])
    self.add_output(output)

model = DummyModel()
model.build()
```
produces the following error message:
```
 File ".../tensor_graph.py", line 764, in build
    layer.name, layer.shape, layer.out_tensor.get_shape().as_list())
AssertionError: ReduceMean_1: Expected shape [2] does not match actual shape [None, 2]
```
I believe this is due to the way the `Reduce*` layers calculate the `_shape` property
```
class ReduceMean(Layer):

  def __init__(self, in_layers=None, axis=None, **kwargs):
    if axis is not None and not isinstance(axis, Sequence):
      axis = [axis]
    self.axis = axis
    super(ReduceMean, self).__init__(in_layers, **kwargs)
    if axis is None:
      self._shape = tuple()
    else:
      try:
        parent_shape = self.in_layers[0].shape
        self._shape = [
            parent_shape[i] for i in range(len(parent_shape)) if i not in axis
        ]
      except:
        pass
```
which does not take into consideration the increase in rank of the tensor on which the `tf.reduce_*` methods are called due to the use of `tf.stack`, which increases the rank by one along the first dimension. I fixed this locally by replacing the relevant sections of code above with:
```
      try:
        parent_shape = [len(self.in_layers)] + self.in_layers[0].shape
        self._shape = [
            parent_shape[i] for i in range(len(parent_shape)) if i not in axis
        ]
      except:
        pass
```

<!-- You can also ask questions on the DeepChem Gitter
https://gitter.im/deepchem/Lobby
-->
'

Title: b'vsomnath'
Body:
b'Hi, 
If you look at the error, it says `expected shape [2]` (which is the correct one), and I would recommend not changing this section.

What should instead be done, in my view is turn the `tf.stack` function in `create_tensor` to `tf.concat`'

Title: b'Alwin-Bucher'
Body: b'Thank you for the swift reply. I am in fact using the ReduceMean layer to perform the kind of averaging that could not be accomplished with `tf.concat` (that which would as it stands require `axis=0`) , but I suppose I could just sum my layers and divide by their number. It does seem more intuitive for the `axis` keyword to refer to the dimensions of the original layers passed in.'

Title: b'vsomnath'
Body:
b'What I wanted to say was, in the `create_tensor` definition for `ReduceMean` layer, `tf.stack` is replaced with `tf.concat`.

```
def create_tensor(self, in_layers=None, set_tensors=True, **kwargs):
    inputs = self._get_input_tensors(in_layers)
    if len(inputs) > 1:
      out_tensor = tf.concat(inputs, axis=0)
    else:
      out_tensor = inputs[0]

    out_tensor = tf.reduce_mean(out_tensor, axis=self.axis)
    if set_tensors:
      self.out_tensor = out_tensor
    return out_tensor
```

If I use this definition, your code (below) runs without any errors.
```
from deepchem.models import TensorGraph
from deepchem.models.tensorgraph.layers import Feature, ReduceMean

class DummyModel(TensorGraph):
  def __init__(self, **kwargs):
    super(DummyModel, self).__init__(**kwargs)
    feature1 = Feature(shape=(None, 2))
    feature2 = Feature(shape=(None, 2))
    output = ReduceMean(in_layers=[feature1, feature2], axis=0])
    self.add_output(output)

model = DummyModel()
model.build()
```

Let me know if the above doesnt work for you.'

Title: b'Alwin-Bucher'
Body: b"I agree. What I meant was that I am in fact creating multiple layers of the same shape and averaging their output tensors, such that the resulting shape is once again the shape of the original layers' output tensors (I.e. in this case `(None, 2)`). I was using `ReduceMean` for this, which worked with the modification I made to the way the `_shape` property was set, and is not possible when `tf.stack` is replaced with `tf.concat`. However, I can see how the intention of the `ReducedMean` layer is more in line with your proposition, and I can of course average my layers using the `Add` layer."

Title: b'vsomnath'
Body:
b'Ah I see what you mean now!
This is a valid point yes. I checked out `tf.reduce_mean` to see what their behavior is.
They give out (None, 2) shaped tensor as well. Expected shape for ReduceMean should be modified, yes.

@rbharath: What do you think?'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'Sounds reasonable to me. @peastman what do you think?'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"I'm not really sure what behavior makes sense when there are multiple inputs.  In fact, I'm not sure it really even makes sense to allow it.  What should happen if the inputs are multiple tensors of incompatible shapes?  I'd be inclined to say ReduceMean should only accept a single input.  If you have multiple inputs, it should be up to you to combine them first in whatever way is appropriate for your problem (such as with a Stack or Concat layer)."

Title: b'vsomnath'
Body:
b'A couple of questions:
1. When you say atomic featurized pdbbind dataset, do you mean you used `ComplexNeighborListFragmentAtomicCoordinates` or the `AtomicConvFeaturizer`?

2. Do you featurize the test-set using `AtomicConvFeaturizer` before running `model.predict()`?

`ComplexNeighborListFragmentAtomicCoordinates` is supposed to prepare the pdbbind_dataset into a format where an `AtomicConvModel` can directly be used to call model.fit()

`AtomicConvFeaturizer` returns the co-crystal embeddings of a trained AtomicConvModel and use it for some tasks. There are a couple of problems with this method right now, not in working but the idea and hence I would recommend not to use it.

So your workflow would look like:
1. Featurize using `ComplexNeighborListFragmentAtomicCoordinates` --> (train, valid, test), transformers
2. Fit an `AtomicConvModel` to this featurized dataset --> model.fit(train)
3. Predict on test dataset --> model.predict(test)
'

Title: b'Data Augmentation Support'
Body:
b"Currently, `dc.trans` only supports simple transformations. There's support for various label transformations to stabilize learning and some limited support for molecular transformations.

![transformers](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1057676/47610148-bc600800-da02-11e8-8ff9-3b8334c383bd.png)

However, there's a lack of support for data augmentation transformations. For example for images, there's a rich family of known perturbations (crops, shifts, rotations, reflections and more) that can help when there's only a small amount of data available. As we add increasing support for image data, we should support such data augmentation techniques."

Title: b'SeanXiaoyuSun'

Title: b'zealseeker'
Body:
b'Hi Sean,
In your code, the (single) model would be fitted five times by the five `train_set`, which are the five "4/5 of the whole dataset".
Let's imagine that in the second loop, the `train_set` becomes `[0, 2, 3, 4]` while the val_set is `[1]`. However, the model object has already trained in the first loop, in which the `train_set` was `[0, 1, 2, 3]`. Say, the model has been trained by all the data in the whole data set and the performance will be overestimated. In real cross validation, we want to use the val_set `[1]` to validate the performance of the model trained by `[0, 2, 3, 4]`.
We should never make model trained by validation set.'

Title: b'SeanXiaoyuSun'
Body: b"Thank you for your explanation @zealseeker ! \r\nI'm confused about how to conduct cross-validation now. As you explained, when doing CV, we should give every split a model object, which means we don't have learned model left after conducting CV. Then which model object should we use to run the test data set? Should we train a model object by the training set again and run test set on this learned model?"

Title: b'zealseeker'
Body: b'@SeanXiaoyuSun You are right. Cross-validation is used to evaluate the rubostness of the "final model" trained by the whole training set. However, during cross-validation, the `n` models actually are not trained by the whole training set, but `n-1/n` for each fold.'

Title: b'Reuse model.fit may overestimate the performance in cross-validation'
Body:
b"I was trying to evaluate a model via cross-validation,
here is my code:
```python
def tf_graph_model(dataset, transformers=None, testset=None):
    # Batch size of models
    batch_size = 50
    model = GraphConvTensorGraph(
        1, batch_size=batch_size, mode='classification')
    spliter = dc.splits.RandomSplitter()
    split_datas = spliter.k_fold_split(dataset,5)
    scores = {m.name:[] for m in metrics}
    for train_set, val_set in split_datas:
        # Fit trained model
        model.fit(train_set, nb_epoch=10)
        valid_scores = model.evaluate(val_set,metrics,transformers)
        for name in valid_scores:
            scores[name].append(valid_scores[name])
    for name in scores:
        scores[name] = np.mean(scores[name])
    return scores
```

In this function, I created only one model instance and fed it repeatedly during 5-fold cross-validation.
I found that the performance of the model will be overestimated according to the result that the scores (metrics) would keep increasing in cross-validation (i.e. the performance of the 2nd fold was better then the 1st; the 3rd was better than the 1st and the 2nd ...). So the mean of the five scores cannot represent the real performance of the model.

I guess that when the model was fed by another training set, the variables/weights of the model were not initialed again, instead, the optimization was based on the previous fed model.

An alternative way is to create a new model instance for each split data. But Is there any way better like 
 `model.init()`"

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"Each split should have its own model object. The current design leaks information since weights are shared. For example:

```
def tf_graph_model(dataset, transformers=None, testset=None):
    # Batch size of models
    batch_size = 50
    spliter = dc.splits.RandomSplitter()
    split_datas = spliter.k_fold_split(dataset,5)
    scores = {m.name:[] for m in metrics}
    for train_set, val_set in split_datas:
        model = GraphConvTensorGraph(
            1, batch_size=batch_size, mode='classification')
        # Fit trained model
        model.fit(train_set, nb_epoch=10)
        valid_scores = model.evaluate(val_set,metrics,transformers)
        for name in valid_scores:
            scores[name].append(valid_scores[name])
    for name in scores:
        scores[name] = np.mean(scores[name])
    return scores
```"

Title: b'SeanXiaoyuSun'
Body: b"@rbharath Sorry for this novice question. If we want to conduct cross validation, why should we give every split a model object? Shouldn't we train a single model with these 5 train/val splits and test this model by using an additional test set?"

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"That's not what cross validation is.  In cross validation, you divide your dataset into N parts.  You then train N models, each time using N-1 of those parts as the training set and the final part as the test set.  So in this case, you would train the model on 4/5 of the data then test it on the remaining 1/5.  And you would do that 5 times, each time using a different 1/5 of the data as the test set."

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"The next step is to debug those failures to figure out what's going on.  That will involve adding debugging code to get more information.  For example, consider the error in `test_delaney_graphconvreg()`.  Here's the code where it's failing:

```python
    with open(os.path.join(out_path, 'results.csv'), 'r') as f:
      reader = csv.reader(f)
      for lastrow in reader:
        pass
      assert lastrow[-4] == 'valid'
```

It just skims through the file to the last line and checks that it has the expected values in it.  That test is failing, perhaps indicating that the CSV reader isn't processing it correctly.  So print out `lastrow` and see what it actually contains.

Or consider the error in `test_weave_regression_model()`.  Here's the full code of that test case:

```python
  def test_weave_regression_model(self):
    tasks, dataset, transformers, metric = self.get_dataset(
        'regression', 'Weave')

    model = WeaveModel(len(tasks), mode='regression')

    model.fit(dataset, nb_epoch=80)
    scores = model.evaluate(dataset, [metric], transformers)
    assert all(s < 0.1 for s in scores['mean_absolute_error'])

    model.save()
    model = TensorGraph.load_from_dir(model.model_dir)
    scores2 = model.evaluate(dataset, [metric], transformers)
    assert np.allclose(scores['mean_absolute_error'],
                       scores2['mean_absolute_error'])
```

It trains a model, saves it to disk, and produces evaluation metrics from it.  Then it reloads the model from disk, evaluates the reconstructed version, and checks that it produces identical results.  That test is failing.  Possibly this indicates a problem in saving and loading models?  Or perhaps it's just an overly strict numeric tolerance?  The first thing to do is add code that prints out the values being compared:

```python
print(scores['mean_absolute_error'])
print(scores2['mean_absolute_error'])
```

See whether they're only slightly different or very different.  If they're very different, that suggests something is going wrong in the saving and loading.  So then you need to start instrumenting the routines that save and load to trace backward and figure out what's going wrong."

Title: b'proteneer'
Body: b"@evanfeinberg \r\n\r\nYou're using an alpha of 20? From the paper - I think for BEDROC to be meaningful it should satisfy the condition that alpha*(ratio of actives to inactives) be significantly less than 1. That is, for something like tox21 where only about 3-5% of the dataset is active, the default choice of 20 seems inappropriate. Intuitively, the alpha parameter is a measure of desired enrichment, which is only meaningful if the ratio of actives to inactives is small. Furthermore, increasing alpha values tends to lead to an increase in the statistical error of the measurement method itself. "

Title: b'proteneer'
Body: b"Also be aware that it's totally nonsensical to compare BEDROCs across different alpha values, so we should document clearly what the chosen alphas are when reporting results."

One issue I have with the 100%/10%/1% FPR cutoffs for evaluation is that it makes things harder for ML people who aren't chemistry experts. Title: b'jisraeli'
Body:
b"@rbharath: Let me start with a huge congrats to you and the team here on putting together MoleculeNet - quality benchmark datasets are invaluable for machine learning in this field.

Equally important are evaluation metrics that reflect what downstream practitioners would want out of the predictions. The field of TF binding imputation has had a clear gap in this regard for quite some time. Below I provide a brief overview of the task at hand, key developments over the past 2 years, and the [ENCODE-DREAM TF binding challenge](https://www.synapse.org/#!Synapse:syn6131484/wiki/402026) in that context:

The human genome has 3E9 bp, processed ChIP-seq data puts the number of reproducible TF sites genome-wide in the ~1K-50K range (varies by TF and celltype), and this data allows TF site detection with ~200 bp resolution: The positive class in these tasks is usually <0.1%. TF site predictions may be used for targeted validation experiments and other downstream models (of gene expression for example). For the purposes of experimental validation, the predictions have to control the false discovery rate (FDR) - a typical FDR experimentalists ask for is 10%. For downstream models, low FDR for TF binding predictions is not as critical as along as those downstream models meet their own FDR requirements - an FDR of 50% in this context could work just fine.

Without these application-specific metrics in mind, a brief survey of recent literature may suggest TF binding is nearly solved. [DeepBind](http://www.nature.com/nbt/journal/v33/n8/full/nbt.3300.html) reported SOTA auROC on the previous DREAM TF binding challenge, and follow-ups to DeepBind such as [Deep Motif](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.01133) and [Genetic Architect](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.07156)  further improve auROC on DeepBind's tasks to 0.95. However, the evaluation of these models is not a good indicator because it is based on 1) a synthetic negative set orders of magnitude smaller than the full human genome, 2) auROC and 3) same test celltype as training celltype. [DeepSEA](http://www.nature.com/nmeth/journal/v12/n10/full/nmeth.3547.html#methods) and followups such as [DanQ](https://academic.oup.com/nar/article/44/11/e107/2468300/DanQ-a-hybrid-convolutional-and-recurrent-deep) report SOTA auROC and auPRC on 17% of the genome on same celltype predictions - this evaluation improves one the first two issues. A [recently published deep learning model](http://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005403) seems to beat both DeepBind and DeepSEA on their respectively test data, but when its evaluated on a full test chromosome (no negative set subsampling as usually done) the sobering truth comes out: its recall is <10% at 50% FDR for most tasks - 10% FDR is not reported most likely because the recall there is effectively 0%. Based on my own evaluation, it is not unusual to get >0.99 auROC and still get 0% recall at 10% FDR on a full test.

The TF binding challenge asks for predictions on an unseen celltype, on unseen chromosomes, on every interval (no negative set subsampling). Participants are ranked by combining their auROC, auPRC, recall at 10% FDR, and recall at 50% FDR (see the challenge wiki for more details on this). We also show their recall at 5% and 25% FDR but do not use those for ranking. I am not familiar enough with this domain to suggest specific metrics at the moment, but I'd be happy to discuss these questions in more detail and help converge on them. By sharing the developments in the TF binding field, I hope that I have clarified the importance of establishing clear evaluation metrics early on."

Title: b'jisraeli'
Body: b"I looked at the figure @agitter pointed to from the overview of footprinting-based methods for TF binding predictions. It suggests the HINT method comes out at the top with an auPRC of ~0.7. HINT participated in the challenge so you can see how well it works - while performance is commendable, it's a long way from auPRC of ~0.7. There are multiple submissions that outperformed HINT, and an auPRC of 0.7 would be a serious breakthrough wrt the top submissions.\r\n\r\nThe FPR-based metrics in this case do not really correspond to the needs of downstream applications. When the negative set is 99.9% of the data, if we assume 100% recall for FPR of 1%, that means that for every 10 true positives detected you get 100 false positives or, equivalently, a 91% FDR. It doesn't make sense to validate predictions >91% of which are not going to work."

Title: b'agitter'
Body:
b"@jisraeli I didn't want to read too much into the conclusions of that benchmarking study, I was mostly referring to it for the visualization and presentation of the results.  I accept your conclusions about HINT.  My main point was that I find it useful when multiple evaluation metrics or thresholds are used in a benchmarking study, even if one of them is given priority.

I see your point about how auROC is still inappropriate at more stringent FPR cutoffs for TF binding.  In the DREAM example, I agree that recall at a fixed FDR is a good evaluation metric.  It still makes sense to look at multiple thresholds (e.g. 10% and 50%) depending on whether the predictions are being used for experimental validation or downstream modeling.

In MoleculeNet, @rbharath and others can say more about what the right metric is.  My main suggestion was to consider more than one metric or threshold, perhaps with a visualization as used in the Gusmao study I linked.  I expect that for MoleculeNet, an experimentalist and an machine learning researcher will have different needs and different preferred metrics."

Title: b'Extract trained weights from TensorGraph Layer'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b'Here's one way to get the variable associated with a layer:
```
variables = model._get_tf("Graph").get_collection("variables", scope=layer.name)

```
weights = model.session.run(variables)
