Title: b'Why my restoring does not work as expected? '
Body:
b'To implement early stopping, I have expanded the `fit()` function in `deepchem/models/tensorgraph/tensor_graph.py` in my customized implementation. The original code can be found here: https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/6f86377d9bff4541ff50ec014743d840a3e230f4/deepchem/models/tensorgraph/tensor_graph.py#L112

Here is a very simplified version of what I wrote inside the body of the function (this code cannot run, just present you with the most relevant information):
```python
if early_stopping:
    # Creating this new field called temp_model_dir 
    self.temp_model_dir = self.model_dir + "/temp"
       
    with self._get_tf("Graph").as_default():
      # The line below is simply added to prevent the error of "nothing to save"
      v1 = tf.get_variable("v1", shape=[3], initializer = tf.zeros_initializer)
      saver = tf.train.Saver()
     
      for _ in range(iterations):              
        # Temporarily overriding the path of saving.
        self.save_file = "%s/%s" % (self.temp_model_dir, "model")
        self.fit_generator(self.default_generator())
        # Validation score.
        val_sc = self.evaluate(valid_dataset, metric, transformers)[metric[0].name] 

        # Resuming the path of saving.
        self.save_file = "%s/%s" % (self.model_dir, "model")
                       
        if val_sc beats the current best score:
          best_score = val_sc
          # Saving in the resumed path
          saver.save(self.session, self.save_file, global_step=self.global_step)
       
      self.restore() # From source code it seems to only restore from the self.model_dir
      self.evaluate(valid_dataset, metric, transformers)
    return
```

As is shown, I have overriden the saving path (`self.save_file`) with `self.temp_model_dir` when running the `fit_generator()`, and only saving the session to `self.model_dir` after confirming that it is indeed the best model. When running the model, I also confirmed that it has the desired behavior: only the models producing the best scores (at the time) are saved in (the directory corresponding to) `self.model_dir`, while `self.temp_model_dir` has the whole collection of models saved automatically by `fit_generator()` function.

The `self.restore()` function which is defined in the same script restores the session from `self.model_dir` by default. So I would expect that only the model with the optimal number of training epochs should be restored by the `self.restore()`. However, by examining the results of the ensuing `self.evaluate()` function, it becomes clear that this is not the case: whether or not the last training epoch yields the best model, the `self.evaluate()` function in the second last line always produces a result identical to the last run of `self.evaluate(valid_dataset, metric, transformers)`.   

If any of you needs a runnable version of the code, please don't hesitate to ask me.

I really need your help in this. Thank you very much!'

Title: b'simonfqy'
Body:
b'I think I have found out the source of the problem. The code below would behave as I desired:
```python
if early_stopping:
    # Creating this new field called temp_model_dir 
    self.temp_model_dir = self.model_dir + "/temp"
       
    with self._get_tf("Graph").as_default():  
           
      for _ in range(iterations):              
        # Temporarily overriding the path of saving.
        self.save_file = "%s/%s" % (self.temp_model_dir, "model")
        self.fit_generator(self.default_generator())
        saver = tf.train.Saver()
        # Validation score.
        val_sc = self.evaluate(valid_dataset, metric, transformers)[metric[0].name] 

        # Resuming the path of saving.
        self.save_file = "%s/%s" % (self.model_dir, "model")
                       
        if val_sc beats the current best score:
          best_score = val_sc
          # Saving in the resumed path
          saver.save(self.session, self.save_file, global_step=self.global_step)
       
      self.restore() # From source code it seems to only restore from the self.model_dir
      self.evaluate(valid_dataset, metric, transformers)
    return
```
The reason my previous code does not work is that I have initialized the `saver` before the `fit_generator()`, at which point the graph only has 1 global variable, which is `v1`, and the `saver` is actually saving nothing else but the value of `v1` each time `saver.save()` is called. 

Now that I put the initialization of `saver` right after the `fit_generator`, so when `saver.save()` is called, it saves the variables of the graph that constitute the neural network.'

Title: b'evanfeinberg'
Body:
b'In case it's useful, reiterating what I mentioned in a subgroup meeting
last year: one can take matrix powers of the NxN adjacency matrix "A" to do
atrous graph convolution. So for those graph convolutional models that use
the basic update (or some variation): h = W * A * x, one can instead just
do h = W * (A^p) * x, where x is the input feature matrix, p is an integer
representing just how atrous you want your graph convolution to be, and W
is a weight matrix. For example, a "1" at the (i, j) position of (A^2)
indicates that atom_i and atom_j are two bonds away from each other. This
simple formulation could lower the bar significantly for coding.

Anecdotally, I haven't seen significant improvements in performance with
atrous vs. normal graph conv, at least on Tox21 and PDBBind, though perhaps
with more hyperparam searching it's possible. Interesting to see what comes
out of this!

Title: b'Why training by default starts from scratch, while evaluation/prediction does not?'
Body:
b"This could be more of a TensorFlow question. Please don't laugh at me if it is too simple.

In the `deepchem/models/tensorgraph/tensor_graph.py` script, in the documentation of the `fit_generator()` function, it says this for the `restore` parameter of the function: 

> restore: bool
      if True, restore the model from the most recent checkpoint and continue training
      from there.  If False, retrain the model from scratch.

https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/6f86377d9bff4541ff50ec014743d840a3e230f4/deepchem/models/tensorgraph/tensor_graph.py#L149

In the function, if `restore == True`, `self.restore()` is called.

And we can see that for the `predict_on_generator()` function in the same file, there is no need for calling `self.restore()` and the model predicts the output value given the input, using the most updated parameter values in the network. Why is this the case?

And I don't quite understand the `_enqueue_batch()` function and the `enqueue_thread` variable which is based on that. Maybe they have some roles to play in this?

Thanks for reading!"

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body:
b'This is a documentation error.  When restore=False we simply do not restore the model.

TensorgGraph is a two step process
1) Construct the Graph
2) Build the Graph

Constructing the graph is done via TensorGraph.add_output(), TensorGraph.set_loss().

Before fitting we have to "build" the graph via TensorGraph.build().  This puts all of the ops in the Graph into a Tensorflow Session.  build() also calls  self.session.run(tf.global_variables_initializer()).   Restore restores all the variables from a checkpoint, but the graph is still computed via the same python mechanisms.'

Title: b'simonfqy'
Body: b'@lilleswing Thanks for your reply. \r\nIf I want to really retrain the model from scratch, is it that I need to call the `fit()` function in `tensor_graph.py` from the caller again, with `restore=False` argument? If not, what is the correct and reasonably easy way to retrain a model from scratch? (I guess that reinstantiating a `TensorGraph` object, like creating one using `WeaveTensorGraph()` function with the same parameters as the first time and calling the fit() function would work. However it is a more tedious and "dirty" way, and I wonder whether their exist "cleaner" methods.)'

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b'We changed some of this behavior a while back, and it looks like that docstring didn't get updated at the time.  Here's how it actually works.

1. When you first create a model, all its variables get initialized based on whatever initializers the layers specify.  (Actually this gets done in `build()`, which happens the first time you call any method that requires the graph.)

2. By default, `fit()` performs fitting starting from whatever values the variables currently have.  If this is the first call to `fit()` and you haven't done anything else to change them (like calling `restore()`), they'll have the values set by the initializers.  But you can override this behavior by specifying `restore=True`, in which case it will restore from the most recent checkpoint.

3. Usually you call `fit()` before `predict()`, so the model will already have the right variables.  But sometimes you run fitting, it saves the variables to a checkpoint, and then later (in a different run of the program) you want to do prediction.  In that case, call `restore()` before calling `predict()`.

There isn't a function to reset the variables to their initial values.  Usually it's easiest to just throw out the old model and create a new one.  But you could try this:

```python
with model._get_tf("Graph").as_default():
  model.session.run(tf.global_variables_initializer())
```

I haven't tried it, but it seems like it ought to work.'

Title: b'Do the batch normalization functions implemented differentiate between training and evaluation?'
Body:
b'**Note that some questions in this post are not correctly raised. I deleted those from my post below.**
In the script `deepchem/models/tensorgraph/layers.py`, there are two classes for batch normalization, `BatchNorm` and `BatchNormalization`, which you can see from here.
 https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/6f86377d9bff4541ff50ec014743d840a3e230f4/deepchem/models/tensorgraph/layers.py#L2870 

However, I think that in the `create_tensor()` functions of both classes, the cases between training and evaluating are not differentiated. Especially in the `create_tensor` function of the `BatchNorm` class which calls `tf.layers.batch_normalization()`, the "training" flag of this `TensorFlow` function is not specified. So I suppose that it will not work entirely properly.

I tried including the flag myself. I inserted one line of code (the second line below) in `create_tensor()` function of the `BatchNorm` class:
```Python
parent_tensor = inputs[0]
self.training = tf.equal(tf.constant(1.0, dtype=tf.float32), kwargs['training']) # Newly inserted
out_tensor = tf.layers.batch_normalization(parent_tensor)
```

in which the `kwargs['training']` should be `self._training_placeholder` of TensorGraph class, which should have a value of 1.0 for training case and 0.0 for evaluation/testing case. '

Title: b'Move dc.dock out of core library'
Body:
b"Compared with the other core submodules of `deepchem`, `dc.dock` is a little anomalous. Most of the other submodules (`dc.feat`, `dc.models`, `dc.hyper` etc.) have to do with providing core machine learning functionality. Since this is DeepChem, the functionality in these modules is geared towards scientific applications, but everything is written in a general manner that would allow for use in arbitrary machine learning applications.

`dc.dock` is different though. Docking is a specialized application that's of primary interest to computational structure-based drug design. As a result, `dc.dock` is one of the loneliest submodules in DeepChem with only limited development effort.

I propose we move `dc.dock` out of the core library and either into `contrib/` or a separate package in the DeepChem organization. Since I suspect there are a few users of `dc.dock` around, if we proceed, this should be a slower change with a deprecation cycle warning of the coming change."

Title: b'Integrating tf.data and dc.data'
Body: b"Continuing our architectural discussions, it's starting to become clear we should integrate dc.data and tf.data in some manner. dc.data is one of the hackier parts of DeepChem and has caused us a good number of scaling and portability headaches. Swapping out this code for optimized tf defaults seems generally useful.\r\n\r\nAt the same time, we need to plan a transition that doesn't entirely break backwards compatibility. Let's use this thread to brainstorm possible implementation paths."

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b'tf.data is very flexible but also awkward to use.  There's nothing nearly as simple as just passing a Dataset object to a model.  Instead, every time you use a dataset you have to write an "input function" that's responsible for gathering up the data and packaging it in whatever way is required.

I think this feature request involves two pieces:

1. Allow a DeepChem Dataset to be used with models designed for use with tf.data.  I don't think this should be hard, especially given that you're expected to write adapter code anyway.  A simple implementation would be to add a `make_iterator()` method to Dataset.  It would return a tf.data.Iterator, which exposes tensors for reading the data.  I'll try implementing this.

2. Allow TensorGraph models to work with tf.data data sources.  This will require more thought.  Possibly we want to redesign TensorGraph to be a subclass of tf.estimator.Estimator.  Or we might create a way to wrap a TensorGraph in an Estimator, similar to how `tf.keras.estimator.model_to_estimator()` works.'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'I think we can close this since addressed by #1091 and the new tutorials on using Dataset and tf.data together.'

Title: b'Reusing pieces of models'
Body: b"Most of DeepChem is based on the assumption that you want to create a model, then train that model, then make predictions based on that trained model.  But sometimes that isn't what you want.  Rather than making predictions with the trained model directly, you might want to reuse part or all of it as one piece of a larger model.\r\n\r\nHere's an example I'm dealing with right now.  I want to start with a SeqToSeq model and train it as an autoencoder.  Then I want to take just the encoder portion of that trained model, and use it as part of a policy for RL.  I can hack something together that will do that, but it will be ugly, and it seems to me this is a common problem.  Do we want to consider ways to make this sort of thing easier?"

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"Since no one has commented on this, let me offer a candidate proposal.

1. We'll add an optional field to Layer that stores the initial values of all its variables.  When you create a TensorGraph containing that layer, it starts by setting the variables to those values.  For layers that already have configurable initializers, this will override them.  The idea is that this lets a Layer object describe a *pretrained* layer.

2. We might consider adding an option to `TensorGraph.save()` that tells it to include the values of all trainable variables in the saved layers.  That would allow you to store a complete trained model, both the model structure and the parameter values, in a single file.

3. We'll create a function to clone a tree of Layer objects.  You call it on a single Layer, and it recursively creates a copy of that Layer and every parent Layer it depends on.  You can optionally specify a TensorGraph, and the cloned Layers will include the values of all trainable variables from that graph.  This lets you clone a piece of a trained model and have the variables get copied with it.

4. We also might consider adding a StopGradient layer that passes its input through `tf.stop_gradient()`.  That way you could incorporate a pretrained model into a larger model, and tell it that the pretrained layers shouldn't be optimized any further.  It also could be useful in other contexts, like GANs."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"As a counterproposal, I suggest we implement Keras's functional API. In this API, models themselves can be invoked as layers:

https://keras.io/getting-started/functional-api-guide/

This should allow for an elegant solution to the resuse problem and has some buy-in already from larger deep learning community as a standard API"

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"I don't see how that solves the problem.  In the example above I don't want to reuse the whole model, just one piece of it.  More generally, pretraining involves training a set of layers in the context of one model, then reusing those trained layers in the context of a different model.  It requires fine control to be able to pull out just the specific pieces you want.\r\n\r\nAlso, I think you're only suggesting that as an alternative to number 3 above?  I don't think it has much to do with numbers 1, 2, and 4."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"For Seq2Seq, in the functional API, we would define it as the composition of two models, an encoder model and a decoder model. Then to reuse the encoder, you can just pull out the encoder subcomponent of the Seq2Seq model.

For the pretraining problem in general, you'd just define submodels in places where you think you might want to pull out pieces later. In this view, models are basically generalized layers, so it allows for elegant decompositions.

I think the functional API is a healthy high level API evolution in general. If we decide it's worthwhile, we should think about spec-ing out the concrete changes needed"

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b'I think we're talking about orthogonal things.  The "submodels" you suggest might be a useful abstraction to introduce, but they're a different sort of entity from "models" in DeepChem.  A TensorGraph model specifies a loss function and an optimizer.  It's associated with a particular Tensorflow graph, and it owns a session that it uses to store its variables.  None of those would be true of submodels.

I think what you're talking about is just having a "metalayer" that groups a bunch of layers together and lets you work with it as a single layer?  That's potentially useful, but it doesn't replace the need for any of the things I suggested above.  You still need a way to copy layers from one model to another while preserving their variables, whether or not those layers have been grouped into a submodel.

What I'm talking about is something much closer to Tensorflow's [graph_replace()](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/contrib/graph_editor/graph_replace) function.  A way of telling it, "Make a copy of these layers while hooking them up to new inputs."'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'Ah, I see your point now. I agree we\'re talking about orthogonal issues. Yes, I think the "metalayer" is the correct replacement for 3 above (since we might not want to clone the entire tree but rather parts of it), but the overall proposal seems sound to me.'

b"I wanted to open this one up to discussion.

DeepChem has built up a variety of high-quality models, some of which can actually get quite far with the limited public data out there. Today, we can take in an arbitrary molecule and estimate its properties reasonably well. What's missing imo is a good way of going from molecule to molecule, which is holding back our ability to do drug optimization here.

I'm not sure about autoencoders. It seems like a nice idea, but they don't really have much respect for synthesizability. I'm not sure hallucinating LSTMs are much better? In some ways I think matched molecular pairs might be the easiest option for now [link](http://rdkit.blogspot.com/2014/08/mmpa-on-chembl-herg-data-using-pandas.html).

Thoughts?

Edit by @rbharath: Fixed link "

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b'I agree that a way of systematically exploring chemical space would be of high value (perhaps a deepchem 1.3 target? #669).

I like the idea of starting with matched molecular pairs. Simple chemoinformatics techniques are often the best baseline before trying more complicated ideas.

PRs welcome!'

Title: b'Definition of save() and reload() inconsistent between TensorGraph and other models'
Body:
b"Copying over @peastman's comment from #522 to kick off the discussion

> TensorGraph doesn't implement reload(), so I'm trying to implement it. In the process, though, I've found there's some ambiguity in what save() and reload() are supposed to do. For other Model subclasses, save() means to write out the current values of all parameters. That is, write a checkpoint. reload() then loads those saved parameters back in. But in TensorGraph, save() does something completely different: it pickles the TensorGraph object itself, so a description of all the layers that make up the model. It then has a load_from_dir() method for reconstructing pickled models, but as far as I can tell, no method for loading checkpoints. Instead, it automatically reloads the most recent checkpoint (if there is one) when you call fit() or predict().
>
> How should this work?

I agree that we should figure out a consistent semantics for all models otherwise we'll have some confused users"

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body:
b'I might be biased -- but I do like the internal weights of a model being part of its internal state and as hidden from the user as possible.

That is how TensorGraph currently does it --
#save() saves the whole object, including weights
#fit() and #predict() use the most up to date weights at all times.'

Body: b'Following up on https://twitter.com/rbhar90/status/970075142586974208 - am I reading the documentation right, in that k=2 for the default in HER? Is there a particular reason for this (the paper prescribes 4, but it is a very different task)? An experiment where k=2 worked much better?\r\n\r\nI am looking at using HER in a very different scenario than the paper (music generation in my case) so I was intrigued by how it is used in deepchem. Thanks'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'CC @peastman '

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"Sorry, I'm not sure what you're referring to.  What is k?"

Title: b'kastnerkyle'
Body: b'In the paper, k is the number of "false state/goals" that are introduced during HER, relative to the "true" goals. They talk about the importance of the choice for k in section 4.5 of the paper https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.01495 , and specifically prescribe k=4. I\'ve been looking around at various implementations, and yours is the first I saw for something that wasn\'t the same experiments as the paper. So I figured I would ask about the differences/how HER came to be used in deepchem, and why the defaults seem different (it looks like k=1 or possibly 2, based on this comment https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/e20c14513ffccb8883a84aa1ef908a9c9c5ea576/deepchem/rl/a3c.py#L91, but maybe I am just reading the code wrong)'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"You're reading it correctly.  That setting doesn't really apply to A3C.  All of the methods they consider involve a replay buffer, so they're free to take whatever set of states and goals they want from the buffer.  But A3C doesn't have a replay buffer.  It just generates a rollout, processes it exactly once, and then throws it away.  When using HER, we process it a second time using the alternate goal."

Title: b'Tutorial Demonstrating using TensorGraph layers with TensorFlow Eager'
Body:
b"[TensorFlow eager](https://research.googleblog.com/2017/10/eager-execution-imperative-define-by.html) has been out as `tf.contrib.eager` since TensorFlow 1.5. It would be great to add a tutorial that demonstrates how TensorGraph layers can be used with TensorFlow eager. This would be a great first contribution for a newcomer to the library and would add a lot of value to the community.

Here are the steps needed to submit this PR:

- As with our other tutorial, this one should be an IPython notebook added to the folder https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/tree/master/examples/notebooks
- Explain how to construct a TensorGraph layer with a few examples. For example
  - `dense_layer = Dense(5)`
- Explain that constructing the layer doesn't actually perform any tensor ops. This is done when `create_tensor()` is called. 
  - `dense_layer.create_tensor(in_layers=[input])`
- Note that as syntactic sugar, layer.create_tensor can be invoked via `__call__()`
  - `Dense(5)(input)` has the same effect as the function call above
- Provide an example of using the function invocation style with TensorFlow eager code. For example, something like the following code snippet.
```
import tensorflow as tf
import tensorflow.contrib.eager as tfe

tfe.enable_eager_execution()

x = [[2.]]
out = Dense(3)(x)
print(out)
```
- Demonstrate how to take gradients of eager code that uses TensorGraph layers.

If you're interested in implementing this tutorial, please make a comment on this thread and raise an issue marked [WIP] that tracks your in-progress implementation."

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'Does this actually work?  If so, that\'s really cool.  Though I suspect "write a tutorial" will turn into "discover lots of edge cases that don\'t work correctly, which we can then figure out ways to fix."  But it definitely sounds like something we want to support.'

Title: b'Batch normalization in convolution'
Body:
b"I just spent a few days tracking down a problem that ultimately turned out to be caused by the fact that the Conv2D layer applies batch normalization.  This can cause really subtle, hard to identify incorrect behaviors.  In my case, I had an RL model that contained both a Conv2D and a GRU.  When it was executing a rollout, it would take one step at a time (batch size of 1).  Then it would evaluate the loss function on the whole rollout, which meant the batch normalization would produce different values, and hence the sequence of internal states in the GRU would be different.  So effectively it was selecting steps based on one policy but computing the loss as if it had used a different policy.  The only visible sign of the error was that it didn't do a very good job of learning.

Obviously the Conv2D layer needs an option to select the normalization function.  I'll add that.  I also notice that AtomicConvolution applies batch normalization.  Should it have the same option?

Is batch normalization even a good default behavior?  It can help in some cases, but as seen above, it can also produce really subtle errors.  I'm inclined to say the default normalization function should be None.  That's the default for `tf.contrib.layers.conv2d()`."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"I'm inclined to turn off batch norm as default too. As you point out there are many subtle batch norm bugs, and having opt-in seems better."

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body: b"I'm inclined to turn off batch norm as default as well."

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"#655 addresses this as far as Conv2D is concerned.  I haven't changed AtomicConvolution because I'm less clear on how that works.  Perhaps someone who knows the atomic convolution code can fix that?  Until it's fixed, any RL model that includes both an AtomicConvolution and a GRU won't work correctly."

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body: b"@peastman I can add batch norm as a flag to atomic conv. \r\n\r\nThe batch norm helps performance but it isn't integral to the atomic conv architecture."

Title: b'Computing gradients w.r.t input in TensorGraph'
Body:
b"In order to implement pose-generation algorithms for docking, we need to be able to take the derivative of the deep score function with respect to the atomic coordinates of the molecule. If the score function is implemented as a `TensorGraph` model, we will consequently need a way to take a derivative of the loss w.r.t a `Features` node. I can see a couple ways to make this happen:

- Define a general `gradients(layer_1, layer_2)` method that returns `tf.gradients(layer_1.out_tensor, layer_2.out_tensor)`.
- Define a special purpose method for taking gradients w.r.t `Features` instead of arbitrary layers.

@lilleswing, @peastman, would love to hear your thoughts on which API you'd prefer. "

Title: b'Does TensorGraph need to be pickled?'
Body: b"I know it's supposed to be a major feature of TensorGraph that you can pickle it, but why?  I haven't yet come across any situations where I actually wanted to pickle one, and I can't think of any use cases where it's a big advantage.  And supporting this feature comes at a cost.  First, of course, it makes the code more complicated.  All the shuffling around of tensors before and after pickling is a bit confusing.  It also make the API messier.  We can't pickle optimizers or initializers, which requires users to work through the TFWrapper class.  And then there are some things we just can't do because of it.  I'd really like to be able to use lambdas to define new layers.  But lambdas can't be pickled, so that just isn't an option.\r\n\r\nWhat are the reasons for wanting this feature?  And do they really outweigh the costs?"

Title: b'proteneer'
Body: b'I think the main reason was that we want to be able to restore the weights for a trained model without having to re-train it.'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"That doesn't require pickling the TensorGraph itself, just using a Saver to record the variables (same as we do with all other models)."

Title: b'proteneer'
Body: b'How do you recommend the topology itself being serialized out then?'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"That's the question: what are the use cases where it's important to be able to serialize the graph topology?  Instead of just having Python code that builds the model (again, as you would with any other model class)?"

Title: b'proteneer'
Body:
b"Having topologies being constructed by code means that graph topology is now versioned by code (i.e. git) as opposed to GraphDef/protobuf.

Suppose someone trained a bunch of models on an older version of deepchem and for various reasons, wanted to re-use/re-deploy the model on a newer version of deepchem (which may change the code for the construction of the graph of interest), then having an orthogonal backwards-compatible serialization format makes sense. Granted, it's not a *super* common use-case, and for model deployment you presumably don't need semantics like optimizers anyways.

I'm going to defer this to @lilleswing and @rbharath "

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"Pickling is a very brittle format.  Unless you put in a lot of work to define how all your classes should be serialized, It's at least as likely to get broken by code changes as is source code, maybe more likely."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"I think the main idea was to let users make use of pretrained models without having to know the details of how the model was initialized. We do have some pretrained models on AWS, but I think that effort never picked up steam; models don't generalize well, so easier to build a custom model for each new use case right now.

Title: b'Implement MaxMin Diversity based splits'
Body:
b"Roger Sayle has improved the speed of the maxmin diversity picker in RDKit by like a factor of 100x. Long story short, it allows one to pick a fraction K molecules out of N such that K is maximally diverse from the the N molecules. It also allows for a constrained variant where you have a precursor M that you know _a priori_

It's conceivable that we can use this to generate better splits where give a dataset of N molecules, we:

Maximize the diversity of the test set, i.e. M using the vanilla MaxMin diversity picker. Then,
we set M to be our constrained set, and pick another K to be maximally diverse under M. Everything else, N-K-M, are our training data.

This *may* be better than Murcko-Scaffold decomposition (i.e. no hand written fragmentation rules), and Butina (unequal sized cluster/lump problem).  

Note that this generates test sets that are maximally diverse (which is different maximally dissimilar)"

Title: b'patrickhop'
Body:
b'@evanfeinberg It's definitely hard to say anything about monotonicity in general here. For example, for a fixed learning rate, the update need not be contractive for all batch sizes - it need not converge at all.

From the paper you linked to: "The mini-batch size (B in Eq. (1)) is typically chosen between 1 and a few hundreds, e.g. B = 32 is a good default value, with values above 10 taking advantage of the speed-up of matrixmatrix products over matrix-vector products."

Below is a newer paper that you might like. Larger batch sizes seem to considerably restrict the range of acceptable hyperparameters. This suggests that if we want to select a default batch size, we should probably pick one on the smaller side.
https://arxiv.org/pdf/1508.02788.pdf

Another consideration is smaller datasets. For the delaney dataset, a batch size of 1000 brings us up to nearly full blown gradient descent.'

Title: b'Converting Models to TensorGraph'
Body:
b'#753 deprecates all non-`TensorGraph` TF models. A number of these models should be converted over to `TensorGraph` in time for the DeepChem 1.3 release.

- Molecular Autoencoder (Old classes `TensorflowMoleculeEncoder`, `TensorflowMoleculeDecoder`)
- Influence Relevance Voting (Old classes `TensorflowMultiTaskIRVClassifier`)
- Progressive Models (Old classes `ProgressiveMultitaskRegressor`).

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"I've copied over your changes, plus added some synchronization that should be very lightweight so it doesn't hang at the end.  I'm not seeing any speed improvement, and if anything it seems to be slightly slower.  Here's the test I'm using.

```python
import numpy as np
import deepchem as dc

muv_tasks, muv_datasets, transformers = dc.molnet.load_muv()

Title: b'proteneer'
Body:
b'Interesting.

I'm using the ANI model (viewable via my PR). I pinpointed the FIFOQueue op when I did a timelines profile. The NN itself is quite simple, so it's possible the data IO was more exacerbated. It is weird that SatgingArea made things slower though. Are you sure the threadig implementation was lightweight enough? (Try having it block so you don't have to worry about the threading overhead).

As for why I chose StagingArea to start with:

https://www.tensorflow.org/versions/r1.3/performance/performance_models

"The dominant part of each stage is executed in parallel with the other stages using data_flow_ops.StagingArea. StagingArea is a queue-like operator similar to tf.FIFOQueue. The difference is that StagingArea offers simpler functionality and can be executed on both CPU and GPU in parallel with other stages. Breaking the input pipeline into 3 stages that operate independently in parallel is scalable and takes full advantage of large multi-core environments. The rest of this section details the stages followed by details about using data_flow_ops.StagingArea."'

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"Here's how I did the synchronization.  I start by creating two lists (really just references to two numbers) for communicating between the threads:

```python
n_enqueued = [0]
final_sample = [None]
```

The enqueue thread increments `n_enqueued[0]` for each batch, and sets `final_sample[0] = n_enqueued[0]` when it's done.  The main thread executes the following at the start of each iteration:

```python
if self.use_queue:
  # Don't let this thread get ahead of the enqueue thread, since if
  # we try to read more batches than the total number that get queued,
  # this thread will hang indefinitely.
  while n_enqueued[0] <= n_samples:
    if n_samples == final_sample[0]:
      break
    time.sleep(0)
  if n_samples == final_sample[0]:
    break
```

I verified that `time.sleep(0)` (which is Python's idiom for forcing a thread to yield) only gets executed very infrequently: about 11,000 times during over 6 million steps of fitting.

The paragraph you quoted may not be relevant.  Here are the three stages they're using StagingArea to coordinate:

> - I/O reads: Choose and read image files from disk.
> - Image Processing: Decode image records into images, preprocess, and organize into mini-batches.
> - CPU-to-GPU Data Transfer: Transfer images from CPU to GPU.

They're letting TensorFlow handle all their disk I/O, which doesn't involve the GPU at all.  That's why they need something that can execute on the CPU and GPU in parallel.  That doesn't apply to us."

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"I just tried another test: do synchronization as described above, but with a FIFOQueue instead of a StagingArea.  That didn't make any difference.  I'm not sure the StagingArea is actually slower: the times fluctuate a bit, and the difference is likely within the noise level.  But it certainly doesn't seem to be any faster."

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'Regardless of which class we use, it might be a good idea to do the synchronization this way.  The current implementation throws an exception if you call `fit()` more than once on a model.  That will be a problem for GANs where you want to call `fit()` repeatedly (see #535).'

Title: b'No Easy Way To Shuffle DiskDataset Shards'
Body:
b"When dealing on datasets which don't fit into RAM we have to use deepchem.data.DiskDataset. 

The FeedDict Generator when deterministic=False shuffles entries within a shard.

Title: b'Minimizing use of  dc.data.Dataset'
Body:
b"One of the biggest hurdles for newcomers to the project is dealing with `dc.data.Dataset`. This object adds an extra layer of abstraction to working with datasets that isn't found in other popular python open source projects. I think this extra step puts off beginners who're looking for a quick entrypoint into the library since they have to learn an unfamiliar API to use our models.

I propose that we minimize use of `dc.data.Dataset` in DeepChem. For smaller datasets, where we use `NumpyDataset` currently, this won't cause a large disruption since we can just Numpy arrays `(X, y, w)` like other open source packages.

For larger datasets, this gets a lot trickier since we use `dc.data.DiskDataset` to store large datasets on disk for MoleculeNet and we've put significant effort into making this function. It's probably most feasible to leave this as-is for now, since I'm not sure there's a dominant abstraction for storing ML data on disk right now. 

Concretely though, I propose we modify `Model.fit` and `Model.predict` to accept Numpy arrays `(X, y, w)` by default (can also continue accepting `Dataset` for backwards compatibility for now) and we should remove uses of `dc.data.Dataset` from all our examples and tutorials."

Title: b'Simplify TensorGraph API'
Body:
b"I'm finding the TensorGraph API kind of cumbersome to work with.  This is mainly because you have to call `add_layer()` for every layer, which forces you to create a variable for every layer.  For example, suppose `a` and `b` are two layers.  As your loss function, you want to multiply them together and take the mean of all elements.  (This is a real example I came across.  `a` contains the cost function for every task, and `b` is the weights.)  Currently, you have to write something like this:

```Python
graph.add_layer(a)
graph.add_layer(b)
mult = Multiply()
graph.add_layer(mult, parents=[a,b])
reducemean = ReduceMean()
graph.add_layer(reducemean, parents=[mult])
graph.set_loss(reducemean)
```

I suggest getting rid of `add_layer()`.  You would only need to tell the graph about layers that have special roles, like with `set_loss()` or `add_output()`.  The parents of each layer would be passed as arguments to its constructor.  With this change, the above code could be simplified to

```Python
graph.set_loss(ReduceMean(Multiply(a, b)))
```"

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"Hmm, this is an interesting suggestion. The current structure of `TensorGraph` uses `add_layer()` to add nodes to the underlying graph structure for the model. While it is admittedly a little cumbersome, it gives us the power to construct arbitrary graph structures (arbitrary DAG to be precise). Once the graph structure is constructed, it's linearized, and the layers are called in bottom-up order to add the ops to the underlying tensorflow graph belonging to the model object.

As I understand it, this proposal is close to the [Keras functional API](https://keras.io/getting-started/functional-api-guide/). This API requires no explicit add calls, but the downside is that layers are evaluated in the scope of the default graph. If users want to prevent this, they have to explicitly manage Tensorflow graphs, which is painful.

The tradeoff seems then to be between the more onerous `add_layer`, which allows for neat hiding away of Tensorflow graphs, or the more free functional API, which exposes graphs to the user. I'm currently leaning towards `add_layer` since requiring users to deal with the underlying Tensorflow graph seems like a leaky abstraction.

Perhaps there's a nice intermediate design that works around these limitations though. Would love to hear your thoughts @peastman and @lilleswing "

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"I don't see the connection.  I'm not suggesting any change to how it would do computations.  You could still construct arbitrary DAGs, and you wouldn't need to directly interact with the underlying Tensorflow objects.  This is just a simplification to the API.\r\n\r\nThe main point is that we don't actually gain anything by calling `add_layer()`.  The graph can already discover every layer in the graph just by tracing backward from the outputs."

Title: b'rbharath'
b'peastman'
Body: b"That's exactly what I had in mind."

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body:
b'
These changes sound good to me.

One thing that I would want to take into account when we change the API is handling of sharing weights.  The current architecture does not support it, and we know we have multiple architectures with sharing weights coming up.  

I would prefer to make this change only if we can also see how it can handle "sharing" a layer between multiple inputs/outputs.

Keras solves this by the object you are creating when called twice shares the weights.
https://keras.io/getting-started/functional-api-guide/#shared-layers'

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"If I understand that example, the Keras API treats layers as function objects?  And instead of passing the parents to the constructor, you invoke the object and pass the parents then?  So instead of `Multiply(a, b)`, you would write `Multiply()(a, b)`?

That's one way of doing it, though I find it a little obtuse.  It creates a confusing distinction between the layer itself and the result of invoking the layer.  An alternative would be for each layer to have a `shared()` method to create a shared copy with different parents.  So following their example of two LSTM layers with shared weights, you would write

```Python
lstm1 = LSTM(parent1)
lstm2 = lstm1.shared(parent2)
```

That keeps the API simpler for the most common case (not shared weights), and makes it clear where you do share weights.  Another option would be to have a `Shared` layer that does the same thing:

```Python
lstm1 = LSTM(parent1)
lstm2 = Shared(lstm1, parent2)
```"

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body:
b'I like 
```python
lstm2 = lstm1.shared(parent2)
```

Then its each layers responsibility to allow sharing (the technical details will not come for free for any given layer.'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"Now that I've read that Keras example, I think I understand some aspects of TensorGraph better that were confusing me before.  Like why you create the Tensorflow objects in `__call__()` instead of a private method like `_create_tensor()`.  I see now you were copying that from Keras.\r\n\r\nWe should decide what kind of API this is supposed to be.  Is it an API for creating Tensorflow objects, and those objects are explicitly exposed to the user?  If so, then making layers callable makes sense.  Though in that case, why don't we just use the Keras layers rather than creating our own versions that do the same thing?  On the other hand, if the layers are supposed to be opaque objects, and the Tensorflow objects are an implementation detail that's hidden from the user, using a private method would make more sense."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b'Thinking about this, here are a couple points to figure out:

1. In both the current/proposed setup, the parents of layers are other layers. How can a DeepChem layer be invoked in pure Tensorflow code where the parents will just be Tensors?
2. Should we remove `__call__()`? In the new design, the parents are passed into the constructor and invoking a layer via function-call like Keras is less meaningful. Perhaps we should just have a `create_tensor()` or `build()` method that adds the layer to the graph in scope and remove `__call__()`.

@peastman, @lilleswing Would love your thoughts here'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"> How can a DeepChem layer be invoked in pure Tensorflow code where the parents will just be Tensors?\r\n\r\nHow about a `Tensor` layer class that wraps an arbitrary tensor and allows it to be passed as a parent?  That would let you use a layer in Tensorflow code, but it would not work correctly going in the other direction (using an arbitrary tensor in a TensorGraph), so the graph should throw an exception if it sees you've tried to use one."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"Ok, here's an summary of design changes for a `TensorGraph` API Change:

1. Remove `TensorGraph.add_layer()`. Move responsibility for getting parents to the contructors of `Layer` objects.
2. Retain functions like `TensorGraph.set_loss(layer)` or `TensorGraph.add_output(layer)` to tell `TensorGraph` what the outputs from the model are (make sure to support GANs, which have 2 different losses). 
3. Add `Layer.shared(parents)` method which allows for weight-sharing between layers. For example, `lstm2 = lstm1.shared(parents2)`. Each layer takes on responsibility for implementing its own `shared(parents)` method since weights differ depending on the layer.
4. Make it possible to invoke `Layer` objects on Tensorflow tensors (so DeepChem code can be easily used with pure Tensorflow Code). Perhaps via use of a `Tensor` layer class as @peastman suggests above.
5. Remove `Layer.__call__()` and replace with `Layer.create_tensors()` that adds tensors to the graph currently in scope.

@lilleswing Does this API change look good? If so, would you be game to take on the refactor? You have the best knowledge of the `TensorGraph` code :-)"

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"> (make sure to support GANs, which have 2 different losses).

Maybe replace `set_loss()` with `add_loss()`?  Then when you call `fit()`, you specify which loss to use.  If there's only one loss you can omit that argument.  But if there are multiple losses, I suggest the argument should be required.  Arbitrarily picking one of them if the argument is omitted would create opportunities for bugs.

Then again, implementing GANs might take something a little more complicated than that.  You have to tell it not just which loss to use, but also which parameters to optimize and which to hold fixed."

Title: b'lilleswing'
Body:
b"@rbharath , @peastman I'm not sure if (4) is possible.

 under the hood tensorflow instantiation of a Tensor is a mutative effect on the global graph.  It would not work unless you are already scoped in the graph of the Model.

It would have to be a lambda which gets executed while inside the appropriate Graph Scope."

For example, is there a case where the set of `Input` layers contained in the graph is different from the set passed to `add_input()`?  If the two could be different, we need to distinguish them in some way.  But if they'll always be the same, it's not necessary."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"Here's an example of what a 2-hidden layer fully connected network would look like under the new API.

```
# Define Layers
in = Input((32, 1024))
h1 = Dense(64, in)
h2 = Dense(64, h1)
logits = Dense(1, h2)
loss = SoftmaxCrossEntropy(logits)
out = Softmax(logits)

# Define Model
model = TensorGraph()
model.add_input(in)
model.add_output(out)
model.add_loss(loss)
model.fit()
```

Looks pretty slick. Having `add_input()`, `add_output()`, and `add_loss()` methods in `TensorGraph` should let us control the 3 types of inputs needed by `TensorGraph`"

b"I think the main problem is just that your network is much bigger and more complicate than it needs to be.  I simplified it down to this:

```Python
    d1 = Flatten(in_layers=state)

        activation_fn=tf.nn.relu,
        out_channels=64)

    value = Dense(in_layers=[d2], activation_fn=None, out_channels=1)
    return {'action_prob': probs, 'value': value}

Title: b'miaecle'
Body:
b'@rbharath I think the problem is from GraphGather layer, which use a tf.dynamic_partition. 
As in ```deepchem/deepchem/models/tensorgraph/layers.py```:
```python
class GraphGather(Layer):

  def __init__(self, batch_size, activation_fn=None, **kwargs):
    self.batch_size = batch_size
    self.activation_fn = activation_fn
    super(GraphGather, self).__init__(**kwargs)

  def create_tensor(self, in_layers=None, set_tensors=True, **kwargs):
    inputs = self._get_input_tensors(in_layers)

    # x = [atom_features, deg_slice, membership, deg_adj_list placeholders...]
    atom_features = inputs[0]

    # Extract graph topology
    membership = inputs[2]

    # Perform the mol gather

    assert self.batch_size > 1, "graph_gather requires batches larger than 1"

    # Obtain the partitions for each of the molecules
    activated_par = tf.dynamic_partition(atom_features, membership,
                                         self.batch_size)

    # Sum over atoms for each molecule
    sparse_reps = [
        tf.reduce_mean(activated, 0, keep_dims=True)
        for activated in activated_par
    ]
    max_reps = [
        tf.reduce_max(activated, 0, keep_dims=True)
        for activated in activated_par
    ]

    # Get the final sparse representations
    sparse_reps = tf.concat(axis=0, values=sparse_reps)
    max_reps = tf.concat(axis=0, values=max_reps)
    mol_features = tf.concat(axis=1, values=[sparse_reps, max_reps])

    if self.activation_fn is not None:
      mol_features = self.activation_fn(mol_features)
    out_tensor = mol_features
    if set_tensors:
      self.out_tensor = out_tensor
    return out_tensor
```
This layer constantly outputs `batch_size` in the first dimension(which maybe less than that in case of `pad_batches=False`).
'

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b"To do this, we need to be able to provide three calculations:

1. Given the output of the policy, select an action by sampling from some distribution.

2. Given the action that was selected, calculate what the probability was of selecting that action.  This needs to be implemented in Tensorflow so that it can backpropagate through it.  It needs to be able to compute derivatives of the probability with respect to the model parameters.

3. A3C and PPO each include an entropy term in the loss, so we need to compute the entropy of the action distribution given the policy output.

I could try to implement all of this in a generic way.  That would probably take a lot of new infrastructure.  Alternatively I could just assume a gaussian distribution, which is what's used in all the examples I've found.  The policy would output a set of means and a set of variances, and we would select the action based on them."

Title: b'Consistent dimensions in tensorgraph'
Body:
b"Implementing the fully connected models in tensorgraph, I ran into a lot of inconsistencies between the dimensions of different tensors that make the process a lot more difficult.  Let's consider how to improve the situation.

In an offline discussion with @rbharath and @lilleswing last week, we reached one tentative conclusion: all models in deepchem (not just tensorgraph ones) should have outputs of dimension three or higher: (batch_size, n_tasks, something).  For regressors, the third dimension is 1.  For classifiers, it's n_classes.  For some models, there might be more dimensions.  But there will always be at least three, and the first two will always be batches and tasks.  The goal of this is to let other code handle regression and classification models in a more uniform way.

That's fine  as far as it goes, but it immediately creates a problem: the `y` vector in a dataset has dimension 2, not 3.  So should the `Label` layer be dimension 2 or 3?  If 3, that guarantees you always have to override `default_generator()` to reshape it when building the feed dict.  If 2, then it's inconsistent with the output, which means you immediately have to wrap it in a `Reshape` layer before you can send it into a `L2LossLayer` or `SoftMaxCrossEntropy`.

Assume you've done that and computed a loss.  For multitask networks, you'll usually want to put that into a `WeightedLoss` layer.  But here we have another problem: the losses and weights have different dimensions.  So you either need to a) override `default_generator()` to reshape the weight vector, b) wrap the weights in a `Reshape` layer, or c) wrap the losses in a `Reshape` layer.  It's very confusing and creates obstacles for anyone trying to use it for the first time.

Can we improve the situation?  Here are a few possibilities I've thought about.

 - `default_generator()` could do some reshaping automatically.  It knows the dimensions of the `Label` and `Weight` layers, so it could reshape the inputs as necessary.

- Alternatively (or in addition?) it could call a `_transform_labels()` method that subclasses could override.  That would also simplify other cases.  For example, classifiers need to convert the labels to one hot representation.  This way they would only need to override a one line method to do that, rather than having to completely reimplement `default_generator()`.

- `L2LossLayer`, `SoftMaxCrossEntropy`, and `WeightedLoss` could all be made more intelligent.  They could inspect the shapes of their inputs and automatically reshape them as necessary."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"I like the idea of making `L2LossLayer`, `SoftMaxCrossEntropy`, and `WeightedLoss` more intelligent. Ideally, I'd like to make the issue of ~~weights~~ dimensions something beginners don't have to deal with, and pushing more intelligence into layers we can implement seems a nice plan.\r\n\r\nEdit: Wrote weights instead of dimensions above."

The layer has separate `n_hidden` and `out_channels` properties, which confused me since a GRU doesn't have separate outputs that are distinct from its internal state.  But looking at the implementation, it adds a linear layer (which is hardcoded to use a sigmoid activation function) to its output, and the `out_channels` argument sets the size of that layer.  What's the reason for that?  If I want to add a linear layer after the GRU I can do that as a separate layer.  But I may not always want that, and even when I do want it, I won't always want a sigmoid activation function.

The code for it also confuses me:

projection = lambda x: tf.contrib.layers.linear(x, num_outputs=self.out_channels, activation_fn=tf.nn.sigmoid)
out_tensor = tf.map_fn(projection, rnn_outputs)
```

But `rnn_outputs` is a single tensor, not a list of tensors, so why the need for the `tf.map_fn()`?  Also, the Tensorflow documentation doesn't mention any such function as `tf.contrib.layers.linear()`.  But after a bit of searching online, I found the definition of it in the source code: https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/master/tensorflow/contrib/layers/python/layers/layers.py#L2242.  It's an alias to `fully_connected` that hardcodes the activation function to `None`.  Which makes me even more confused about what's going on here!"

Title: b'Better Hyperparameter Searching'
Body:
b"The current `HyperparamOpt` class accepts lists of values for each hyperparameter, and then searches over the product space. For example
- learning rate: `.001`, `.0003`
- hidden layer size: `100`, `1000`

Would generate 4 combinations of hyperparameters `(.001, 100), (.001, 1000), (.0003, 100), (.0003, 1000)`. This type of product expansion is not always desirable. We might for example want to try just `(.001, 100), (.0003, 1000)`. (This particular example doesn't make much sense, but it is common for groups of hyperparameters to be tied together). Allowing the user to specify tied hyperparameter settings, in a list, would be a nice complement to the product based search currently supported.
"

Title: b'Making benchmark Numbers more reproducible'
Body:
b'CC @miaecle 

Currently, the benchmark performances vary by a few percentage points between runs. Some of this is natural, due to the random initializations of the matrices used in training, and in the random sampling of mini-batches. Here are a few potential solutions to make the benchmark runs more stable:

1. Set numpy random seed.
2. Set tensorflow random seed.
3. Repeat benchmark runs on datasets multiple times and return average.

Options 1. and 2. are easy to implement, but 3. will be inconvenient, especially for larger benchmarks like PCBA which take ~6hrs/run already.'

Title: b'DeepChem Development Roadmap'
Body:
b"I thought it would be useful to lay out a rough development roadmap for DeepChem to give users a sense of the relatively stability of parts of the DeepChem API. Since DeepChem is alpha software, users should be willing to put up with some amount of breakage, but I'd like to make things as painless as possible by explicitly noting which parts of API are fair game for future refactoring.

- `dc.data` - **Relatively Stable**: The abstract `Dataset` API seems to be holding up well, so I don't anticipate any major changes here. It is likely that we'll continue tweaking things here and there though (I think `NumpyDataset` is missing a little functionality and `DiskDataset` may be simplified a bit. Might also add other subclasses as need arises).
- `dc.dock` - **Highly Unstable**: This is the newest part of DeepChem and the API is not at all settled. Any and all parts of API may change without warning for foreseeable future.
- `dc.feat` -  **Relatively Stable**: While I anticipate us adding on new `Featurizer` objects, I don't think we will make any major changes to existing code. The one exception is `GridFeaturizer`, which will likely be refactored at some point.
- `dc.hyper` - **Deprecated**: The current hyperparameter search framework is a little kludgey. I anticipate that we may clean this up, or remove outright (it's easy enough to do hyperparam search, so we might just have a basic example instead). This isn't high on my priorities list, so might stick around for a few months or more though.
- `dc.metrics` - **Stable**: No major changes anticipated. May add a couple new metrics as need arises.
- `dc.models` - **Unstable**: The DeepChem model building framework is outdated and a little kludgey. I'd like to support `Keras` style model construction, but I'd like to be able to do it entirely within DeepChem without Keras (#296). Refactoring `dc.models` will be tricky though, so won't start until we solidify the benchmark suite (so we can refactor without harming performance).
- ` dc.nn` - **Relatively Stable**: I don't anticipate removing primitives, but we will likely add a good number more primitives moving forward.
- `dc.splits` - **Relatively Stable**: No major refactoring anticipated. However, @joegomes has reported that the `RandomSplitter` may have issues (doesn't behave deterministically even when seed is set), so likely will need a couple bugfixes.
- `dc.trans` - **Relatively Stable**: No major refactoring anticipated, but will likely add more transformers and debug existing transformers.
- `dc.utils` - **Deprecated**:  This submodule is currently a dumping bin. I'd recommend avoiding using anything in here. I'll try to clean-up here. Will likely greatly trim or outright remove this module."

Title: b'DeepChem Documentation Roadmap'
Body:
b"Now that parts of the deepchem API are starting to stabilize (see development roadmap #343), we need to start prioritizing documentation. We currently have auto-generated API documentation, but we don't have tutorials on how to do simple tasks with DeepChem. Here's a list of the types of docs I'm thinking:

1. CSV file loading tutorial: Show how to load and featurize dataset in a CSV file with DeepChem.
2. Dataset tutorial: Demonstrate how to work with `DiskDataset` and `NumpyDataset` in DeepChem.
3. Train/Valid/Test + Cross Validation Tutorial: Show how to split a dataset up into train/valid/test or k-fold splits. Give an overview of different types of `Splitter` objects.
4. Featurizer Tutorial: Walk through the available `Featurizer` classes and discuss how they work.
5. Classification Tutorial: Walk through the construction of a simple classifier. Show how to fit a model to a dataset, evaluate its performance with `Metric` objects on validation sets. Demonstrate how to make predictions on new compounds.
6. Regression Tutorial: Same, but for a regression dataset.
7. One-shot tutorial: Show how to train a one-shot dataset and use it to make predictions.
8. Docking tutorial: Walk users through using `dc.dock` to perform docking.
9. **Edit:** Standardizing docstrings: As @peastman points out in thread below, docstrings aren't present for every class. We should make sure that all public-facing functions and classes have useful docstrings (with examples if possible)

@miaecle, @joegomes, @peastman : Would you mind helping out with documentation writing? It would be great to get volunteers to help write subsections :-). All the documentation lives on github at https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/tree/master/docs, so can be added via small pull requests as people find time to contribute.

Also, if there are any other suggestions for useful tutorials, please add on to this thread."

Title: b'Initialization of Dense layers'
Body: b"TensorGraph's Dense layer now lets you specify initializers for weights and biases, but it does it in a way that makes it not very useful.  Instead of specifying an initializer object, you just specify the class.  It then constructs an instance of that class by calling the constructor with no arguments.  That means you can't use any initializer that requires constructor arguments (`constant_initializer`, `random_normal_initializer`, etc.).\r\n\r\nI tried modifying it to let you pass in an initializer object instead, but that caused `model.save()` to throw an exception because initializer objects can't be pickled.  It looks like this requires a somewhat more involved fix."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'Keras has `Initializer` objects which let users specify initializations that require constructor arguments. Perhaps we could to the same, and make sure the initializer objects are implemented in a pickle-able fashion?'

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"We discussed passing in a lambda to get around this problem, but it turns out that doesn't work either: lambdas also can't be pickled.  Apparently there are a couple of libraries that implement pickling of lambdas: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/16626429/python-cpickle-pickling-lambda-functions.  Possibly we could use one of those, or maybe we want to rethink the whole approach here."

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b'For the moment, I've created the following class to work around the problem:

```Python
class Initializer(object):
  """This class exists as a workaround for Tensorflow initializers not being picklable."""

  def __init__(self, initializer_class, **kwargs):
    """Create an Initializer for constructing Tensorflow initializers.

    Parameters
    ----------
    initializer_class: class
      the type of initializer to create
    kwargs:
      any other arguments will be passed on to the Tensorflow initializer's constructor
    """
    self.initializer_class = initializer_class
    self.kwargs = kwargs

  def __call__(self):
    return self.initializer_class(**self.kwargs)
```'

Title: b'PyTorch Support'
Body:
b"We've debated PyTorch versus TensorFlow a couple times already, but I think we should re-open the debate. PyTorch has been maturing and is starting to get buy-in from organizations (http://www.fast.ai/2017/09/08/introducing-pytorch-for-fastai/ for example, and I know of many good corporate teams making a transition more quietly).

I think it's time for us to add PyTorch support into DeepChem head. Cutting edge work on models isn't happening on TF as much these days, and I want to make sure we can keep up with the edge of the field.

To avoid causing pain to users who don't want to use PyTorch, we can use local imports to ensure that only users using PyTorch submodules actually need to have it installed."

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"What exactly are we discussing doing?  Most of the core classes like Dataset, Model, Metric, etc. already don't have any explicit dependence on Tensorflow, so there's no obstacle to creating new ones based on PyTorch.  But as we've discussed before, that will be very limiting for interoperability.  We've standardized on TensorGraph as the base for all models.  That makes it easy to connect up different types of modelling elements and use them together.  If we start adding new models based on PyTorch, they'll be incompatible with all TensorGraph models, which seems like a bad idea to me.\r\n\r\nAlternatively we could convert TensorGraph (and all our other code) from Tensorflow to PyTorch.  That would be a huge project, but might be worth it in the long run if we think PyTorch is what everyone will be using in the future."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b'My current feeling is that PyTorch will be the source of cutting edge work for probably the next couple years, while TensorFlow will dominate the enterprise and applications market for deep learning. If DeepChem is more research package than an applications project, doing a whole-scale shift might be the correct answer for our future research health even if it will be a painful transition.'

Title: b'proteneer'
Body:
b'I don't think "cutting edge work for next couple of years" is persuasive enough of a reason given that we've *just* standardized on TensorGraph. How much of the cutting edge work is actually relevant to chemistry?

While I'm not against moving to a whole new platform per-se, I'm against a move where it's not clear what the obvious pros and cons are. Even more, the pros have to be greater than 10x the cons to justify it. Alternatively, we can try and maintain both but it's a lot tedious work. You can ask @peastman about having to support both OpenCL/CUDA/CPU-platform for OpenMM :) 

'

Title: b'peastman'
Body:
b'The important questions are, what users are we trying to serve by making this change, and what problems are we trying to solve for them?

Most "DeepChem programs" either don't directly use Tensorflow at all, or they only reference it incidentally, such as to specify an activation function.  If we fully convert DeepChem over to PyTorch, it will make very little difference to the people who write those program.  The code they write will be mostly unchanged.

So the main effect of this decision is on DeepChem developers, not users.  Will the initial cost of making the conversion be outweighed in the long term by easier development?  Will this make it easier or harder to attract new developers?  Do the two packages have equivalent feature sets, or will one of them give us substantially more tools to work with?

Of course, that assumes they both work equally well.  If one of them is faster or less buggy or uses less memory, that will affect all users even if they never see the code directly.'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"I think this tweet makes the case for PyTorch well. Check out the meme within https://twitter.com/karpathy/status/909592435440869376\r\n\r\nThe issue is that there are models easy to construct in PyTorch that are nearly impossible in TensorFlow. For example, while layers will continue to make sense, TensorGraph in it's present form may not since we won't need to only define one graph (could define a unique graph at each time step in PyTorch). Plus, by all reports, debugging models is dramatically easier in PyTorch than TensorFlow since all standard python tools work (no more weird TF stack traces). I was on the fence for a long while, but I'm becoming convinced that PyTorch style is the winner in the long run."

I'm mainly thinking we can move in some contrib pytorch models (with local imports to avoid user issues) and hook them up to tests. It would be a good to get a first hand sense of pytorch stability in case we ever want to re-open the discussion in future."

Title: b'Save/restore for TensorGraph'
Body:
b"In the past, our models have generally had a persistent Session object containing all the variables for the model.  They automatically wrote out checkpoints during training, and provided a `restore()` method to load the variables from the most recent checkpoint into memory.

TensorGraph works differently.  It creates a new Session every time you call `fit()` or `predict()`, loads the variables from the latest checkpoint, then throws away the Session before returning.  I find this behavior has a couple of problems.

First, it's really slow.  If you want to run prediction thousands of times, that means it will load the variables from disk thousands of times.  This is why for both RL and MAML I've basically had to subvert the design of TensorGraph.  I use it to build the Tensorflow graph, but when I need to do any calculations I ignore the corresponding parts of TensorGraph, pull out the needed internal fields, and do the calculations directly.

It also is inflexible, since it enforces that prediction can only ever be done based on the variables in the latest checkpoint file, no others.  A good example of where this causes problems is MAML.  It uses TensorGraph to define the model, but the actual optimization is done with a different optimizer and a different loss function.  That produces a model (which gets saved to disk) that is designed to be easy to train, but isn't optimized for any particular task.  To use it for prediction, you first do a few steps of gradient descent to produce a fine tuned version of the model (which does *not* get saved to disk), and do the prediction based on that.  But I can't use any of TensorGraph's prediction methods for it, because it would just throw away the tuned variables and replace them with the generic ones from disk.

I think we should consider changing this behavior."

Title: b'rbharath'
Body: b"I'd be in favor of changing the behavior. Do you have thoughts on what the new save/restore API should behave?"

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b"I'd suggest something roughly identical to what's currently in A3C.  When you first create the object, it creates a persistent Session.  There's a `restore()` method to load the most recent checkpoint from disk.  I also included a `restore` argument to `fit()` that you can use to have it automatically load the latest checkpoint and continue training from where it left off."

Title: b'Shape of SoftMaxCrossEntropy'
Body:
b"I'm working on some cleanup, and I'm running into lots of problems trying to get the shapes of different TensorGraph layers to match up correctly.  I've tracked part of the problem down to a few layers whose shapes just don't make any sense to me.

`SoftMaxCrossEntropy` and `SparseSoftMaxCrossEntropy` each reshape their output as

```python
out_tensor = tf.reshape(self.out_tensor, [-1, 1])
```

So for example, if you have a batch of 100 samples and 25 values per sample, it reshapes all of them into a [2500, 1] output tensor.  Why?  The very next thing I want to do with it is put it into a `WeightedError` layer, which needs to combine it with a [100, 25] weight tensor."

Title: b'peastman'
Body: b'`L2Loss` has a different but related problem: it does a `reduce_mean()` over all but the first dimension, leaving a single number per sample.  That makes it impossible to apply weights.'

Title: b'proteneer'
Body: b'I ran into this recently. The -1 is for the batch, a WeightedError is applied afterwards which actually does the real reduce.'

Title: b'proteneer'
Body: b"(ie. the L2 doesn't actually compute an L2 at all)"

Title: b'Changes in rdkit_grid_featurizer'
Body:
b'Hi all!

As you might have noticed, I'm working with the `rdkit_grid_featurizer` module. I've already created a few tests and fixed some minor issues (#868 and #873). Now, I want to test the `RdkitGridFeaturizer` class, so I'm trying to figure out what are the possible use-cases.

I found an example in `protein_ligand_complex_notebook.ipynb`, but I'm a little confused. Why is `voxel_width=16.0` used? Do I understand correclty, that it means that a single voxel is used to represent the whole box? Is it a way to sum up all features over coordinates and represent the whole protein-ligand complex with a 1D array?

Apart from providing the tests for this module, I also plan to add docstrings and do a little cleanup (TL;DR: I want to improve readability and fix some inconsistencies). But before I start coding I want to make sure that my assumptions are correct and discuss the changes I propose:

1. I think that the `get_formal_charge` function defined in this module has a misleading name - it actually returns **partial** charge. I propose to change its name to `get_partial_charge`. If you want to change the name, but also provide backward compatibility, we can do it as follows:
```python
def get_partial_charge(atom):
  try:
    value = atom.GetProp(str("_GasteigerCharge"))
    if value == '-nan':
      return 0
    return float(value)
  except KeyError:
    return 0

def get_formal_charge(atom):
  warn('get_formal_charge function is deprecated, use get_partial_charge instead',
       DeprecationWarning)
  return get_partial_charge(atom)
```

2. After reading the code of the `RdkitGridFeaturizer` class I can't figure out what is the relationship between `feature_types` and `voxel_feature_types` arguments. Could you please explain this?

3. Also, I'm not sure whether `feature_types` should be a string or a list. The default value is a string, some parts of the code suggest that we expect a list, but also that we ignore other elements of this list, e.g: https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/a0a586fde9f949cc25ea837907a287a2369c932f/deepchem/feat/rdkit_grid_featurizer.py#L799-L802

4. Another thing that bothers me is how the `flatten` argument is used: https://github.com/deepchem/deepchem/blob/a0a586fde9f949cc25ea837907a287a2369c932f/deepchem/feat/rdkit_grid_featurizer.py#L1087-L1088
Shouldn't we use `feature_tensor.flatten()` here to create flat arrays? `np.squeeze` works for the use-case I found in the examples, but in general it only removes the dimensions of length 1.

5. I would also like to re-write the `_transform` method to make it easier to read and maintain. I will keep its functionality (with respect to the changes I propose in this issue), but change the code structure completely.
The main idea is to create a dictionary, which will map from keyword provided by the user in the `feature_types` or the `voxel_feature_types` argument (e.g. ``"ecfp"``) to the function calculating the feature (`compute_ecfp_features` in this case). This will allow to calculate features in a loop, and simplify the code drastically.
I'm afraid it's quite difficult to discuss this idea in details without actually writing the code. So let me know if you don't want me to change the code structure and if it's not a problem, I'll just implement it and then we'll discuss the details.

6. Using a list as a default argument in a function is a bad idea (see [link](https://docs.quantifiedcode.com/python-anti-patterns/correctness/mutable_default_value_as_argument.html)). I propose to use `None` as a default value and create an empty list:
```python
class RdkitGridFeaturizer(ComplexFeaturizer):
  def __init__(self, ..., voxel_feature_types=None):
    if voxel_feature_types is None:
        self.voxel_feature_types = []
    ...
```
...or use an empty tuple, if this argument doesn't need to be mutable:
```python
class RdkitGridFeaturizer(ComplexFeaturizer):
  def __init__(self, ..., voxel_feature_types=()):
    self.voxel_feature_types = voxel_feature_types
    ...
```

7. I think there are some unused arguments in this class: `save_intermediates`, `voxelize_features`, and `parallel`. Also, `box_x`, `box_y`, and `box_z` are only used in the `_generate_box` method, which is a private method not used anywhere. Additionally, I think this method won't work, because it doesn't use the RDKit Mol class to represent the molecule.
Are those arguments deprecated? Or are they more like TODOs? If they are deprecated, I'm willing to remove them and throw a DeprecationWarning if the User tries to use them (it can be done really easily with `kwargs`). Also I propose to remove `_generate_box` method (or replace its body with DeprecationWarning).

8. There are several parameters in `RdkitGridFeaturizer` that are hard-coded. I think it is a good idea to allow the User to provide custom bins and cutoffs with `kwargs`, e.g.:
```python
if 'hbond_dist_bins' in kwargs:
    self.hbond_dist_bins = kwargs['hbond_dist_bins']
else:
    self.hbond_dist_bins = [(2.2, 2.5), (2.5, 3.2), (3.2, 4.0)]
...
```

Let me know what you think about these changes. Also, if you want me add or change anything else, I'm open to your suggestions! :)


Best,
Marta'

Title: b'rbharath'
Body:
b"@marta-sd Glad to see you're taking on this refactor! Some comments

1. Proposed change sounds good.
2. This is a little unclear to me as well. We might want to combine both of these into just one flag `feature_types`, and remove `voxel_feature_types`.
3. I think we probably want `feature_types` as a list.
4. +1 for moving to `.flatten()`
5. I like this proposed refactor. Better than our explicit listing we have currently.
6. +1 for using `None` as the default argument.
7. Feel free to remove unused arguments.
8. +1 for allowing users to provide values as suggested.

CC @evanfeinberg, @lilleswing who might have more comments on this code."

Title: b'marta-sd'
Body:
b"@rbharath Thanks for your comments :) I think it's a great idea to combine `feature_types` and `voxel_feature_types` into a single flag. I propose the following design:
* `voxel_feature_types` is deprecated and ignored, the User is warned
* `feature_types` is a list
* if the User specifies multiple features, created vectors/tensors are concatenated
* if `feature_types` contains both flat and voxel features, the tensors are flatten
* there are 3 predefined sets of features: 'flat_combined', 'voxel_combined', and 'all_combined'"
